The Creative Idea
The Idea Haus — AI-Transformation guide (Step 6, optional)
A repeatable process for unleashing boundless creativity — for the overall creative concept, or for  
campaign ideation and planning.
July 2026 · builds on the MSLGROUP Idea Haus and Delivering Creativity method
1. What the Idea Haus is — and when to use it
The Idea Haus is a repeatable creative process that lets any team design and deliver big ideas — consistently, not 
by luck. Clients increasingly ask for big, game-changing ideas, and don't much care which agency brings them; the 
Idea Haus is how UP delivers them every time. Creativity without structure is chaos; the Idea Haus is creativity 
with structure.
Optional — and dual-use.  This step is optional in the flow. Use it for the overall creative concept / platform that 
expresses the strategy, or as a self-contained method for campaign ideation and planning. Either way it turns the 
insight and strategy into a Big Idea.
2. A Big Idea, not a tactic
The most common creative failure is presenting a tactic dressed up as an idea. A Big Idea is the elevated purpose; 
a tactic is the activity that serves it.
Tactic (what you do) Big Idea (why it matters)
Provide feminine-hygiene products Help young girls in Africa stay in school
Add a new ingredient to increase flavour (the elevated purpose the ingredient serves)
Secure top-tier media / a celebrity A movement of thousands who change a behaviour
The Big Idea Criteria — validate every concept against these
Simple · Shareable (any-size screen) · Scalable · Memorable / recognisable asset · Ownable · Persuasive
A true Big Idea is also: about the brand's purpose/benefit · stands out in its category · radically opens hearts and minds 
· creates movement.
3. The Idea Haus — six steps
Step What it does Output
1  Internalize the strategy Live and breathe the brief — WHO, WHAT (from → to), HOW A one-sentence strategic 
summary
2  Result-back thinking Start at the end — visualise the epic outcome Top 3 visions of success
3  Embrace insights Empirical + intuitive truths about the WHO (the 5 T's) 3 killer insights (see the Insight 
guide)
4  Elevate the objectives Push the client's ask to its biggest version Elevated objectives
5  Focused ideation Generate many ideas, select and build 1 Big Idea concept
6  Validate the concept Check against the Big Idea Criteria A validated Big Idea
Step 1 — Internalize the strategy (the brief)
The creative brief structure
Challenge: what consumer/stakeholder behaviour or mindset change do we hope to achieve?
Insight starters: why are they behaving this way? why should they care? why would they change? why is it 
relevant to their life?
Benefit: what core thing do we promise them — and why would they tell a friend?
Then write it down: WHO (and how we relate to / change them) · WHAT (from what mindset → to what) · HOW 
(how we deliver it) → one sentence. Look. Internalize. Write.
Step 2 — Result-back thinking
Start at the end. With eyes closed, picture the campaign as a movie and visualise how it ends — if we could have 
any ending possible, what would it be? Every outlet talking about it? A movement of thousands? A million 
engaged? Rate the possible outcomes and pick the top three.
Securing media is not a big ending.  “Top-rated media placements” or “a celebrity at an event” are not big 
endings — they're tactics. Push for endings that are epic: movements, behaviour change, cultural impact. Score 
outcomes across Media / Movement / Engagement / Content / WOM / Influencers / Social / Events / Purpose / 
Cause and Local→Global.
Step 3 — Embrace insights
Big ideas are driven by real, impactful insights — empirical (proven by data) and intuitive (sensed, then 
evidenced) — each passing the 5 T's: True, Tacit, Touches the heart, Tension, Triggers action. A “day in the life” 
of the audience is a fast way to surface them. (Covered fully in the Insight guide.)
Step 4 — Elevate the client's objectives
Big ideas mean big objectives. Take what the client asked for and elevate it. “If you don't know where you're 
going, any road will get you there.” We can always scale down.
NEED + VALUE = POWER
What is the client asking for, really?   +  What is the value we add?   =  the elevated objective.
e.g. “Drive trial” → “Place the brand at the centre of ongoing conversations that make trial irresistible.”
Step 5 — Focused ideation
Generate, then focus. Run it large group → small group:
● Set the stage — share the strategy, the result-back vision, the insights and the elevated objectives.
● Ideate — break into small teams; generate freely; capture everything on Post-its; go for quantity.
● Share & evaluate — play ideas back; assess against the criteria.
● Select 3 → build — the ideas you have the most heart for; build each (~10 min per idea).
● Small group → 1 — push outside the norm, pick the one with most potential, build it, express it in 
words + images.
Ask throughout: how do we achieve the end result? how do we bring the insights to life? how do the elevated 
objectives take shape? are the Big-Idea elements present?
Step 6 — Validate the concept
Check the Big Idea, literally box by box, against the Big Idea Criteria. Missing any? Go back and rework the idea to 
include it. Only a validated idea proceeds.
4. Fuel the ideation — lateral-thinking brain-trainers
When ideas go stale or obvious, break the pattern (Edward de Bono's lateral thinking). Four trainers to unlock 
bolder ideas:
Brain-trainer How it works
Random Entry Pick a random word/object unrelated to the task; list what's true about it; force-fit those truths onto the challenge
Provocation Distortion (distort the challenge), Illusionary (exaggerate the payoff to an ideal), Reversal (ask the opposite of the 
problem, then turn it back). The burger “take it away” idea won a Cannes Lion
Challenge Idea Appoint someone to keep asking “Why?” — list your assumptions about the client's business and challenge each 
one
Movement Extract the principle from another example (e.g. Apple's launch playbook) and apply it to your challenge — 
corporate ↔ consumer cross-pollination
This is the engine's creativity engine.  These brain-trainers are exactly the systematic creativity (M6) that fixes 
the weak spot the bake-off found. The AI can run Random Entry, Provocation, Challenge and Movement at 
volume — generating many bold options — while the human selects the one with the spark.
5. Run a great session
The ten ground rules
● Show up · Read the brief · No censoring · It's OK to be silly
● Practise active listening · Build on each other's ideas
● Use “How can we?” or “I wish…” language · Speak in headlines
● Be current · Blue-sky thinking
Environment & facilitation
● Time pressure is a myth. Harvard research: people are LEAST creative under deadline pressure, with a 
two-day hangover. Creativity needs an incubation period — time to soak in the problem.
● Set the room and the invite. Make the invite fun; mix different perspectives; give pre-work that gets 
people into the audience's head; dress the room with thought-starters; serve food; go for quantity; 
write everything down.
6. Package & present the idea
A big idea badly presented dies in the room. Six principles for selling it:
● Be visual and aspirational — show the idea, don't just describe it.
● Tell a story — take the client on a journey.
● You are the star — never read off the slide; if the audience can read your script, they no longer need 
you.
● Sell the idea, not the tactics — lead with the Big Idea; tactics come after.
● Help the client see it boundlessly — show how far the idea can stretch.
● Prop it up — props, costumes, a creative leave-behind to make it memorable.
7. What the AI does, and what the human owns
The AI does The human owns
Drafts the internalised brief and strategic summary; generates result-
back visions; runs the four brain-trainers at volume to produce many 
bold candidate ideas; elevates the objectives; drafts concepts in words 
+ images; validates each against the Big Idea Criteria
Owns the creative spark and taste; selects the idea with heart; judges 
what's ownable and category-breaking; builds and elevates it; sells it in 
the room
Honest boundary.  This is where the human matters most. The engine reliably raises the creative floor — it 
generates volume, breaks patterns, and rejects tactics-masquerading-as-ideas — but the top of the creative 
ceiling is still human. The Idea Haus makes the floor high and consistent; the strategist makes the ceiling.
8. Quality gate — before the idea proceeds
  ☐ It is a Big Idea (an elevated purpose), not a tactic
  ☐ It flows from the insight, the result-back vision and the elevated objective
  ☐ It passes the Big Idea Criteria (simple, shareable, scalable, memorable, ownable, persuasive)
  ☐ It is ownable — a competitor couldn't run the same idea
  ☐ It was generated from many options and pushed with a brain-trainer, not the first thought
  ☐ It is expressed in words + images, ready to build and present
Bottom line. Creativity can be repeatable without being formulaic. Internalize the strategy, imagine the epic 
ending, ground it in a real insight, elevate the objective, generate many ideas and break the pattern with lateral 
thinking, then validate the one Big Idea against the criteria — and sell it as an idea, not a task list. Do that, and a 
junior team lands a genuinely big, ownable idea more often, because the process supplies the discipline and the 
spark supplies the rest.

Building the Strategic Approach
The AI-Transformation guide to the Strategy phase
Phase 4 of the flow (CUBE · Strategy, Step 7). Where the insight becomes a decision about how to win.
July 2026 · builds on the UP Strategy Masterclass and PR & Reputation Management
1. What the strategic approach is — and why it must be strategic
The strategic approach is the bridge between the insight (what's true) and the plan (what we'll do). It is the single 
organizing idea for HOW communications will change what stakeholders think, feel or do. Get it right and every 
downstream choice — narrative, messages, channels, tactics — flows naturally. Get it wrong and no amount of 
clever execution saves it.
Strategy vs tactics
Tactics are WHAT and HOW — posts, releases, events. Short-term, reactive.
Strategy is WHY and what success looks like — the direction that ties communications to the business. 
Long-term, proactive.
Why this is the hard part.  Only ~26% of communicators say their strategy directly ties to business objectives 
(CMO Council). The strategic approach is where an order-taker becomes a strategic advisor: it asks the diagnostic 
questions, challenges the assumption, and builds the business case — rather than jumping to activity.
2. The Strategy Blueprint — everything must connect
The approach lives inside a cascade with line of sight from the business goal to the metrics. Every level must 
connect to the one above it; if a tactic can't be traced up to the objective, it doesn't belong.
BUSINESS OBJECTIVE   e.g. revenue +15% YoY — what the business must achieve
▼
COMMUNICATION OBJECTIVE   e.g. increase consideration +25% — the shift comms must drive (SMART+I)
▼
STRATEGIC APPROACH   e.g. reposition as the category's innovator — the organizing idea (this step)
▼
MESSAGES · CHANNELS · TACTICS   the narrative, key messages, PESO plan and activities that deliver it
▼
KPIs   how each level is measured back up the chain
3. The Communication Objective (SMART+I)
The approach serves a target. Write it as a SMART+I objective — the difference between a measurable shift and 
an activity.
Letter Test
Specific Clearly defined outcome
Measurable Quantifiable result
Achievable Realistic within resources
Relevant Aligned to the business goal
Time-bound Clear deadline
Impact Drives a business outcome
Example of a strong objective
“Increase brand consideration among the target audience (18–35, urban professionals) by 30% by Q3, 
measured through brand-tracking studies, to drive incremental revenue growth of $2M.”
Objective, not activity.  “Get people to know about us” is an activity. “Shift 45% of stakeholders from unaware to 
actively considering us within 12 months” is an objective. The strategic approach only makes sense once the 
objective is this sharp.
4. Defining the strategic approach itself
The approach is the big organizing idea for how communications will hit the objective — and it must flow directly 
from the insight. The insight named the tension; the approach is the decision about how to resolve it. Articulate 
it two ways:
The strategic-direction statement
GET [the audience]
WHO [their current context / mindset — from the insight]
TO [the shift in what they think, feel or do]
BY [the leverage / organizing idea that makes it happen]
Then a one-line positioning: what the company will stand for, and against, in the eyes of its stakeholders. The 
“BY” and the positioning together are the strategic approach.
The reputation lens
Reputation = experience − expectations (Gary Davies). A reputation approach therefore has only three real 
moves: change the experience, reset the expectations, or close the gap between what the company says and 
what it demonstrably does. Frame the approach as one of: 
● Reposition — claim a new, ownable space (the insight's white space)
● Close the trust gap — attack the specific weak trust driver the research found
● Own the tension — take a defensible stand on the stakeholder tension the insight surfaced
5. Don't take the first idea — generate and select options
Weak strategy is the first plausible approach written up confidently. Strong strategy is chosen from options. Use 
the communications strategy model:
STRATEGIC ANALYSIS   organization–environment · market & competitor · stakeholder (done in Research)
▼
STRATEGIC INTENT   identify the bases of choice · GENERATE several strategic options · evaluate & SELECT
▼
STRATEGIC ACTION   define the role of communications · programme the tactics · organizational arrangements
Selecting between options
Criterion The question
Fit Does it resolve the insight's tension and hit the communication objective?
Distinctiveness Is it ownable — could a competitor run the same approach? (the Distinctiveness Gate)
Feasibility Achievable within budget, timeline, and the company's character and risk appetite?
Line of sight Does it trace cleanly up to the business objective and down to executable tactics?
The engine's role.  This is exactly where the options generator (M5) and the Adversarial Review Board earn their 
place: the AI generates several distinct strategic approaches with rationale; the Board's Competitor persona kills 
the copyable ones; the operator chooses the sharpest — never originating from a blank page, never shipping the 
obvious.
6. Reputation building blocks
For a corporate reputation strategy, the approach draws on a few durable frameworks:
● Identity → Image → Reputation. Reputation is built in phases: corporate identity (what you present) 
shapes image (how you're seen now) which, over time, becomes reputation. The approach must be 
consistent across all three.
● Reputation is holistic. Modern reputation management is strategic, integrated, long-term and involves 
all employees — not just media relations. Build the approach inside-out as well as outside-in.
● Issue management is the backbone. Good reputation management runs on issue management: identify 
→ analyse → choose a change strategy → act → evaluate. Bake the live issues into the approach.
● The stakeholder imperative. The company answers to a plurality of stakeholders, not only shareholders. 
Prioritise them on the power/interest grid and let that shape where the approach concentrates.
● Aim at a real target. Reputation has external yardsticks — RepTrak / Reputation Quotient, Most 
Admired, sustainability indices. Point the approach at a defensible movement on one.
7. From approach to expression (the bridges)
The strategic approach hands directly to the next steps. In this phase, set the architecture; the dedicated guides 
build each out.
Message architecture (→ Narrative & Messages, Steps 8–9)
Core Narrative (the one true story) → Key Messages (3–5, distinct, audience-specific) → Proof Points (data, 
cases, testimony). Ladder each message with the Trident system:
Trident messaging ladder
1° message (the umbrella claim)  →  2° messages (the supporting pillars)  →  3° / killer facts (the specific, 
memorable proof). Example: “A great place to work” → “Good employment opportunities” → “3,000 new 
jobs created annually.”
Channels (→ Channels, Step 11)
Set the PESO shape of the approach — Paid, Earned, Shared, Owned — and which the approach leads with 
(corporate reputation is usually Earned-led). Detail comes later.
8. The deliverable — the Strategy One-Pager
The approach is captured on a one-page north star that everything else flows from. It includes:
  ☐ Executive summary (2–3 lines)
  ☐ Business & communication objectives (SMART+I)
  ☐ Target audience profile & persona
  ☐ The strategic approach + one-line positioning
  ☐ Core narrative & 3–5 key messages
  ☐ Proof points / supporting evidence
  ☐ Channel strategy (PESO)
  ☐ Campaign timeline & phases
  ☐ Success metrics & KPIs
  ☐ Budget allocation summary · risk mitigation
Why the one-pager.  It is the alignment tool — everything (creative, media, partnerships) flows from it, and it 
keeps a novice's strategy as disciplined as a senior's, because a gap on the page is a gap in the thinking.
9. What the AI does, and what the human owns
The AI does The human owns
Drafts SMART+I objectives from the brief; generates several distinct 
strategic approaches from the insight, each with rationale; checks line-
of-sight up and down the cascade; drafts the message architecture and 
the one-pager; runs the Distinctiveness check
Chooses the approach; judges the ownable idea; sets the positioning 
and the stand; confirms fit to the company's character and risk 
appetite; defends it
Why it's operator-independent.  The approach is chosen from vetted, evidenced options, and every candidate is 
checked for line-of-sight (traceable cascade), SMART+I rigour and distinctiveness before the operator sees it. A 
novice picks the sharpest of three sound options; they never have to originate strategy from nothing.
10. Quality gate — before the approach goes to Narrative
  ☐ The communication objective is SMART+I and traces to a business objective
  ☐ The strategic approach flows directly from the insight (resolves its tension)
  ☐ It is expressed as GET/WHO/TO/BY plus a one-line positioning
  ☐ It was chosen from options, not the first idea — and passes the Distinctiveness Gate
  ☐ It is one of: reposition · close the trust gap · own the tension
  ☐ It has clean line of sight up (to business) and down (to executable tactics)
  ☐ It is captured on the Strategy One-Pager, complete for the tier
Bottom line. The strategic approach is a decision, not a description: the one organizing idea for how 
communications will resolve the insight's tension and move the objective. Anchor it in a SMART+I objective, 
generate options rather than grabbing the first, choose the ownable one, and frame it as reposition / close-the-
gap / own-the-tension. Keep the whole cascade in line of sight and land it on the one-pager. Do that, and the 
approach a junior builds carries the same strategic weight a senior would sign — which is exactly what this phase 
of the engine delivers.

The AI-Transformation guide to the message architecture (Steps 8–10)
Where the strategic approach becomes the one story, the messages that carry it, and the themes all content

July 2026 · builds on Content-Centric Communications, P&G storytelling and the UP messaging architecture
The through-line — one cascade, three artifacts
Narrative, key messages and communications pillars are not three separate tasks — they are one connected 
message architecture that flows from the strategic approach. UP's Content Strategy Cascade shows how they 
lock together:
BRAND NARRATIVE   the one story (Step 8)
▼
THEMES = COMMUNICATIONS PILLARS   3–5 territories the narrative earns the right to own (Step 10)
▼
STORIES & MESSAGES   what each audience hears within each pillar (Step 9)
▼
SEQUENCING   onto the roadmap (Step 12)
The rule.  The narrative is the north star; the messages carry it to each audience; the pillars are the few enduring 
themes everything ladders up to. If a message or a pillar doesn't trace back to the narrative, it doesn't belong.
  Part A — The Narrative  (Step 8)
A1. What a narrative is
A brand narrative is the core story you are always telling, in everything you do. It is not a tagline or a message — 
it is the north star beneath them. Strong brands can tell their story a thousand ways and stay recognisable; weak 
brands mean many things and hold nothing together.
The digital-age truth.  In the age of social media, anyone can tell your story and reach a global audience — how 
others tell it now matters more than how you tell it yourself. You can't control the story, but you can shape it to 
be told the way you want. That is what the narrative is for.
A2. Plan the story before you write it
Think of a story as a tree: Story Planning is the roots (why it must be told, and where it lands), the Narrative is 
the trunk, and Story Worlds are the leaves (the elements that adapt over time). Before writing, answer four 
planning questions:
Question How to answer it
What is the context? Survey the external landscape first — communications never happen in a vacuum; how people receive you 
depends on their view of you and what competes for attention
Who is the audience? Think like a journalist (who/what/when/where/why); make them real — a name and a face; write for them, 
not for you
What is the purpose? Awareness (who I am) · Relevance (why I'm here) · Vision (I have a dream) · Education (I'll show you how) · 
Principles-in-action · Dealing with the elephant in the room
How do we tell it? Think like a politician — be Specific, Authentic, Engaging, Appropriate; use real language and real examples, not 
jargon or statistics; repeat with discipline
A3. The narrative structure — World, Tension, Resolution
Every narrative has three movements. Something must be at stake, or there is no story. The company's 
commitment grounds the narrative; the tension is built from what it is willing to do to keep that commitment.
The four-part construction
1 · The world — the world where the focus plays out.
2 · What's at stake — the tension in that world.
3 · What we understand — the truth we grasp about it.
4 · Our role to resolve the tension — what the company does about it.
A4. The UP Narrative Template
The fill-in that turns the structure into a draft. Complete it, then hand it to the copywriters to bring to life.
The Narrative Template (the “Brand Contract”)
We believe in a world where… (the Purpose, as a belief about the world)
We know in that world that… (what we know that brings tension — what's at stake)
So we make sure… (what the company does to resolve the tension)
Which is why we… (the products, services and behaviours that keep the contract)
A5. Make it travel — trailer and tweet
In the digital age the same story is told second by second in “beats.” Compress the narrative so it moves:
● The movie-trailer technique: capture the world, the protagonist and the quest — but not the resolution 
— to pull people into the longer story.
● The tweet: force the whole story into one line. If you can't, it isn't sharp enough yet.
Worked example (the classic Fairy narrative).  “In a world that often pulls people apart, there is one place that 
brings families together: the kitchen. Sometimes things go wrong… But it's also where the small things of family 
life happen. And Fairy is always there — it's our job to keep the kitchen going.” Trailer: “One place brings families 
together again and again. The kitchen.”
  Part B — Key Messages  (Step 9)
B1. From narrative to messages
Messages naturally fall out of the narrative — by audience, by objective. The architecture flows down:
CORE NARRATIVE   the one true story (the why)
▼
KEY MESSAGES  (3–5)   distinct, audience-specific statements (the what)
▼
PROOF POINTS   data, cases, testimony, killer facts (the proof)
B2. The 6-type Messaging Architecture
For corporate work, build a multi-track architecture: one umbrella message supported by six message types, 
each with proof, mapped to the audience's bonds and barriers, and adapted per stakeholder.
The six message types (each with proof points)
Awareness · Relevance · Emotion · Logic · Action · Commitment
Under one Umbrella message. Built by researching value proposition, culture, leadership equity, competitive 
framework, stakeholder attitudes, and the Bonds & Barriers — then tailored for each key audience.
B3. Ladder every message — the Trident system
1° → 2° → 3°
1° message (the umbrella claim)  →  2° messages (the supporting pillars)  →  3° / killer facts (specific, 
memorable proof). E.g. “A great place to work” → “Good employment opportunities” → “3,000 new jobs 
created annually.”
B4. Build, test, guard
● Message Storming — a collaborative workshop to sort research into the sharpest messages.
● Message Testing — test with key audiences before committing.
● Message Training — train spokespeople to deliver them consistently.
● Do-not-say guardrails — name the messages to avoid for legal, regulatory or reputational reasons 
(enforced by the Review Board's GC and Journalist personas).
Ownable, not generic.  Every key message must be ownable — a competitor couldn't put their logo on it — and 
carried by real proof. A message that could belong to any company is not a message; it's a platitude.
  Part C — Communications Pillars  (Step 10)
C1. What a pillar is
Communications pillars (the Themes in the Content Strategy Cascade) are the 3–5 enduring territories the 
narrative earns the company the right to own — the few things it talks about, again and again. They are the 
bridge from the narrative to the content calendar.
How to derive them.  Pillars come straight from the narrative and messages: each pillar is a territory the 
narrative supports, mapped to a stakeholder track and a key message. If a proposed pillar doesn't ladder to the 
narrative, it isn't a pillar.
C2. Balance the pillars — Hero / Hub / Hygiene
Layer Role ≈ Share
Hero Big, ambitious, campaign-level content that drives reach and conversation ~20%
Hub Ongoing, valuable content that builds audience and demonstrates value ~60%
Hygiene Always-on, table-stakes content that maintains presence and relationships ~20%
C3. Classify the stories in each pillar
Within each pillar, plan stories by cadence — which tells you how to resource them:
Story type What it is
Evergreen Always-true brand stories; reusable year-round
Seasonal Tied to calendar moments and cultural events, planned ahead
Real-time Reactive stories riding live news and trends (newsjacking)
The handoff.  Pillars + story types feed directly into Channels (Step 11, the PESO plan) and the Tactical Roadmap 
(Step 12, phased and sequenced). Set the architecture here; sequence it there.
How the AI helps, and what the human owns
The AI does The human owns
Drafts narrative options from the insight & approach using the 
template; generates key messages by audience with proof; proposes 
pillars mapped to the narrative; ladders messages; drafts the trailer and 
tweet; checks every message and pillar traces to the narrative
Owns the story truth and its tension; judges what's ownable vs generic; 
chooses the narrative; approves messages and proof; sets the do-not-
say lines; decides the pillars
Why it's operator-independent.  The tests are checkable — does it have tension? is it ownable? does it trace to 
the narrative? is every message proven? — and the operator chooses from vetted, drafted options. A novice 
lands a coherent architecture because the cascade forces coherence: nothing survives that doesn't ladder to the 
one story.
Quality gate — before this hands to Channels & Roadmap
  ☐ The narrative has genuine tension (World → Tension → Resolution) and uses the template
  ☐ It is ownable and compresses to a trailer and a tweet
  ☐ Key messages: 3–5, distinct, audience-specific, each with proof points
  ☐ Messages are laddered (1°/2°/3°) and carry do-not-say guardrails
  ☐ 3–5 communications pillars, each tracing to the narrative and a message
  ☐ Pillars are balanced Hero/Hub/Hygiene and classified by story type
  ☐ Everything ladders to the one narrative — no orphan messages or pillars
Bottom line. Build one story with real tension, express it as the narrative template, carry it to each audience 
through a multi-track, proof-backed, laddered message set, and distil it into a few ownable pillars that everything 
else grows from. Keep the whole architecture tied to the one narrative, and a junior produces a message system 
as coherent and ownable as a senior's — because the cascade, not the person, holds it together.

The Communications Platform
Channels & Tactics — the AI-Transformation guide (Steps 11–12)
Where the strategy becomes an organized, integrated system of channels and tactics — not a random  
list of activities.
July 2026 · builds on the MSL Platform→Plan→Programs process and the UP PESO / engagement models
1. What a communications platform is
A communications platform is the unifying architecture that turns the strategy, narrative and messages into an 
organized, integrated system of channels and tactics. It is not a list of activities — it is the foundation that 
organizes messaging, priorities and programs into rollout strategies, target audiences, channels and a timeline. It 
is both educational and inspirational, and it is driven by differentiation.
The test of a platform vs a plan.  A plan is a list of things to do. A platform is the organizing logic that makes 
those things add up — so every channel and tactic reinforces one story and one insight. If your channels could 
each belong to a different strategy, you have a list, not a platform.
2. What makes a good platform — the criteria
A strong platform passes five tests (and you should generate several candidate platforms, narrow to two or 
three, and validate with stakeholders before finalising):
● Delivers differentiation — it is ownable, not generic.
● Leverages heritage — it is rooted in what's true about the company.
● Creates extension opportunities — it can stretch across markets, moments and years.
● Sustains competitive advantage — it holds up against what competitors do.
● Is evolutionary, durable and global — it lasts and travels; it isn't a one-campaign idea.
3. Line of sight — the pull-through
The platform connects the brand all the way to the programs, so nothing is orphaned. Every channel and tactic 
must trace up this chain to the strategic approach and the narrative.
VISION / POSITION   where you're going & how you're different
▼
BRAND EXPRESSION   how you look, act, feel — narrative, messages, tone, identity
▼
GO-TO-MARKET   who you focus on — target audiences, geographies, priority segments
▼
COMMUNICATIONS PROGRAMS   how you communicate — the channels, tactics and activations (this phase)
The rule.  If a tactic can't be traced up to an audience, a message, and the objective, it doesn't go in the platform 
— it goes in the appendix.
4. The channel architecture — PESO, orchestrated
Communications don't live in four separate channel reports. The platform orchestrates Paid, Earned, Shared and 
Owned around one insight, each doing the job it does best. For corporate reputation, the platform is usually 
earned-led — third-party credibility is what builds trust.
Channel Primary role Leads for reputation?
Paid Controlled reach & action — puts the story in front of the right audience Support (selective)
Earned Third-party credibility & validation — the reputation engine LEAD
Shared Participation & advocacy — amplification through trusted voices Support
Owned Depth, education & conversion — where the full story lives Foundation
The integrated programming model (4C)
Run the four channels as one program: Unifying Human Insight → Find the Right Moment → Deploy the Right 
Channels (Earned/Shared/Owned) → Engage Influencers → Develop Compelling Content → Evaluate & 
Recalibrate. Paid drives to owned; owned feeds influencers; earned is amplified by paid and shared.
The Pyramid of Influence
Map the voices who carry the story: Professional Influencers (journalists, analysts, named experts) → the Power 
Middle (semi-pro creators, sector voices) → Super Fans & Employees → Fans & Followers. For corporate 
reputation the highest-value influencers are usually credible third parties — analysts, editors, respected alumni 
or partners — and employees as advocates.
5. The engagement model — always-on, not burst
A platform runs continuously; initiatives punctuate an always-on baseline rather than replacing it. UP's 
proprietary rollout model moves through four outcomes:
ALIGN / ENGAGE   set the stage — align internally, mobilise the platform, set direction
▼
DEVELOP / ENHANCE   build visibility — content, moments, thought leadership
▼
CONNECT / ADVOCATE   stakeholder engagement — connect influencers & advocates to the platform
▼
MOBILISE / AMPLIFY   influence perceptions — sustain, amplify, scale
Real-Time Engagement.  Underneath the phases runs an always-on operating rhythm — the Conversation 
Management loop: establish goals → gather assets → develop proprietary content → deploy across 
owned/earned/paid → train advocates → deploy → measure → refine. Supported by an always-on newsroom 
(the Observatory) that runs proactive stories and reactive issues management.
6. From messages & pillars to tactics
Every tactic is placed against an audience, a message and a pillar — the discipline that keeps the platform 
coherent. Build the map before the calendar:
Audience Message / pillar it serves Channel (PESO) Tactic
e.g. Investors / analysts Message 2 · “global-standard & proven” 
pillar
Earned + Owned Analyst briefings · results-linked 
thought leadership

hub
e.g. Media / public Umbrella · “rooted & impact” pillar Earned + Paid Signature report + op-ed · promoted 
amplification
7. The tactics catalogue (corporate reputation)
A menu, not a mandate — pick what the audiences and messages demand. Don't reach for volume; reach for the 
right tactic.
Channel Tactics
Earned Tier-1 business & sector media relations · op-eds & bylines by leaders · executive profiling & speaking · data / report-led PR · 
awards & rankings submissions · analyst & influencer relations · editorial partnerships (e.g. an Economist-style platform)
Owned Corporate newsroom / press room · thought-leadership content hub · flagship reports (annual, sustainability) · investor & 
careers pages · executive LinkedIn presence · podcast · email / newsletters
Shared Corporate & executive social · employee advocacy (e-advocates) · community & stakeholder engagement · partnerships · 
user-generated & third-party content
Paid Sponsored thought leadership · LinkedIn / programmatic to named stakeholders · content amplification (discovery 
platforms) · selective OOH for signature moments
8. Build every tactic as an Activation Card
The atomic unit of the platform. No tactic goes on the calendar until it is a card — this is what stops the platform 
becoming a to-do list.
The Activation Card
Insight → Idea → Engagement (the mechanic) → Desired Outcome   +  named targets  +  hashtag / 
signature
Each card also carries: audience · message/pillar it serves · PESO channel · KPI · phase.
9. Sequencing the platform — phasing & calendar
The platform is sequenced over time, balancing signature moments with always-on presence.
Campaign phasing
Tease → Launch → Sustain → Amplify for each major moment (the corporate rollout overlay: Engage → 
Enhance → Advocate → Amplify).
Content balance — Hero / Hub / Hygiene
Layer Role ≈ Share
Hero Signature moments — flagship reports, executive platforms, signature events ~20%
Hub Sustained programmes — ongoing thought leadership, content hub, recurring engagement ~60%
Hygiene Always-on maintenance — newsroom, investor/careers pages, social presence, issues monitoring ~20%
The content calendar & multi-market
● The 12-month calendar places every activation by date, channel, audience, message, phase and KPI — 
and shows the white space, not just the busy weeks.
● Global toolkit → localised: for multi-market work, build one core toolkit of channel-agnostic content 
that local markets adapt across Paid/Owned/Earned (a small set of global KPIs + local targets).
10. The deliverable — the Communications Plan
The platform is captured as an integrated Communications Plan that organizes, not lists:
  ☐ The platform idea + why it's ownable (passes the five criteria)
  ☐ Rollout strategies and phasing (Tease→Amplify / Engage→Amplify)
  ☐ Target audiences prioritised, each with its channels and tactics
  ☐ The PESO channel architecture, earned-led, integrated
  ☐ The tactics as Activation Cards, each traced to audience/message/pillar/KPI
  ☐ The 12-month content calendar (Hero/Hub/Hygiene), with the always-on newsroom
  ☐ The integrated plan + messages, sequenced and client-approved
11. What the AI does, and what the human owns
The AI does The human owns
Generates candidate platforms and tests them against the five criteria; 
maps tactics to audiences/messages/pillars; drafts Activation Cards; 
builds the PESO plan, the calendar and the phasing; checks every tactic 
for line of sight; drafts the Communications Plan
Chooses the platform; judges what's ownable and integrated; sets 
channel priorities and the earned-led balance; approves the tactics; 
owns feasibility, budget and risk
Why it's operator-independent.  Coherence is enforced by structure: every tactic must be an Activation Card 
traced to an audience, a message and a pillar, and the platform must pass the five criteria — so a novice can't 
produce a random tactic list, and the sharpest of the vetted platform options is what reaches the client.
12. Quality gate — before the platform goes to Measurement & 
delivery
  ☐ The platform passes the five criteria (differentiation, heritage, extension, advantage, durability)
  ☐ Every channel and tactic traces up to an audience, a message and the objective
  ☐ PESO is integrated around one insight — earned-led for reputation — not four silos
  ☐ Every tactic is an Activation Card with a KPI and a phase
  ☐ The calendar is balanced Hero/Hub/Hygiene and shows the white space
  ☐ Always-on presence and the newsroom are in place, not just campaign bursts
  ☐ The Communications Plan is integrated, sequenced and approved
Bottom line. A communications platform is an organizing idea, not a task list: one ownable architecture that pulls 
the brand through to the programs, orchestrates PESO around a single insight, and runs always-on with signature 
moments on top. Generate platform options, pick the one that passes the five criteria, map every tactic to an 
audience and a message as an Activation Card, and sequence it Hero/Hub/Hygiene across the year. Do that, and 
a junior builds a platform as integrated and ownable as a senior's — because the structure forces the coherence.

The Execution Toolkit
Turning the strategy into ready-to-run assets — the AI-Transformation guide to activation
The final phase — how to build the pack any team, market or partner can pick up and execute

July 2026 · builds on the MSL / UP toolkit library (Boots ‘Florence’, Febreze Always-On, Family Care GDM Playbook)
1. What an execution toolkit is — and why it's the last step
An execution toolkit is the bridge from an approved strategy to activity on the ground. It is a self-contained, 
replicable pack that turns the platform, narrative, messages and plan into ready-to-run assets and clear 
guidelines — so any team, any market, or any network partner can execute the strategy consistently and well, 
without the strategist in the room.
Why it matters most for the AI-Transformation.  Everything upstream makes a great strategy; the toolkit is what 
makes that strategy executable by anyone, anywhere, to the same standard. It is operator-independence at the 
point of delivery — flawless activation without depending on who's holding it.
2. The anatomy of a toolkit — what's in it
A complete UP execution toolkit contains these components. Use every one for a full launch; scale down for a 
lighter activation.
A · The strategic foundation (self-contained recap)
  ☐ Platform recap — the idea, the brand truth and the consumer/stakeholder truth on one page
  ☐ Story skeleton — Insight → Reason to Believe / New Discovery → Benefit → Proof
  ☐ Strategy recap — objectives, the proof/credentialing model (the pillars), priority audiences & influencers, KPIs
B · The plan
  ☐ The phased plan — Pre-Seed / Launch / Sustain (or Tease→Launch→Sustain→Amplify), each with objective, audience, 
messages, activities, available tools and leverage tactics
  ☐ The editorial / content calendar — by audience track, month by month, with message, hook and tool per slot
  ☐ A signature / experiential IP (optional) — an ownable programme and its activation guidelines
C · The messages & assets
  ☐ Message tracks — key messages by audience segment, each with insight, benefit and proof
  ☐ “What they will say / what they will see” — verbatim messaging by phase and audience
  ☐ The collateral library — press release, 30-second pitch, advertorial, Q&A / FAQ, key-message table (KMT), fact sheet, 
social posts, infographics, spokesperson materials, images
D · Activation & execution
  ☐ Channel activation guidelines (PESO) — owned, earned, shared, paid
  ☐ Influencer / creator activation — outreach guidelines, targets, mechanics, golden rules, disclosure
  ☐ Localisation guidance — what's fixed vs. locally adaptable (global toolkit → local markets)
  ☐ Execution logistics — roles (RACI), timeline, approvals, the content lifecycle and always-on newsroom
  ☐ Measurement hooks — tagging / UTM, KPIs per tactic, reporting cadence
  ☐ Governance — do-not-say lines, legal / disclosure, and the pre-publish quality checklist
3. The build workflow — assembling the toolkit
Step What you do Output

2  Phase the plan Break the roadmap into Pre-Seed → Launch → Sustain → Amplify with objectives

Every toolkit is organised by phase. For each phase, the toolkit specifies the objective, the audience in focus, the 
key messages, the activities, the available tools and the suggested leverage tactics.

5. The editorial / content calendar
A month-by-month grid per audience track (e.g. media, stakeholders/experts, consumers/public). Every slot ties 
a moment to a message and a ready asset.
Field What it captures

Always-on + moments, global → local.  Balance signature moments (Hero) with always-on presence

6. Message tracks & “what they'll say / see”
The toolkit gives each audience segment its own message track — not one set of messages for everyone. For 
each track, provide the copy at three depths, plus the verbatim a spokesperson would say and the audience 
would see.
Per-audience message track

Plus: “What the [spokesperson] will say” (verbatim quotes) and “What the audience will see” (headlines / 
creative directions), by phase.

The heart of a toolkit: the assets a team can pick up and use immediately, built from consistent templates.

8. Influencer / creator activation
Give local teams a repeatable way to activate creators, with clear targets and guardrails.
Example activation targets (per creator)
1 blog / long post · 3–5 social updates over ~14 days · 2–3 posts per day during a live challenge · agreed number 
of pieces committed up front.
Golden rules: be relevant & targeted · crowd-source their expertise · personalise (never cut-and-paste) · make it 
easy (ready assets, local adaptation) · be transparent and require disclosure of gifted product · be persistent with 
relevance.

Localisation — global toolkit → local markets
Build one core toolkit of channel-agnostic assets that local markets adapt. Mark clearly what is fixed (the 
platform, the narrative, the do-not-say lines, the global KPIs) and what is flexible (local hooks, spokespeople, 
language, local proof, market-specific tactics).
10. Execution logistics — how the work actually runs
The content lifecycle

Roles (RACI): who briefs, creates, approves, publishes and reports each asset. Always-on newsroom: a standing 
team for real-time stories and issues. Approvals: the sign-off path (incl. legal / client) before anything publishes.
11. Measurement hooks & governance
Wire in measurement from the start
Bake the AMEC measurement framework into the toolkit: campaign IDs / UTM conventions, tagged links, landing 
pages and CRM fields; a KPI against every tactic; and the reporting cadence (daily for paid, weekly headline KPIs, 
executive scorecard at the end). Measurement is a component of the toolkit, not an afterthought.
The pre-publish quality gate (the Publishing checklist)
  ☐ Fits a defined content pillar / message track
  ☐ On brand purpose, personality and narrative
  ☐ Provides real value to the audience (what's in it for them?)
  ☐ Within the do-not-say / legal / disclosure rules
  ☐ Clear call to action · conversational and shareable
  ☐ Correctly tagged for measurement · assets approved
Enforced by the engine.  The Adversarial Review Board's GC and Journalist personas screen assets for 
unsubstantiated claims, disclosure and greenwashing before they publish — so a local team can activate fast 
without a compliance miss.

Campaign Measurement Framework
AMEC-based · Engine Measurement Module (CUBE Face 6 · Flow Step 13)
Start with the business change, then work backwards to activities and metrics.
Adapts AMEC's Integrated Evaluation Framework into a repeatable UP operating model for B2B, B2C, corporate, 
public-sector and multi-market campaigns.
How this fits the engine
This is the definitive methodology for the CUBE's Measurement face and Step 13 of the guided flow. It replaces 
the lighter measurement summary in the Master Blueprint (§13) and becomes the engine's measurement 
standard.
Central rule: start with the business change, then work backwards to activities and metrics. Reach and coverage 
remain useful diagnostics, but success is judged through audience response, behaviour change and 
organizational impact.
Why it is operator-independent
● The Measurement Brief is a hard gate. No campaign enters creative development without an approved 
brief (baseline, target, source, owner) — so a novice can't skip it.
● The KPI ladder and campaign-type modules are fill-in templates. The operator selects the right KPIs 
from a vetted set rather than judging what to measure.

1. Purpose & the goal
The UP AI Transformation turns United Partners' expertise, methodologies and proven client workflows 
into a structured, AI-powered operating system. It guides a team member — or a network partner, or an 
in-house team — through the complete client-delivery process, from collecting and validating inputs 
through research, strategy development, quality control, approvals and final deliverables, using UP's 
frameworks, templates, case studies and accumulated experience.
AI supports the research, analysis, synthesis and drafting. UP professionals retain responsibility for strategic 
judgment, client decisions, reputation risk and final approval. The first pilot is the corporate & brand 
communications strategy, tested on real client cases.
The goal, precisely.  Not to train people — to make anyone deliver the same high-quality strategy regardless of 
knowledge or seniority. The metric is operator-independence: a novice and a 30-year veteran should produce 
the same excellent strategy. The number we drive to zero is the variance between operators.

3. Design principles
● Quality lives in the system, not the person. Every judgment is a system procedure, not the operator's 
call — that is what makes output operator-independent.
● Co-pilot, not autopilot. A named senior Strategy Owner carries accountability at four judgment gates; 
the engine does everything between them.
● Reason from reputation, don't template. Every step is grounded in UP's theory of reputation, so the 
output withstands scrutiny.
● One insight, integrated. Great communications can't be great on its own — everything flows from one 
human insight, orchestrated across all channels.
● Every step makes an artifact and has a gate. You never advance until the step's quality check passes.
● Depth scales to the client. An SME runs a lean version; an enterprise runs the full, governed version.
● The engine compounds. Every completed strategy feeds the knowledge base, so the next one starts

5. The theory — Economics of Reputation
Every strategy rests on an explicit theory of reputation, encoded as reasoning the engine applies from the 
first step.
Question The UP position
What is reputation? A dynamic construct — perception + judgement + asset. Fluid, never “solved.”
Why does it matter? Digital voice, transparency and scandal have made it a board-level asset.
How is it created? Partnerships (borrow prestige) · Initiatives (awards, innovation, symbolic acts) · Associations (leaders' 
reputations). Consumers co-create it.
How does it create value? Externally — price premium, lower cost of capital, loyalty. Internally — talent, retention, motivation.
How is it measured? Ranking · Rating · Multiple-Stakeholder (RepTrak / Reputation Quotient).

17. Honest limits
Two things resist full systematization, and naming them is the difference between a credible plan and a 
sales pitch. First, perceiving a specific client's unspoken internal politics — the system can force the input 
but can't perceive what the operator doesn't know to enter. Second, breakthrough creative originality — 
the engine reliably delivers strong-and-distinctive, occasionally brilliant; the top few percent of genius 
stays human.
For this pilot's goal, that is the right trade. The aim is not occasional superhuman brilliance but that a novice 
and a veteran produce the same excellent strategy. Consistency at “excellent” is worth more to the firm than 
high-variance genius — and it is reachable. The engine raises the floor, refuses to let the obvious pass, forces 
the choices strategy requires, and leaves the true ceiling to the strategist. That is a defensible, honest, and 
valuable claim — and it is exactly what the AI Transformation set out to build.

The Adversarial Review Board
Mechanism M3 — Specification
Senior-grade scrutiny with no senior in the room. A panel of AI adversaries attacks the strategy; it must  
survive them before it ships.
July 2026 · builds on v1.0
What it is — and its honest boundary
After the engine drafts a strategy (or a key artifact), a panel of AI personas each attacks it from a specific 
adversary's point of view — the people who, in the real world, would try to tear it apart. The strategy must 
survive them. This is how a novice operator gets the same scrutiny a 30-year strategist would apply, 
without a strategist present.
The honest boundary.  The Board delivers senior-grade SCRUTINY — it finds the problems a senior would find. It 
does not deliver senior-grade CREATION — it doesn't originate the brilliant fix. Pair it with the options generator 
(M5/M6): the Board finds the flaw, the generator proposes fixes, the operator chooses. And it tests logic and 
exposure, not ground truth — so real audience validation (M7) stays essential; the Board can't catch a wrong-
but-plausible insight if the data feeding it is wrong.
1. Where it runs
Placement Board convened Why here
Insight mini-board (Step 5B) Competitor + Target Audience + Activist Kill a weak insight before a whole strategy is 
built on it — cheap to fix early
Pre-ship full board (Step 14) All personas Final gauntlet on the complete strategy before 
the human ship gate
2. The personas
Each persona owns one failure mode. Together they cover the ways a reputation strategy dies.
The Competitor   “I can say that too.”
Catches:  Table-stakes positioning; weak distinctiveness and ownability.
Attacks:  Which of your claims could I make word-for-word? How do I counter-position you tomorrow? What's your 
defensible ground versus mine? Is your “white space” actually contested?
Pass when:  At least one position no named competitor can credibly claim, plus a stated defense against counter-
positioning.
The CFO / Board   “So what — where's the business and the number?”
Catches:  No business linkage; vanity or vague measurement; unrealistic budget/timeline; over-claimed value.
Attacks:  How does this move the business objective? What's the KPI, baseline, target and benchmark? Prove the 
reputation-to-value link — or stop claiming it. Why fund this over the alternative?
Pass when:  Every objective traces to a business goal; measurement has baseline/target/benchmark; value stated as 
contribution, not attribution; budget realistic.
The Journalist   “Where's the substance? I'm going to check.”
Catches:  Unsubstantiated claims; the gap between narrative and behaviour; greenwashing / hypocrisy exposure; spin.
Attacks:  What's the proof behind this line? What does your actual record show? Where does the narrative outrun the 
truth? What's the story when I dig?
Pass when:  Every claim carries a proof point; no demonstrable gap between narrative and behaviour; no 
greenwashing exposure (CSRD-safe).
The General Counsel / Risk   “Can you substantiate that — and what's the exposure?”
Catches:  Legal/regulatory exposure; unsubstantiated or regulated claims; defamation; a stand that invites an 
unwinnable fight; hidden tripwires.
Attacks:  Is this claim substantiable and compliant? Does it create liability? Does the stand invite a fight we can't win? 
Is there a litigation / disclosure / deal tripwire hiding here?
Pass when:  Claims substantiable; do-not-say guardrails intact; no undisclosed tripwire; the stand fits the company's 
risk appetite and character.
The Target Audience   “Why do I care? I don't believe you.”
Catches:  Weak relevance and resonance; brand-centric not audience-centric; an unvalidated audience truth.
Attacks:  What's in this for me? Is this about you or me? Do I actually feel the tension you claim? Does this change 
what I think, feel or do?
Pass when:  A Unifying Human Insight the audience genuinely holds (M7-validated); messages framed as audience 
value; a real perception/behaviour shift.
The Hostile Stakeholder / Activist   “Here's how this blows up.”
Catches:  Backlash and vulnerability; who gets alienated; crisis exposure; a stand that becomes a target.
Attacks:  Who does this anger? What's the worst-case headline or tweet? What vulnerability does it expose? Can you 
withstand the counter-attack?
Pass when:  The backlash surface is identified and acceptable; the sacrifice is deliberate; the position can withstand 
scrutiny; crisis exposure is mapped.
The Employee / Insider   “We don't actually do this.”
Catches:  Internal-credibility gap; inside-out authenticity; internal misalignment. (Enterprise / any values-led strategy.)
Attacks:  Is this who we actually are? Will staff believe it or roll their eyes? Have the people who must deliver it bought 
in?
Pass when:  The narrative is authentic to the lived culture; internal alignment is addressed; employees could advocate 
it honestly.
3. The verdict model
Every persona returns a structured verdict — never a vague opinion.
Field Values / rule
Verdict PASS · CONCERN · BLOCK
Severity Low · Medium · High · Critical (anchored to examples so “Critical” means the same thing every time)
Finding The specific line, claim, competitor or audience at fault — quoted. No vague criticism allowed.
Suggested fix A concrete direction the options generator can act on
Specificity is enforced.  An attack with no quoted target is discarded by the referee pass (§5). This stops the 
Board being vague or sycophantic — it must point at the exact weakness or it doesn't count.
4. Aggregation & pass/fail rules
The system — not the operator — triages the Board's findings by fixed rules:
Condition Outcome
Any CRITICAL finding (legal red line, factual falsehood, 
greenwashing, reputational landmine)
HARD BLOCK — fix before anything else, regardless of all other verdicts
Competitor returns BLOCK on distinctiveness RETURN to Insight/Strategy — a table-stakes strategy cannot ship
Target Audience returns BLOCK (insight not held / 
unvalidated)
RETURN to Insight — trigger M7 validation
≥ 2 High concerns, or ≥ 4 Medium MUST REVISE — auto-revise loop
Only Low concerns, or all PASS CLEARS the Board → proceeds to the human ship gate with the Board 
report attached
The Board never ships to the client.  It clears the strategy to the final human gate (the Strategy Owner). But 
because the scrutiny is already done and documented, that human's job shrinks from “review everything” to 
“confirm the Board's clearance” — which is what makes the senior time affordable and, at SME tier, often 
unnecessary beyond a spot-check.
5. The review loop
Step What happens
1  Draft Engine produces the artifact / strategy
2  Attack All personas run in parallel, each grounded in real data (competitor's actual positioning, the client's actual record, 
real audience data)
3  Referee A meta-pass strips hallucinated or ungrounded attacks, de-duplicates, and ranks by severity
4  Triage Rules in §4 decide: Block / Return / Revise / Clear
5  Fix Auto-revise where the fix is determinate; where a genuine fork exists, the options generator (M5) presents 
vetted choices to the operator
6  Re-review Bounded to 3 rounds. If it still can't clear, escalate to a human — the one place seniority is invoked, and only on 
genuinely hard deadlocks
7  Clear Attach the Board report; proceed to the human ship gate
Keeping the Board honest (it's AI, so it can flatter or hallucinate)
● Grounding. Each persona is fed real data, not imagination — the competitor's real positioning, the 
client's real record, actual audience evidence.
● Specificity requirement. No attack counts unless it quotes the exact target; the referee discards the 
rest.
● Severity calibration. Anchored to worked examples so verdicts are consistent run to run — no drifting 
standards.
● Validate the validators. Periodically check the Board's findings against real senior reviews: does it catch 
what seniors catch, without crying wolf? Feed the result back (Outcome Library).
Operator-independence — how the operator never judges
The operator never scores the Board and never adjudicates a finding. The system triages by rule; it auto-
revises where it can; and where a real choice exists, it presents the Board's reasoning plus vetted options 
and the operator simply chooses. A novice and a veteran get the same scrutiny and the same fix set — 
which is the entire point of M3.
6. Tier scaling
Tier Board composition
SME / Standard Core 4 — Competitor · CFO · Journalist · Target Audience
Enterprise / Regulated Core 4 + General Counsel · Activist · Employee, grounded in fuller research
Regulated sectors Add a Regulator persona (sector rules, disclosure, advertising standards)
Bottom line. The Adversarial Review Board is the closest thing to putting a demanding senior in the room 
without one being there. Six or seven adversaries, each owning a way reputation strategies fail, each forced to 
quote the exact weakness, triaged by fixed rules into block / return / revise / clear — with the operator only ever 
choosing among vetted fixes, never judging. It won't originate genius and it can't see past bad input data, so it 
lives alongside the options generator and real validation. But for the goal that matters — the same tough 
scrutiny on every strategy, whoever is at the desk — the Board is the mechanism that delivers it.

# Real Client Case For AI Workflow Demo

Selected case: Corporate brand strategy, built from scratch

Client: A real United Partners telecom client, sanitized. No client name is used.

Status: Sanitized, confidential, for AI workflow demo.

## Short Ask

This case is a corporate brand and corporate communications strategy built from a blank slate. The client has no approved corporate brand strategy, and positioning, narrative, and pillar architecture are not pre-decided. The workflow must reason from evidence to a defensible strategy and show what is fact, what is missing, and what is strategic judgment.

## Client Type

Industry/category: Telecommunications: fixed line, mobile, broadband internet, TV/entertainment, and B2B solutions such as IoT, smart cities, cloud, and digital education.

Market/country: A single mid-sized European national market. The client is a subsidiary of a larger regional telecoms-and-media group.

B2B or B2C: Both. Mass-market consumer is the revenue core. B2B, enterprise, and public-sector solutions are strategic growth areas.

Current business situation: Market leader by revenue and the incumbent operator. Operationally strong, with leading network, fixed infrastructure, and entertainment assets. Stable and profitable, but operating in a mature, saturated, price-pressured market where the three main operators have converged on near-identical positioning. The company operates beyond core connectivity, but is not yet recognized for that broader role.

## Real Challenge

Trigger: A leadership transition requiring a narrative reset. The specific transition details are excluded from AI use.

What the client wants to change: Move from reactive, campaign-by-campaign communications to one coherent corporate brand strategy. The client must decide on a corporate positioning and narrative that do not currently exist in approved form. Prior agency proposals were liked but never adopted, so the company is effectively starting fresh.

Business/reputation problem:

- Differentiation: the three main operators recycle technology leadership, ESG, and employer-brand claims.
- Affinity: the category is trusted but not loved.
- Contested leadership: share of voice has moved from clear dominance to a tight race.
- Latent strength: national scale, infrastructure, digital-economy role, CSR, and skills programmes exist, but are communicated as episodes rather than one corporate story.

## Objectives

- Re-establish corporate reputation and leadership trust after the transition.
- Build a differentiated corporate brand platform the market can recognize.
- Lift affinity and preference in a trusted-but-not-loved category.
- Strengthen employer brand for digital and engineering talent.
- Establish credible, ownable ESG and societal-contribution leadership.

## Audiences To Prioritize

These audiences are not pre-ranked. The strategy must prioritize them.

- Media: national news, business/financial press, tech media, consumer media.
- Regulators, policy stakeholders, and government stakeholders.
- Talent and future talent: students, STEM graduates, tech community.
- Business and enterprise customers and partners.
- General public and consumer base.
- Parent-group corporate stakeholders.

## Must-Say And Must-Avoid

Because positioning is open, these are guardrails, not the message itself.

Must-say guardrails:

- Use verifiable and ownable proof.
- Show a genuine role in the country’s digital progress.
- Build one company story rather than disconnected activity claims.

Must-avoid guardrails:

- Do not fall back into state-utility or former-monopoly framing.
- Do not recycle shared category claims around technology leadership, ESG, or employer branding as the central idea.
- Do not use competitive price-war messaging as corporate positioning.
- Do not introduce political framing.

## Decision Setup

Primary approval owner: client-side Corporate Communications lead.

Final sign-off: CEO and parent-group corporate communications function.

Consulted teams: Marketing, HR/People, Product, Regulatory Affairs, Legal, and parent-group communications.

Internal alignment tension: Marketing owns consumer brand and advertising budget. Corporate Communications owns reputation and PR. The corporate platform must sit above and feed consumer campaigns without colliding with them. Parent-group requirements add an approval layer. Because positioning is genuinely undecided, the strategy must force and document the positioning decision the client still owes itself.

## Competitive And Market Context

Main competitors: two strong rivals in a three-player market. One is positioned around technology/network leadership and social-impact programming. The other is positioned around customer experience and independently certified network quality. Both invest heavily in corporate narrative and are closing the share-of-voice gap.

Reference brands: major European incumbent operators that repositioned from utility to digital enabler. These are directional benchmarks only, not targets to copy.

Market pressure: mature, saturated, price-competitive market; streaming pressure on traditional TV consumption; convergence pressure from over-the-top players. Growth must come from preference and value, not volume.

Known audience-perception problem: the category is trusted but not admired. The client is respected for reliability and scale but is not associated with a distinctive idea. Competitors out-narrate it on innovation and customer experience, while the client’s relative strength appears more in corporate, sustainability, and CSR coverage than product buzz.

Open strategic question: Is incumbent scale and infrastructure a liability to move away from, or, retold in human and national terms, the one position rivals cannot match? The strategy must take a view; the brief must not assume one.

## Channels And Components

PESO direction:

- Earned: core driver for corporate reputation.
- Owned: newsroom, reports, internal channels, and thought-leadership content.
- Shared: professional social, executive social, consumer social where relevant.
- Paid: supporting role only.
- Partnerships, CSR, and ESG: high relevance.
- Crisis sensitivity: regulatory proceedings, outages, data security, and leadership-transition sensitivities.

## Constraints

Legal/regulatory:

- The client operates under a national communications regulator.
- Claims touching market share, pricing, or competitive position require Legal/Regulatory review.
- ESG claims must align with group-verified data.
- GDPR applies to audience targeting, campaign data, and influencer data handling.
- EU AI Act, DSA, and DMA awareness is required where relevant.

AI-use limits:

- Exclude leadership-transition specifics.
- Exclude real commercial or retainer terms.
- Exclude competitor-by-name intelligence.
- Exclude unannounced strategic plans.
- Use only publicly grounded facts plus this sanitized brief.
- Treat prior unadopted agency positioning ideas as tone reference only, never approved positioning.
- Replace client and individual names with generic stand-ins or role titles.
- Replace financial specifics, budgets, and retainer terms with ranges or TBC.

## Expected Outputs

- Evidence base and readiness check: what is known, what is missing, and what must be decided before strategy can proceed.
- Positioning options: two to three reasoned territories with a recommended direction and rationale, not a single pre-baked answer.
- Corporate brand platform/message architecture: core idea, narrative, and message house framed as a first build for client decision.
- Pillar architecture: derived from evidence and argued, including how many pillars and why.
- Stakeholder and executive thought-leadership map.
- Twelve-month roadmap/campaign platform linked to business moments.
- Measurement framework aligned to AMEC Barcelona Principles 4.0 and the AMEC Integrated Evaluation Framework.

## What Good Looks Like

- Input discipline: surfaces gaps before writing and flags that positioning is undecided.
- Strategic structure: pillars and positioning are reasoned from evidence, not borrowed from competitors.
- Review trail: every recommendation traces to input and separates fact from judgment.
- Honest about unsettled decisions: presents options for client decision rather than asserting a finished answer.
- Practical first artifact: message architecture small enough for a client decision meeting, but substantive enough to test the central strategic bet.

## Safety Note

This brief uses sanitized facts plus publicly grounded context. No confidential client documents, real names, real financials, or specifics of the leadership transition are included. The strategic problem is preserved while identifying and sensitive details are removed or generalized. The account team should review anything pulled into a live demo before it runs.

Smart-city platform. Vivacom says it works on Internet of Things and smart-city services and has smart solutions for more than 130 Bulgarian municipalities (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata). (bears on: programme, narrative and channels)

Customer data exposure. The My Vivacom Google Play listing says the app may share personal information and may collect location, personal information and two other data types (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en_IE&id=bg.vivacom.mobile). (bears on: constraints and guardrails)

Self-claim verdict. Vivacom says, exactly, “Vivacom е иноватор” and says it has invested nearly 3 billion leva in technology, innovation, people and the Bulgarian economy; Pikasa did not test that exact innovation claim, but its Q1 2026 social audit found Vivacom strongest on Instagram and weak at converting YouTube reach into response (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata; https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war). (bears on: reputation problem / desired perception)

Self-claim verdict. Vivacom says its 5G network is the largest in Bulgaria and covers 92% of the population; OpenSignal’s January 2026 Bulgaria mobile report corroborated a related strength by awarding Vivacom the Time on 5G award with 26.3%, two percentage points ahead of A1 (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata; https://insights.opensignal.com/reports/2026/01/bulgaria/mobile-network-experience). (bears on: reputation and stakeholder context)

Channels. Vivacom GAME ON had a wider live-stream channel set than the banked 2026 YouTube evidence shows: in September 2024 the first two rounds were streamed in 9 online channels across YouTube, Twitch, Kick and TikTok (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/parvite-dva-runda-na-vivacom-game-on-s-blizo-180-000-gledania-online). In October 2025 a Roblox round was streamed in 11 channels across YouTube, Twitch, Kick and TikTok, so GAME ON uses creator and streaming channels beyond Vivacom's main owned social accounts (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/virtualniyat-svyat-na-roblox-otpravi-novo-izpitanie-za-otbornite-v-tretiya-onlain-rund-na-vivacom-game-on-2025).

Presence. The first two Vivacom GAME ON rounds in 2024 generated about 180,000 online views and more than 24,000 viewer hours, showing that the gaming platform can draw measurable audience attention outside ordinary telecom product posts (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/parvite-dva-runda-na-vivacom-game-on-s-blizo-180-000-gledania-online). The 2025 GAME ON YouTube series had more than 250,000 views after six episodes, according to Vivacom's own news centre; no independent source found in this pass tested that figure (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/virtualniyat-svyat-na-roblox-otpravi-novo-izpitanie-za-otbornite-v-tretiya-onlain-rund-na-vivacom-game-on-2025).

Presence. United Group said in July 2026 that Bulgaria's telecoms market reached 2.16 billion euros in the prior year and that IPTV had passed one million households nationally; this places Vivacom's EON presence inside a visible market shift toward IPTV (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/).

Tone of voice. Asen Velikov's 2019 interview used a customer-first and technology-change frame, calling Vivacom a "customer-oriented company" and saying customer experience had become a focus of investment because customers compare telecoms with Amazon and Google (https://www.economic.bg/bg/a/view/change-is-the-only-invariable-112562). This supports a voice route around customer experience and digital change, not only network scale (https://www.economic.bg/bg/a/view/change-is-the-only-invariable-112562).

Tone of voice. The Netcracker release carried a technical but customer-facing executive voice: Asen Velikov linked billing-system modernization to long-term stability, growth and the customer experience, while Netcracker framed the work around 5G monetization, AI, automation and vertical industries (https://www.netcracker.com/news/press-releases/netcracker-and-vivacom-extend-long-term-partnership-for-innovative-it-modernization-program).

Tone of voice. The GAME ON news voice is youth-culture and gaming-led, using named creators, Roblox, Minecraft, live streams, fan voting, prizes, finals and YouTube episodes to translate fibre-network proof into entertainment participation (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/parvite-dva-runda-na-vivacom-game-on-s-blizo-180-000-gledania-online; https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/virtualniyat-svyat-na-roblox-otpravi-novo-izpitanie-za-otbornite-v-tretiya-onlain-rund-na-vivacom-game-on-2025).

Community. The 2024 GAME ON format made viewers active participants: more than 100 audience-selected participants joined the second online battle, viewers voted in Vivacom's social channels, and the final carried a 15,000 leva prize fund (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/parvite-dva-runda-na-vivacom-game-on-s-blizo-180-000-gledania-online). In the 2025 Roblox round, two fans won 1,000 leva each and a chance to stand with their preferred captain at the November 1 final in Joy Station, Sofia (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/virtualniyat-svyat-na-roblox-otpravi-novo-izpitanie-za-otbornite-v-tretiya-onlain-rund-na-vivacom-game-on-2025).

Community. United Group said Job Lab began in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2021, then expanded to Slovenia and Croatia before Bulgaria became the fourth market in 2026; this makes Vivacom's Job Lab a local version of a group youth-skills programme rather than a stand-alone Bulgarian invention (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/united-group-b.v._joblab-unitedgroup-vivacom-activity-7425125424449511424-1jtJ).

The visibility of its executives. Asen Velikov appears as a customer-experience and IT-modernization spokesperson beyond Vivacom's owned channels: Netcracker quoted him on February 11, 2026 saying Vivacom was entering the "next phase of our IT evolution" through its revenue-management upgrade (https://www.netcracker.com/news/press-releases/netcracker-and-vivacom-extend-long-term-partnership-for-innovative-it-modernization-program). This is partner-channel visibility tied to service systems and customer experience rather than only corporate announcements (https://www.netcracker.com/news/press-releases/netcracker-and-vivacom-extend-long-term-partnership-for-innovative-it-modernization-program).

The visibility of its executives. Asen Velikov had executive media visibility before becoming CEO: Economic.bg published a 2019 interview with him as Financial Director and Management Board member, covering customer experience, e-shop updates, customer-centre platform replacement, SAP, electronic sourcing and supplier relationship management (https://www.economic.bg/bg/a/view/change-is-the-only-invariable-112562).

The visibility of its executives. The banked record makes a new pattern visible: Asen Velikov is visible through owned Vivacom pages, parent-group pages, partner releases, employer content and public events, while the banked non-CEO executive visibility is mainly HR and public-affairs content (banked findings: The visibility of its executives).

EON platform provenance. United Group said in July 2026 that Vivacom backs Bulgaria's IPTV shift through EON, a TV platform developed by United Cloud; this adds parent-group platform provenance to Vivacom's entertainment story (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/). United Group separately says EON was built in-house by United Cloud and is available across the markets where United Group operates; Broadband TV News independently reported that Vivacom added BBC First and BBC Earth to EON in Bulgaria in March 2026, so the presence of EON in Vivacom's offer is corroborated while the parent claim that it is an "award-winning TV platform" was not tested there (https://united.group/united-group-brings-southeast-europes-leading-television-platform-eon-to-greece/; https://www.broadbandtvnews.com/2026/03/17/vivacom-adds-bbc-first-and-bbc-earth-to-eon-in-bulgaria/). (bears on: programme, narrative and channels)

Customer and revenue systems. Netcracker said on February 11, 2026 that Vivacom would upgrade to the latest version of Netcracker Revenue Management as part of an IT modernization programme affecting postpaid mobile and fixed lines for both B2C and B2B customers (https://www.netcracker.com/news/press-releases/netcracker-and-vivacom-extend-long-term-partnership-for-innovative-it-modernization-program). Netcracker said the suite automates the lead-to-cash process across billing, invoicing and revenue processes, which makes customer and revenue systems a likely evidence source to request in the intake conversation (https://www.netcracker.com/news/press-releases/netcracker-and-vivacom-extend-long-term-partnership-for-innovative-it-modernization-program). (bears on: baseline data & measurement access)

(bears on: reputation problem / desired perception)

Community.
