guided_interview.prompt: Read the Context scan findings and gaps below. Do the findings hold up on the client you know, and is any gap the one that would change how you walk into the client conversation?
findings: Regulatory context. Bulgaria’s telecom sector is governed by EU rules including the European Electronic Communications Code, ePrivacy Directive, Net Neutrality Regulation, Roaming Regulation, Gigabit Infrastructure Act and EU termination-rate rules; Bulgarian core laws include the Electronic Communications Act and Electronic Communications Networks and Physical Infrastructure Act (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).

Regulatory context. Telecom and adjacent digital activity in Bulgaria is also affected by the General Data Protection Regulation, Digital Services Act, Digital Markets Act, Cybersecurity Act, Artificial Intelligence Act, NIS2 Directive and Critical Entity Resilience Directive; this confirms the supplied brief’s legal and AI-policy constraints (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).

Regulatory context. The Communications Regulation Commission is the independent telecom regulator; the Ministry of Transport and Communications and Ministry of e-Government set ICT, digital administration and cybersecurity policy; the National Radio Frequency Spectrum Council handles national spectrum-planning proposals (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).

Regulatory context. CRC Decision No. 220 of 30 July 2024 found no effective competition in wholesale access to passive physical infrastructure, named Vivacom as having significant individual impact, and imposed access, non-discrimination, transparency, reference-offer and price-control duties (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Regulatory context. CRC launched a fourth-round analysis of local access at a fixed location, and by Decision No. 251 of 29 August 2025 ordered extra information on fixed access via mobile network for 2021-2023; this keeps fixed access and 5G-based home internet inside active review (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Regulatory context. CRC says Vivacom met all universal-service quality target values in 2024, did not request unfair-burden compensation by the 30 June 2024 statutory deadline, and had a 46% drop in universal-service complaints versus the prior period (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Regulatory context. CRC says 2024 universal-service complaints to Vivacom were mainly technical failures at 27% of complaints; termination complaints rose to 16% from 2% in 2023, and the other category rose 18 percentage points to 29% (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Regulatory context. CMS says CRC awarded 20-year 3.6 GHz licences to A1, Vivacom and Yettel in April 2021, and assigned 700 MHz and 800 MHz bands to the same three operators in December 2023 for 15 years; CMS says total licence payments were about BGN 13.4 million (https://cms.law/en/int/expert-guides/cms-expert-guide-to-5g-regulation-and-law/bulgaria).

Regulatory context. Bulgaria’s Supreme Administrative Court issued a final ruling in February 2026 clearing United Group’s acquisition of Bulsatcom telecom infrastructure assets after appeals by A1 Bulgaria, Yettel Bulgaria and Cetin Bulgaria; the court said the deal and base-station infrastructure asset deal were not a notifiable concentration under Bulgarian competition law (https://seenews.com/news/bulgarias-supreme-court-clears-united-groups-acquisition-of-bulsatcom-1290035).

Regulatory context. A1 Group publicly objected in July 2023 to CPC approval of Vivacom acquisitions of Networx-Bulgaria and six smaller operators, saying the deals could give Vivacom more than 60% of TV distribution and nearly 40% of internet; CRC’s 2024 market data later reported Vivacom at 59.6% of pay-TV subscribers and 39.4% of fixed internet subscribers (https://newsroom.a1.com/news-a1-group-deeply-unsettled-by-an-unexpected-decision-of-the-bulgarian-commission-on-protection-of-competition?id=182022&l=english&menueid=14594; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

ESG context. United Group says its 2024 sustainability results included 61% electricity from renewable sources, a 52% cut in Scope 1 and 2 emissions against its 2020 baseline, a 13% improvement in its Network Efficiency Index, 25% refurbished customer premises equipment among installed devices, more than 2,300 kg of e-waste recovered, and more than 1,500 smartphones recovered through customer take-back programs (https://united.group/united-group-releases-2024-sustainability-report-highlighting-tangible-progress-across-esg-priorities/).

ESG context. United Group says it is building three solar plants and one wind farm in Bulgaria; by 2027 these assets are planned to supply 160% of electricity needed for the Group’s Bulgarian operations, cover 65% of total Group electricity use, remove about 120,000 tonnes of CO2 from Bulgaria’s grid each year, reach 124 MW combined capacity, and produce 310,000 MWh a year (https://united.group/united-group-enters-renewable-energy-production/).

ESG context. A Vivacom careers page says United Group Energy develops renewable power plants to supply United Group telecom and media operations with 100% green electricity, and says Bulgaria has more than 120 MW of renewable projects under development, construction and operation (https://www.vivacom.bg/bg/residential/za-nas/karieri/obiavi-za-rabota/31166/senior-electrical-engineer-high-voltage-substations-sofia).

ESG context. Vivacom says its management system is certified to ISO 9001:2015, ISO 14001:2015, ISO 45001:2018, ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, and ISO/IEC 27018:2019; I did not find an independent certificate register for each standard in this pass, so this is a client claim awaiting document proof (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata).

Geopolitical context. United Group is Netherlands-based and majority owned by BC Partners; it completed Vivacom’s acquisition on 31 July 2020 after European Commission approval in April 2020 and a November 2019 agreement (https://united.group/united-group-welcomes-vivacom-the-largest-telecom-operator-in-bulgaria/).

Geopolitical context. BC Partners said Vivacom had over 1.8 million unique customers at the time of the 2019 acquisition agreement, and described the deal as part of United Group’s expansion from six Southeast European countries (https://www.bcpartners.com/news/bc-partners-owned-united-group-acquires-vivacom/).

Geopolitical context. United Group agreed in February 2025 to sell SBB Serbia to e& PPF Telecom and to sell NetTV Plus and Western Balkan sports rights to Telekom Srbija; the announced combined enterprise value was EUR 1.5 billion, and United Group said the move completed its aim of exiting non-EU telecom assets (https://united.group/united-group-agrees-to-sell-sbb-serbia-as-well-as-net-tv-plus-business-and-its-sports-broadcasting-rights-for-western-balkans/).

Geopolitical context. A May 2026 SeeNews report said United Group was considering selling some or all Bulgarian assets, including Vivacom’s fixed network and Nova Broadcasting Group; the article says the process was early and based on local media reporting, so this is a live ownership-watch item, not a completed event (https://seenews.com/news/see-focused-united-group-mulls-selling-bulgarian-assets-report-1294890).

Geopolitical context. Bulgaria, Kosovo and North Macedonia signed 5G security declarations with the United States on 23 October 2020 under the Clean Network initiative; RFE/RL reported the initiative was aimed at limiting equipment from companies such as Huawei in telecom networks (https://www.rferl.org/a/bulgaria-kosovo-north-macedonia-join-us-initiative-to-block-chinese-equipment-in-5g-network/30909512.html).

Geopolitical context. CRC reported that A1, Vivacom and Yettel provided annual reports in 2024 on their Multivendor Strategy; this makes supplier mix and network security a regulator-visible issue for Vivacom (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Category context. Bulgaria’s electronic communications market reached EUR 2.06 billion in 2024, up 5.7% on 2023, according to the ICLG Bulgaria telecoms chapter citing CRC data (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).

Category context. United Group said in July 2026 that Bulgaria’s telecom market grew close to 5% last year to EUR 2.16 billion, and said the growth came in fibre, 5G and television (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/).

Category context. CRC reported bundled-service revenue of BGN 2.064 billion in 2024, up 10.6% year on year; A1, Vivacom and Yettel accounted for 97.8% of bundled-service revenue and 98.3% of bundled-service subscribers (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Category context. Vivacom’s bundled-service subscriber share rose from 30.7% in 2023 to 32.9% in 2024, and its bundled-service revenue share rose from 27.6% to 30.2%; CRC says Bulsatcom was deleted from the CRC register and its activity was reported by Vivacom (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Category context. CRC reported retail fixed internet and data-transfer revenue of BGN 1.879791 billion in 2024; Vivacom led retail fixed internet access with 39.4% of subscribers and 37.1% of revenue, up 7.2 and 8.3 percentage points year on year (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Category context. CRC reported 2.02 million pay-TV subscribers at the end of 2024; Vivacom led pay TV with 59.6% of subscribers and 56.5% of revenue after the incorporation of Bulsatcom and TVN Distribution Bulgaria (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Category context. CRC reported IPTV subscribers grew 9.4% in 2024 and IPTV reached 47.8% of pay-TV subscribers; Vivacom, A1 and Yettel together made up 95.0% of IPTV subscribers (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Category context. CRC reported satellite TV subscribers fell 8.4% in 2024; after Bulsatcom was incorporated into Vivacom, Vivacom’s satellite-TV subscriber share exceeded 80.0% by the end of 2024 (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Self-claim verdict: 5G coverage. Vivacom says it has the "5G мрежата с най-голямо покритие в България" and that its 5G covers 92% of Bulgaria’s population; CMS confirms Vivacom has extensive 5G coverage but does not rank it first, so the ranking claim needs proof before use (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata; https://cms.law/en/int/expert-guides/cms-expert-guide-to-5g-regulation-and-law/bulgaria). (bears on: reputation problem / desired perception)

Self-claim verdict: fibre speed. Vivacom says it has the fastest fixed fibre network for home internet in Bulgaria as of 23 May 2025 based on CRC’s tariff comparison tool; nPerf’s public awards page confirms a 2024 Bulgaria fixed-line performance award page exists, but the page opened in this pass did not expose the winner text, so the claim needs the CRC comparison record or nPerf report before it is used as a fact (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata; https://www.nperf.com/en/awards/bg/2024/broadband/bulgaria). (bears on: reputation problem / desired perception)

Platform dependency. United Group selected Eutelsat as the single future satellite operator for its next Direct To Home platform; the move covers Telemach, NOVA, Bulsatcom, VIVACOM, SBB and Total TV across eight countries and is expected to finish by the end of 2025 (https://united.group/united-group-and-eutelsat-develop-next-gen-dth-platform/). (bears on: programme, narrative and channels)

Ownership history. Vivacom’s ownership history is a reputation asset and a risk: Viva Ventures bought 65% of BTC for EUR 230 million in 2004, AIG bought 90% of BTC for 2.8 billion levs in 2007, Spas Roussev bought Vivacom at auction for EUR 730 million in 2015 including EUR 400 million of debt, and United Group completed its acquisition in 2020 after agreeing the deal in 2019 (https://euobserver.com/88022/bulgarias-phone-company-from-state-to-private-monopoly; https://seenews.com/news/aig-closes-acquisiion-of-90-percent-of-bulgarian-telco-btc-for-2-8-bln-levs-904186; https://developingtelecoms.com/telecom-business/operator-news/6155-bulgarian-operator-vivacom-acquired-at-auction-for-730m.html; https://united.group/united-group-welcomes-vivacom-the-largest-telecom-operator-in-bulgaria/). (bears on: business and organizational context)

Acquired-customer handling. Vivacom’s customer-integration pages for Networx customers say service provision moves to Vivacom, existing prices and conditions continue during current contract terms, first Vivacom invoices would be issued after 8 March 2024, and support continues through current Networx numbers and acquired offices; this bears on customer anxiety after acquisitions (https://www.vivacom.bg/networx). (bears on: priority audiences & current state)

Regulatory context. The banked record shows a regulatory pattern: Vivacom is being treated both as a regulated infrastructure holder and as the main object of consolidation scrutiny. The banked record says CRC imposed access, non-discrimination, transparency, reference-offer and price-control duties on Vivacom for passive physical infrastructure; rivals objected to or appealed Vivacom-linked acquisitions; and the Supreme Administrative Court cleared United Group’s acquisition of Bulsatcom infrastructure assets as not notifiable under Bulgarian competition law (banked findings: CRC Decision No. 220 of 30 July 2024; A1 objection; Supreme Administrative Court Bulsatcom ruling).

Regulatory context. On 27 June 2025, the Commission on Protection of Competition, the Commission for Consumer Protection and CRC signed a cooperation agreement for consumer protection, market transparency and price-increase scrutiny before and after euro adoption. CRC said it had agreements with telecom undertakings on a working model. The consumer regulator said mobile-service prices would be included in the unified consumer portal, and that rules for consumer protection in electronic communications had already been revised with CRC. The competition authority said it was about to start a sector analysis of the telecommunications services market (https://crc.bg/en/news/1699/cpc-ccp-and-crc-join-forces-for-better-consumer-protection-and-market-transparency).

Regulatory context. Bulgaria’s amended Cybersecurity Act entered into force on 13 February 2026 and transposed NIS2, 16 months after the original deadline. Public electronic communications network providers are classed as essential entities. Regulated entities must give an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notice within 72 hours and a final report within one month. Essential-entity penalties can reach EUR 10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, with manager liability also introduced (https://www.schoenherr.eu/content/bulgaria-implements-nis-2-directive-key-changes-to-the-cybersecurity-act).

Regulatory context. The European Commission sent Bulgaria a reasoned opinion on 7 May 2025 for failing to notify full NIS2 transposition by the 17 October 2024 deadline. The Commission says NIS2 covers public electronic communications services and other critical sectors (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/nis2-directive-bulgaria; https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-calls-19-member-states-fully-transpose-nis2-directive).

Regulatory context. The AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024 and became applicable on 2 August 2026, with earlier rules for prohibited practices, AI literacy and general-purpose AI. From 2 August 2026, the AI Office and member-state authorities enforce the Act. High-risk systems in sensitive areas now apply from 2 December 2027, and high-risk systems embedded in regulated products apply from 2 August 2028 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai).

ESG context. The banked record shows a proof split: United Group has quantified group-level environmental proof, while Vivacom-specific certificates still need document proof. United Group reported 61% renewable electricity, a 52% Scope 1 and 2 cut against 2020, 25% refurbished customer premises equipment among installed devices, and e-waste and phone take-back figures; Vivacom’s ISO claims were not independently proved in the banked pass (banked findings: United Group 2024 sustainability results; Vivacom certification claim).

ESG context. United Group says its 2040 net-zero target was approved by the Science Based Targets initiative in February 2024. United Group says its near-term targets are a 90% absolute Scope 1 and 2 cut by 2030 from 2020 and a 40% Scope 3 cut by 2030 from 2022. United Group says its long-term target is a 90% Scope 3 cut by 2040 from 2022. The Science Based Targets initiative says targets in its dashboard are reviewed and validated by SBTi Services, but this pass did not extract the United Group row from the dashboard itself (https://united.group/united-groups-net-zero-target-gains-approval-from-the-science-based-targets-initiative-sbti/; https://sciencebasedtargets.org/target-dashboard).

ESG context. Vivacom says it follows United Group targets including 100% renewable electricity sourcing by 2027, zero waste to landfill by 2030, 40% women in managerial positions by 2030, average 40 learning hours per employee annually by 2030, annual Code of Responsible Business Conduct and Ethics training for 100% of employees, and five annual on-site supplier-standard audits through 2030. Independent public proof in this pass corroborated the climate target validation only, not the social and governance targets (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/ustojchivo-razvitie; https://united.group/sustainability-our-vision-esg-targets-progress/).

ESG context. United Group’s H1 2026 update says Vivacom ran the Bulgarian pilot of Job Lab with 120 students in Sofia, Varna, Veliko Tarnovo and Blagoevgrad. The same update says Vivacom completed the 16th Technical Academy with new artificial-intelligence and cybersecurity courses, held a Private 5G Hackathon, took 55 people into its Summer Internship Programme, and extended its partnership with the Association of Olympic Teams in Natural Sciences to 2028 with an extra EUR 30,000 donation (https://united.group/updates-from-united-groups-operations-h1-2026/).

Geopolitical context. The banked record shows a geopolitical ownership pattern: Vivacom is now part of an EU-focused regional group, but Bulgarian assets remain on sale watch. The banked record says United Group is Netherlands-based and majority owned by BC Partners; United Group completed the Vivacom acquisition after European Commission approval; United Group agreed to sell Serbian telecom and sports-rights assets for EUR 1.5 billion; and SeeNews reported in May 2026 that United Group was considering selling Bulgarian assets, including Vivacom’s fixed network and Nova Broadcasting Group (banked findings: United Group Vivacom acquisition; BC Partners acquisition statement; United Group Serbia sale; SeeNews Bulgarian asset-sale report).

Geopolitical context. Bulgaria adopted the euro on 1 January 2026 and became the 21st euro-area member. The fixed conversion rate is EUR 1 to BGN 1.95583. The European Central Bank says the euro area is Bulgaria’s main trading and financial partner and that Bulgaria had a high degree of euroisation before adoption (https://www.ecb.europa.eu/press/economic-bulletin/focus/2026/html/ecb.ebbox202508_01~b4379b735b.en.html; https://economy-finance.ec.europa.eu/euro/eu-countries-and-euro/bulgaria-and-euro_en).

Geopolitical context. ICLG says Bulgaria’s telecom and audiovisual distribution sectors are fully liberalised and generally open to foreign investment. ICLG says foreign direct investment screening can apply when an investment reaches at least 10% of capital, exceeds EUR 2 million, or concerns high-tech activity; the Screening Council may permit, condition or prohibit the investment (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).

Category context. The banked record shows a category pattern: growth, consolidation and concentration are moving together. The banked record reports market growth in fibre, 5G and TV; Vivacom share gains in bundled services, fixed internet, pay TV and satellite TV; Bulsatcom and TVN activity incorporated into Vivacom; and rival objections to acquisitions and market shares (banked findings: CRC 2024 market data; United Group July 2026 market growth statement; A1 objection; Bulsatcom incorporation findings).

Category context. ICLG says 62.4% of fixed internet subscribers in Bulgaria used fibre-optic access at the end of 2024. ICLG says Vivacom and A1 served 39.4% and 29.9% of fixed internet subscribers, respectively, while the rest of the market included many regional operators. ICLG says Bulgaria has strong infrastructure-based competition in broadband, and mobile shares sit in the 30% to 37% range across A1, Yettel and Vivacom (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).

Category context. Vivacom says it is an "иноватор" and says it invested close to BGN 3 billion in technology, innovation, people and the Bulgarian economy. Vivacom says more than 2 million clients use more than 5.5 million services. Independent sources in this pass corroborate Vivacom’s leading shares in fixed internet and pay TV, but did not verify the BGN 3 billion investment claim (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata; https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).

guided_interview.prompt: The provisional hypothesis is written to be tested. Read it with the confirms/overturns test beside it: is this the claim you want the research to test, and would the confirm/overturn actually settle it?
guided_interview.hypothesis: Vivacom's reputation problem is that its public story does not yet turn its strongest assets into one trusted national role. The open space is a clear story about useful Bulgarian digital infrastructure, grounded in fixed internet, television, coverage, satellite capacity, public-service duties, skills programmes and local digital projects. The claim must stay inside the evidence: Vivacom can credibly support leadership in fixed internet, pay TV, coverage and satellite growth, but it cannot claim total telecom leadership across every mobile, internet or customer-experience measure. A1, Yettel, CETIN and Neterra all carry credible network, quality, infrastructure or specialist claims, so Vivacom should not compete with another broad technology claim. It should prove the national outcomes that only its mix of incumbent infrastructure, United Group scale, EON, Bulsatcom, satellite assets, public-sector work and skills programmes can connect. (rests on: The white space)(rests on: Vivacom self-claim verdict)(rests on: The narratives running about it)(rests on: Category context)(rests on: Each peer's narrative)

hypothesis_test.confirms: The hypothesis holds if client data and stakeholder interviews show that decision-makers, employees, public-sector customers, and media accept Vivacom's infrastructure scale as useful national progress when it is tied to named outcomes rather than broad leadership language.
hypothesis_test.overturns: The hypothesis fails if audience research shows that Vivacom's scale mainly triggers former-incumbent, market-power, pricing, or service-friction associations that cannot be offset by fixed internet, television, satellite, public-sector, and skills proof.

guided_interview.prompt: The style note is the engine's read of how the client speaks about itself. Take each field in turn: does the observation match the client's own voice, and are the do/don't words the ones you would flag?

style_note.tone: Vivacom's own voice is direct, service-led, and confident. It often opens with the customer benefit, then supports it with network scale, product detail, or programme proof.
style_note.sentence_length: The client uses mostly short to medium sentences in public-facing copy, with longer sentences when it lists service features, coverage figures, or programme details.
style_note.vocabulary: The client's vocabulary centres on connectivity, customers, digital services, innovation, technology, coverage, speed, education, skills, entertainment, support, and Bulgaria's digital development.

The public record shows strong fixed internet and pay-TV positions, Bulsatcom integration, and United Group backing, but it does not give a current Vivacom-only revenue split by consumer, enterprise, public sector, mobile, broadband, television, and information and communications technology services; what internal split can we use to keep the strategy tied to the business model? (builds on: Its business model)

questions.question: The record shows positive proof in coverage, fixed internet, satellite, and employer signals, but customer reviews, outages, data-protection cases, consumer-law rulings, and competition concerns pull the other way; which risk line must the strategy address openly? (builds on: The sentiment of that coverage)

Vivacom's strongest defensible story is infrastructure scale, while that same scale feeds former-incumbent and market-power concern; how far can we lean into scale before it starts to hurt the desired perception? (builds on: The narratives running about it)

The peer map shows A1 and Yettel as national retail rivals, Neterra as an enterprise and infrastructure specialist, and CETIN as a wholesale network-infrastructure peer; which competitor set should the corporate platform be built to beat? (builds on: Three to five peers)

A1 can claim breadth and speed, Yettel can claim certified mobile quality and employer trust, Vivacom can claim fixed internet, pay TV, coverage, and satellite proof, and Neterra can claim specialist infrastructure; which leadership claims are worth making, and which should we avoid? (builds on: The white space)

A1 and Yettel have both challenged Vivacom-linked consolidation, while the Supreme Administrative Court cleared the Bulsatcom infrastructure-assets transaction; how should the corporate story handle market-power scrutiny without repeating competitor framing? (builds on: Competition clearance development)

guided_interview.prompt: Confirm what the work must say, must avoid and must prove. The proof ladder is ordered from strongest to weakest and no claim may outrun its evidence.

must_say: Show a genuine role in the country's digital progress.
Build one company story rather than disconnected activity claims.
must_avoid: Do not fall back into state-utility or former-monopoly framing.
Do not recycle shared category claims around technology leadership, environmental, social and governance performance, or employer branding as the central idea.
Do not use competitive price-war messaging as corporate positioning.
Do not introduce political framing.

do_not_say: Do not say Vivacom is the telecom leader without naming the metric.
Do not say Vivacom is the best mobile network when independent sources split speed, reliability, and coverage across operators.
Do not say Vivacom is an innovator unless the claim is tied to a named proof point.
Do not claim environmental, social and governance leadership without group-verified or Vivacom-specific proof.
Do not invent clients, revenue splits, market shares, campaign results, budget, timeline, or approval status.
Do not present prior agency ideas as approved positioning.
claim_rules: Separate client claims, parent-group claims, regulator data, third-party rankings, and strategic judgement.
Use the narrowest claim that the evidence supports.
Name the source and date for market share, ranking, and performance claims.
Treat hypotheses as hypotheses until audience research or client data tests them.
Keep legal, regulatory, pricing, competition, cyber, data, and environmental claims under review before client-facing use.
Do not turn a proof point from one segment into a claim about the whole company.

findings: What the company does. Vivacom is a Bulgarian telecommunications provider serving households, businesses, and institutions (https://amcham.bg/member/vivacom/).

What the company does. Vivacom offers mobile voice, fixed voice, mobile broadband, fixed broadband, interactive TV, satellite TV, Internet of Things, smart-city, digital education, and cloud services (https://amcham.bg/member/vivacom/).

What the company does. Vivacom says it provides telecommunications solutions for private and business clients, including mobile and fixed voice, high-speed optical internet, satellite TV, interactive TV, and tailored offers for corporate clients (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata).

What the company does. United Group describes Vivacom as a leading provider of mobile, fixed broadband, and television services in Bulgaria (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgaria-telecoms-market-expands/).

What the company does. United Group said in 2020 that Vivacom was the first telecommunications company in Bulgaria and supplied fibre broadband, mobile communications, and digital TV to private and commercial customers (https://united.group/united-group-welcomes-vivacom-the-largest-telecom-operator-in-bulgaria/).
What the company does. Vivacom says its own infrastructure includes mobile, fixed, terrestrial, copper, and satellite assets (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata).

What the company does. Vivacom says its 5G network covers 92% of Bulgaria’s population, its 4G LTE network covers 99.95%, and its 2G and 3G networks cover 99.99% (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata).
What the company does. Vivacom says its fixed network covers 1.6 million homes and includes the first and only 10 GIGA network in Bulgaria (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata).
What the company does. Vivacom says it has more than 200 own retail stores across Bulgaria (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata).

Its business model. Vivacom serves both private and business customers with mobile and fixed voice, high-speed fixed broadband, mobile broadband, interactive TV, satellite TV, Internet of Things, smart-city, digital education, and cloud services (https://amcham.bg/member/vivacom/).

Its business model. Vivacom’s revenue model is a telecom bundle model built around mobile, fixed broadband, fixed voice, pay TV, devices, business services, and public-sector solutions (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata; https://amcham.bg/member/vivacom/).

Its business model. United Group says Vivacom has backed the shift to IPTV through EON, a TV product developed by United Cloud, and that IPTV has passed one million households nationally (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgaria-telecoms-market-expands/).

Its business model. Netcracker says Vivacom uses Netcracker Revenue Management for billing, invoicing, and other revenue-related processes across postpaid mobile and fixed lines for B2C and B2B customers (https://www.netcracker.com/news/press-releases/netcracker-and-vivacom-extend-long-term-partnership-for-innovative-it-modernization-program).

Its business model. United Group completed the acquisition of Bulsatcom in February 2024, adding a direct-to-home satellite TV and broadband internet business in Bulgaria to the group’s Bulgarian perimeter (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/united-group-compretes-the-acquisition-of-bulsatcom).

Its performance. Vivacom says it has invested nearly BGN 3 billion in technology, innovation, human resources, and the Bulgarian economy; this pass found no independent source that restates the full BGN 3 billion figure (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata).

Its performance. Vivacom says more than 2 million customers use more than 5.5 million services from the company; this pass found no independent source that restates those exact customer and service counts (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata).

Its performance. CRC’s 2024 Annual Report says Vivacom held 37.1% of fixed Internet access retail revenue in 2024, up 8.3 percentage points from 2023 (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Its performance. CRC’s 2024 Annual Report notes that Bulsatcom EOOD was incorporated into Vivacom Bulgaria EAD as of 10 July 2024 (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Its performance. United Group said on 15 July 2026 that Bulgaria’s telecom market grew close to 5% in the prior year to EUR 2.16 billion and that market Internet revenue rose more than 9% to EUR 1.21 billion (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgaria-telecoms-market-expands/).

Its performance. United Group said on 15 July 2026 that Vivacom grew its mobile service-revenue share over the prior year (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgaria-telecoms-market-expands/).

Its performance. United Group said in 2020 that Vivacom had been Bulgaria’s largest domestic operator by revenue for the previous seven years (https://united.group/united-group-welcomes-vivacom-the-largest-telecom-operator-in-bulgaria/).
Its leadership. Vivacom’s management page names Asen Velikov as member of the management board and chief executive officer (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/ekip).

Its leadership. United Group’s leadership page says Asen Velikov is both chief executive officer and chief financial officer of Vivacom, joined the company in 1999, became chief financial officer in 2013, and has been a management-board member since 2014 (https://united.group/leadership/asen-velikov/).
Its leadership. Vivacom’s management page names Nikolay Gavrilov as management-board member and chief technical officer (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/ekip).

Its leadership. Vivacom’s management page names Stoyan Karanlakov as management-board member and chief commercial officer, with the role taken on 15 September 2021 (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/ekip).
Its leadership. Vivacom’s management page names Ognyan Toshmakov as management-board member and chief financial officer from 13 July 2026 (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/ekip).
Its leadership. Vivacom’s management page names Ivo Zlatev as management-board member and chief legal officer, in that role since 2017 (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/ekip).

Its leadership. SeeNews reported on 5 August 2025 that United Group appointed Asen Velikov as CEO, replacing Nikolai Andreev, who was dismissed (https://seenews.com/news/bulgarias-vivacom-names-ceo-1279653).

Its leadership. SeeNews reported that Stan Miller was named chair of Vivacom’s supervisory board, Spas Rusev and Stan Miller were appointed as new board members, and Nikolaos Statopoulos was re-elected for five years (https://seenews.com/news/bulgarias-vivacom-names-ceo-1279653).
Its ownership. Vivacom says it has been part of United Group since 2020 (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata).

Its ownership. United Group says it completed the acquisition of Vivacom on 31 July 2020 after European Commission approval in April 2020 and a signed agreement in November 2019 (https://united.group/united-group-welcomes-vivacom-the-largest-telecom-operator-in-bulgaria/).

Its ownership. Schoenherr says the 2020 United Group acquisition of Vivacom was valued at EUR 1.2 billion and was Bulgaria’s largest 2019 deal by value and asset size (https://schoenherr.eu/content/bulgaria-schoenherr-advises-united-group-on-eur-1-2-bln-acquisition-of-vivacom).

Its ownership. United Group says it is majority owned by BC Partners, and BC Partners says the group is majority owned by BC Partners (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/united-group-compretes-the-acquisition-of-bulsatcom; https://www.bcpartners.com/portfolio/united-group/).

Its ownership. Vivacom says it is the successor to BTC, the first telecommunications company in Bulgaria, and says BTC moved from a long state-owned period to privatization in 2004 (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata).

Its ownership. Private Equity International reported that Advent’s 2004 BTC agreement covered a EUR 230 million purchase price plus a EUR 50 million capital increase (https://www.privateequityinternational.com/advent-finally-wins-bulgarian-telco/).

Its ownership. A SeeNews telecom sector report says the 2004 privatization sale of a 65% BTC stake was formally completed in June 2004, with Vienna-registered Viva Ventures GmbH remitting EUR 280 million (https://cdn.seenews.com/reports/TELECOMMUNICATIONS_Telecommunications%20Sector%20-%20Bulgaria%20%282006%29.pdf).
Its ownership. The Bulgarian Industrial Association reported that NEF Telecom Bulgaria sold a 93.99% stake in Vivacom to Viva Telecom Bulgaria in 2012 (https://en.bia-bg.com/service/view/14419/).

Its ownership. Developing Telecoms reported that Vivacom was sold at auction in November 2015 for about EUR 730 million (https://developingtelecoms.com/telecom-business/operator-news/6155-bulgarian-operator-vivacom-acquired-at-auction-for-730m.html).

findings: Three to five peers. A1 Bulgaria is a direct peer for Vivacom across mobile, fixed broadband, TV, entertainment, business ICT and IoT. A1 was founded in 1994, acquired by Telekom Austria Group in 2005, and A1 Group says it is second-largest in mobile and fixed-line segments and overall number one in the market (https://a1.com/a1-group-and-markets/a1-in-bulgaria/).

Three to five peers. A1's predecessor Mobiltel was bought by Telekom Austria in a 2005 transaction valued at up to EUR 1.6 billion. A1 later bought STEMO, with SeeNews citing industry sources that put the price around BGN 50 million, equal to about EUR 25.6 million (https://www.novinite.com/articles/48248/Telekom%2BAustria%2BAcquires%2BBulgaria%27s%2BMobiltel; https://seenews.com/news/a1-bulgaria-closes-buy-of-local-stemo-in-boost-to-corporate-it-services-1214760).

Three to five peers. Yettel Bulgaria is a direct peer for Vivacom in mobile, fixed wireless broadband and TV. It started as Globul in 2001, was sold by OTE to Telenor in 2013 for EUR 717 million, was bought as part of Telenor's CEE assets by PPF in 2018 for EUR 2.8 billion, and is now owned by e& PPF Telecom Group (https://www.telekom.com/en/media/media-information/archive/greece-ote-agrees-to-sell-globul-for-717-million-to-telenor-358962; https://en.yettel.hu/press/press-release/ppf-group-completes-acquisiton; https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/yettel-bulgaria).

Three to five peers. Yettel's current parent was formed after e& bought control of PPF Telecom assets outside Czechia, with the announced consideration at EUR 2.15 billion plus a possible earn-out of up to EUR 350 million. The European Commission conditionally approved the acquisition under the Foreign Subsidies Regulation on 24 September 2024 (https://en.yettel.hu/press/press-release/ppf-group-press-release-ppf-closes-a-major-transaction-and-forms-a-partnership-with-e-a-global-technology-group; https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/api/files/document/print/en/ip_24_4842/IP_24_4842_EN.pdf).

Three to five peers. Neterra is a narrower peer for Vivacom's enterprise, wholesale, satellite, cloud, data-center and managed-service audiences. Neterra was founded in 1996 in Sofia, owns and operates four data centers and a global network of over 220 points of presence, according to SeeNews (https://seenews.com/news/bulgarias-neterra-invests-12-mln-euro-in-data-network-upgrade-1289377).

Three to five peers. Neterra's own history says it built the first Bulgarian alternative connection to Turkey, created a Frankfurt point of presence, launched a large DWDM optical network in Bulgaria and operates Neterra.TV for Bulgarians abroad. CRC data places Neterra among the leading leased-line undertakings, which makes it a real B2B choice even if it is not a national mass-market mobile operator (https://neterra.net/about-us; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

How each peer positions and communicates. A1 positions as a full-service market leader. Its own description covers communications, payment, entertainment, mobile, fixed, broadband, satellite TV, its interactive TV platform, MAX Sport, financial services, ICT, cloud and IoT (https://newsroom.a1.com/news-a1-group-deeply-unsettled-by-an-unexpected-decision-of-the-bulgarian-commission-on-protection-of-competition?id=182022&l=english&menueid=14594).

How each peer positions and communicates. A1 communicates by splitting channels by role. In Q1 2026, Pikasa found A1 used Facebook for sports and occasions, LinkedIn for 5G projects, network awards and its internal academy, and YouTube for self-service tutorials (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war).

How each peer positions and communicates. Yettel positions around certified network quality and customer trust. Its owner says Yettel's network reaches over 99% of the population and has nine umlaut Best in Test certificates; SeeNews reports one such certificate at 926 points out of 1,000, first in reliability, coverage, voice and latency (https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/yettel-bulgaria; https://seenews.com/news/seventh-consecutive-best-in-test-certificate-outlines-yettels-network-as-the-best-1254822).

How each peer positions and communicates. Yettel communicates through employer, sustainability and original content themes. Pikasa found its strongest platform was LinkedIn, supported by CEO transition announcements, Top Employer certification and intern programme content (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war).

How each peer positions and communicates. Neterra positions as an enterprise and carrier-grade connectivity provider. Its homepage sells Enterprise Internet with 99.99% uptime, seven-day rapid deployment and 24/7 expert support, while its services list covers business internet, backup internet, Starlink satellite internet, dedicated internet, NetIX, colocation, cloud, DDoS protection and audio-video services (https://neterra.net/).

How each peer positions and communicates. Neterra communicates through infrastructure proof and customer quotes. Its site cites over 75 countries of network presence, European industry memberships, awards, data centers, NetIX traffic records and testimonials from the National Palace of Culture, WebIT foundation and Unimasters Logistic (https://neterra.net/about-us; https://neterra.net/).

Each peer's narrative. A1's narrative is breadth plus market scale: mobile, fixed, TV, sport, payment, ICT, cloud and IoT under one provider. A1 calls itself "overall, the number one in the market"; CRC corroborates A1 as the largest mobile voice operator by subscribers, but CRC shows Vivacom leading fixed internet and pay-TV, so the self-claim is segment-dependent (https://a1.com/a1-group-and-markets/a1-in-bulgaria/; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Each peer's narrative. A1 also runs a challenger-regulator narrative against Vivacom concentration. It says Vivacom acquisitions could create a dominant TV and broadband player, and CRC later shows Vivacom's 2024 pay-TV share near 60% after Bulsatcom and TVN Distribution Bulgaria were incorporated (https://newsroom.a1.com/news-a1-group-deeply-unsettled-by-an-unexpected-decision-of-the-bulgarian-commission-on-protection-of-competition?id=182022&l=english&menueid=14594; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Each peer's narrative. Yettel's narrative is mobile quality, reliability and employer credibility. Yettel calls itself the "largest mobile telecommunications provider in Bulgaria by revenue"; CRC corroborates that Yettel held the highest 2024 retail mobile voice revenue share at 40.9% (https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/yettel-bulgaria; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Each peer's narrative. Yettel also publishes a human-use narrative around accessibility, digital literacy, volunteering, sustainability content and original YouTube series. Pikasa says this gave Yettel the most genuinely varied media coverage among the three national operators in Q1 2026 (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war).

Each peer's narrative. Neterra's narrative is business-grade infrastructure rather than mass consumer telecom. It says its mission is to empower customers everywhere through information technology and customer care, and CRC corroborates its business-network role through a 10.4% share of retail leased lines by line count and a 33.7% share of wholesale leased-line revenue in 2024 (https://neterra.net/about-us; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

What each peer publishes to be known for. A1 publishes to be known for full-service breadth and market leadership. It lists mobile and fixed services, broadband, satellite TV, interactive TV, MAX Sport, financial services, ICT, cloud and IoT, and A1 Group reports EUR 821 million revenue for Bulgaria in 2024 (https://newsroom.a1.com/news-a1-group-deeply-unsettled-by-an-unexpected-decision-of-the-bulgarian-commission-on-protection-of-competition?id=182022&l=english&menueid=14594; https://a1.com/a1-group-and-markets/a1-in-bulgaria/).

What each peer publishes to be known for. A1 publishes to be known for ICT leadership after the STEMO deal. A1 said STEMO would help it become the ICT market leader in Bulgaria, and SeeNews reports the acquisition was completed in August 2022 after competition approval (https://newsroom.a1.com/news-a1-telekom-austria-group-announces-100-acquisition-of-stemo-a-bulgarian-ict-company?id=158471&l=english&menueid=14594; https://seenews.com/news/a1-bulgaria-closes-buy-of-local-stemo-in-boost-to-corporate-it-services-1214760).

What each peer publishes to be known for. Yettel publishes to be known for certified network quality. It cites nine Best in Test certificates from umlaut, and SeeNews reports Yettel scored 926 out of 1,000 in one 2024 umlaut test across Bulgaria (https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/yettel-bulgaria; https://seenews.com/news/seventh-consecutive-best-in-test-certificate-outlines-yettels-network-as-the-best-1254822).

What each peer publishes to be known for. Yettel publishes to be known as an employer and social-impact operator. Its owner says it is the first and only Bulgarian telecom certified as a Top Employer, and Pikasa reports Yettel coverage around tactile strips, digital literacy reaching 60,000 children, volunteering culture, Super People and sustainability content (https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/yettel-bulgaria; https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war).

What each peer publishes to be known for. Neterra publishes to be known for global connectivity, business internet, cloud, colocation, DDoS protection, satellite and NetIX. Its site says it has a network in over 75 countries, and SeeNews reports a EUR 12 million optical data network upgrade in 2026 using Infinera equipment from Nokia (https://neterra.net/about-us; https://seenews.com/news/bulgarias-neterra-invests-12-mln-euro-in-data-network-upgrade-1289377).

What each peer publishes to be known for. Neterra publishes to be known for awards and critical infrastructure. Its history lists Best CEE Connectivity Provider awards, NetIX traffic above 4 Tbps, a second Sofia data-center building and DDoS protection for the Bulgarian Presidency of the EU Council (https://neterra.net/about-us).

Each peer's share of voice. A1 had the largest social voice in Pikasa's Q1 2026 telecom dataset: 277 posts, 48,682 total engagements and 176 average engagements per post. A1 had 137 press articles in the same dataset (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war).

Each peer's share of voice. A1's business voice is large. A1 Group reports 2024 Bulgaria revenue of EUR 821 million, EBITDA of EUR 341 million and CAPEX of EUR 121 million (https://a1.com/a1-group-and-markets/a1-in-bulgaria/).

Each peer's share of voice. Yettel had the smallest social footprint in Pikasa's Q1 2026 dataset: 115 posts, 4,870 total engagements and 42 average engagements per post. Yettel had 157 press articles and the most genuine media coverage of the three operators in that analysis (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war).

Each peer's share of voice. Yettel's business voice is smaller than A1 but strong in mobile. It reports 2025 revenue of EUR 557 million, EBITDA of EUR 162 million, 3.208 million mobile subscribers, 141,000 fixed broadband subscribers and 104,000 pay-TV subscribers (https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/yettel-bulgaria).

Each peer's share of voice. Neterra's voice is strongest in enterprise connectivity measures rather than mass media. CRC reports Neterra held 10.4% of retail leased lines by line count, 8.4% of retail leased-line revenue, 25.9% of wholesale leased lines by line count and 33.7% of wholesale leased-line revenue in 2024 (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

The white space. The main national operators converge on network, technology, entertainment, ESG and employer claims. The supplied brief already flags that sameness, and the public record supports it through A1's market-scale and service-breadth claims, Yettel's certified network-quality claims and Vivacom's fibre, 5G and TV growth frame (SOURCE DOCUMENT: sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md; https://a1.com/a1-group-and-markets/a1-in-bulgaria/; https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/yettel-bulgaria; https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/).

The white space. A less occupied space is a national digital-infrastructure story that connects scale to people's daily and economic progress, not only to network claims. Vivacom has the assets for that story, but Pikasa's Q1 2026 analysis says much of its press volume was PR-led announcements with weak audience response (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war; SOURCE DOCUMENT: sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md).

The white space. Another open space is useful public service content. Pikasa says Yettel earned more varied coverage from tactile strips, digital literacy reaching 60,000 children, volunteering culture and entertainment stories, while A1 and Vivacom were more often present through sponsorship, product or announcement material (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war).

The white space. A B2B white space sits between mass telecom and specialist infrastructure. A1 owns ICT breadth through STEMO, Neterra owns enterprise-network credibility, and Vivacom can credibly connect national network scale with smart cities, cybersecurity, education, EON and fibre if it proves the role through named projects (https://newsroom.a1.com/news-a1-telekom-austria-group-announces-100-acquisition-of-stemo-a-bulgarian-ict-company?id=158471&l=english&menueid=14594; https://neterra.net/about-us; https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/).

Vivacom origin. Vivacom was Bulgarian Telecommunications Company before the entity was renamed Vivacom Bulgaria EAD after 30 years using the BTC name. Its roots are the former state fixed-line operator, and this history explains why former-monopoly framing is a live positioning risk (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivacom; SOURCE DOCUMENT: sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md). (bears on: Business problem / organizational objective)

Vivacom privatization. Viva Ventures, linked to Advent International, bought 65% of BTC in 2004 for EUR 230 million and paid another EUR 50 million for a mobile licence. A separate company profile gives the 65% sale price as EUR 275.356 million, so the precise privatization figure should be checked before client use (https://euobserver.com/88022/bulgarias-phone-company-from-state-to-private-monopoly; https://seenews.com/companies/profile/vivacom-bulgaria-ead-formerly-known-as-bulgarian-telecommunications-company-ead-4525). (bears on: Business problem / organizational objective)

Vivacom current ownership. United Group agreed in 2019 to acquire Vivacom, and the 2020 closing was reported as a EUR 1.2 billion acquisition of Bulgarian Telecommunications Company EAD. United Group says Vivacom has been part of United Group since 2020 (https://www.bcpartners.com/news/bc-partners-owned-united-group-acquires-vivacom/; https://ceelegalmatters.com/bulgaria/14224-united-group-s-acquisition-of-vivacom-closes; https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/). (bears on: Business problem / organizational objective)

Vivacom self-claim verdict. Vivacom's parent presents it as a leading provider of mobile, fixed broadband and television services in Bulgaria. CRC data corroborates leadership in fixed internet subscribers at 39.4% in 2024 and pay-TV subscribers at almost 60%, but not mobile subscriber leadership, where A1 held 36.5% in 2024 (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf). (bears on: Reputation problem / desired perception)

Vivacom growth frame. Vivacom's parent frames the growth story around fibre, 5G and television, and says Bulgaria's market grew close to 5% last year to EUR 2.16 billion. CRC's 2024 report corroborates the same growth areas: fixed internet subscribers rose to 2.643 million, IPTV reached 47.8% of pay-TV subscribers, and Vivacom's fixed internet share rose by 7.2 percentage points (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf). (bears on: Reputation problem / desired perception)

Competition constraint. A1 publicly argued in July 2023 that Vivacom's acquisitions could give it over 60% of TV distribution and nearly 40% of internet. CRC later reported Vivacom at almost 60% of pay-TV subscribers and 37.1% of fixed internet retail revenue in 2024 after Bulsatcom and TVN Distribution Bulgaria were incorporated into Vivacom (https://newsroom.a1.com/news-a1-group-deeply-unsettled-by-an-unexpected-decision-of-the-bulgarian-commission-on-protection-of-competition?id=182022&l=english&menueid=14594; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf). Three to five peers. A fourth direct peer is CETIN Bulgaria for Vivacom's public-sector, wholesale and network-infrastructure audiences. CETIN Bulgaria was established in July 2020 by separating telecom infrastructure from Telenor Bulgaria. It provides mobile network services for Yettel Bulgaria. Its parent reports 2025 revenue of EUR 170 million, EBITDA of EUR 123 million and CAPEX of EUR 76 million. It won rural digital network contracts alongside A1 and Vivacom under Bulgaria's 2025 BGN 433.6 million programme (https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/cetin-bulgaria; https://seenews.com/news/bulgaria-signs-222-mln-euro-digital-network-deals-with-a1-vivacom-cetin-1276695).

Three to five peers. The competitive set now reads as four practical choices by audience: A1 and Yettel for national consumer and business telecom, Neterra for enterprise, carrier, cloud and data-center buyers, and CETIN for wholesale and public-infrastructure buyers. This pattern is derived from the banked A1, Yettel and Neterra peer findings plus the CETIN findings in this pass (banked findings; https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/cetin-bulgaria).

CETIN International's own heading says, "We drive digital transformation by providing cutting-edge communication infrastructure solutions". Its profile says it serves anchor tenants and other telecom providers. Its Bulgaria page says it provides mobile network services for Yettel. The 2025 government-contract reports corroborate CETIN's infrastructure role by naming it with A1 and Vivacom as an implementation partner, but they do not test the quality claim (https://www.cetin.international/what-we-do/profile; https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/cetin-bulgaria; https://seenews.com/news/bulgaria-signs-222-mln-euro-digital-network-deals-with-a1-vivacom-cetin-1276695).

That challenges any single operator's unqualified network-leadership wording and pushes claims into narrower language (https://insights.opensignal.com/reports/2026/01/bulgaria/mobile-network-experience).

This pattern is derived from banked findings: A1 2005 acquisition; Yettel OTE-to-Telenor-to-PPF-to-e& PPF chain; Vivacom United Group acquisition; Neterra founded in Sofia and expanded through network build-out (banked findings).

The white space. The banked findings create a claim-tiering white space. A1 can claim breadth and speed; Yettel can claim certified mobile quality and employer trust; Vivacom can claim fixed internet, pay-TV and coverage; Neterra can claim specialist enterprise infrastructure. No player can safely own total leadership without qualifiers. This pattern is derived from the banked A1, Yettel, Vivacom and Neterra share and narrative findings plus Opensignal 2026 (banked findings; https://insights.opensignal.com/reports/2026/01/bulgaria/mobile-network-experience).

Bulgaria's Supreme Administrative Court issued a final ruling in February 2026 clearing United Group's acquisition of Bulsatcom telecom-infrastructure assets after appeals by A1, Yettel and CETIN. This changes the constraint from unresolved approval risk to a live concentration narrative that competitors can still use publicly (https://seenews.com/news/bulgarias-supreme-court-clears-united-groups-acquisition-of-bulsatcom-1290035). This supports the brief's pressure to grow through value and enterprise services, not only consumer volume (https://www.mordorintelligence.com/industry-reports/bulgaria-telecom-mno-market). The white space. The open space is not "best network" as a broad claim. SpeedGeo reports Vivacom as fastest fixed broadband in Bulgaria from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026, with 117 Mb/s average download, 85.2 Mb/s upload and 25 ms ping. The same source reports A1 as fastest mobile internet, with 190.7 Mb/s average download. This splits performance proof by service type (https://www.speedgeo.net/statistics/bulgaria).

The white space. A national-infrastructure story must avoid sounding like every peer's proof claim. The banked record shows A1 claiming breadth and speed, Yettel claiming certified quality and trust, Neterra claiming specialist infrastructure, and CETIN claiming wholesale infrastructure. The open space is the human and economic result of the infrastructure, with named local proof (banked findings: A1 narrative; Yettel narrative; Neterra narrative; CETIN narrative; Opensignal 2026 finding).

The white space. The ICLG 2026 Bulgaria chapter says fixed internet has strong infrastructure-based competition and many regional operators outside Vivacom and A1. This leaves room for a local-outcome story by town, school, enterprise or public service, because national share alone does not explain the regional customer experience (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).

Customer complaint pressure. Bulgaria's Ombudsman reported 525 complaints about telephone, internet and television services in 2024. Vivacom had 187 complaints, Yettel had 164, A1 had 158, and others had 16. The main complaint themes were monthly-fee indexation, unwanted service additions, payment for unused services and service quality. This makes customer fairness a shared category risk, not only a Vivacom issue (https://www.ombudsman.bg/storage/pub/files/20250527115030_ANNUAL%20REPORT%20OMBUDSMAN%202024%20SUMMARY%20EN.pdf). (bears on: Reputation problem / desired perception)

It also lists the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, Digital Services Act, Digital Markets Act, Cybersecurity Act, NIS2 and critical-entity resilience rules among laws affecting telecoms and media providers. This supports tight legal review for market, data, cyber and platform claims (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).
