findings: Regulatory context. Bulgaria’s telecom sector is governed by EU rules including the European Electronic Communications Code, ePrivacy Directive, Net Neutrality Regulation, Roaming Regulation, Gigabit Infrastructure Act and EU termination-rate rules; Bulgarian core laws include the Electronic Communications Act and Electronic Communications Networks and Physical Infrastructure Act (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).

Regulatory context. Telecom and adjacent digital activity in Bulgaria is also affected by the General Data Protection Regulation, Digital Services Act, Digital Markets Act, Cybersecurity Act, Artificial Intelligence Act, NIS2 Directive and Critical Entity Resilience Directive; this confirms the supplied brief’s legal and AI-policy constraints (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).

Regulatory context. The Communications Regulation Commission is the independent telecom regulator; the Ministry of Transport and Communications and Ministry of e-Government set ICT, digital administration and cybersecurity policy; the National Radio Frequency Spectrum Council handles national spectrum-planning proposals (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).

Regulatory context. CRC Decision No. 220 of 30 July 2024 found no effective competition in wholesale access to passive physical infrastructure, named Vivacom as having significant individual impact, and imposed access, non-discrimination, transparency, reference-offer and price-control duties (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Regulatory context. CRC launched a fourth-round analysis of local access at a fixed location, and by Decision No. 251 of 29 August 2025 ordered extra information on fixed access via mobile network for 2021-2023; this keeps fixed access and 5G-based home internet inside active review (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Regulatory context. CRC says Vivacom met all universal-service quality target values in 2024, did not request unfair-burden compensation by the 30 June 2024 statutory deadline, and had a 46% drop in universal-service complaints versus the prior period (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Regulatory context. CRC says 2024 universal-service complaints to Vivacom were mainly technical failures at 27% of complaints; termination complaints rose to 16% from 2% in 2023, and the other category rose 18 percentage points to 29% (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Regulatory context. CMS says CRC awarded 20-year 3.6 GHz licences to A1, Vivacom and Yettel in April 2021, and assigned 700 MHz and 800 MHz bands to the same three operators in December 2023 for 15 years; CMS says total licence payments were about BGN 13.4 million (https://cms.law/en/int/expert-guides/cms-expert-guide-to-5g-regulation-and-law/bulgaria).

Regulatory context. Bulgaria’s Supreme Administrative Court issued a final ruling in February 2026 clearing United Group’s acquisition of Bulsatcom telecom infrastructure assets after appeals by A1 Bulgaria, Yettel Bulgaria and Cetin Bulgaria; the court said the deal and base-station infrastructure asset deal were not a notifiable concentration under Bulgarian competition law (https://seenews.com/news/bulgarias-supreme-court-clears-united-groups-acquisition-of-bulsatcom-1290035).

Regulatory context. A1 Group publicly objected in July 2023 to CPC approval of Vivacom acquisitions of Networx-Bulgaria and six smaller operators, saying the deals could give Vivacom more than 60% of TV distribution and nearly 40% of internet; CRC’s 2024 market data later reported Vivacom at 59.6% of pay-TV subscribers and 39.4% of fixed internet subscribers (https://newsroom.a1.com/news-a1-group-deeply-unsettled-by-an-unexpected-decision-of-the-bulgarian-commission-on-protection-of-competition?id=182022&l=english&menueid=14594; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

ESG context. United Group says its 2024 sustainability results included 61% electricity from renewable sources, a 52% cut in Scope 1 and 2 emissions against its 2020 baseline, a 13% improvement in its Network Efficiency Index, 25% refurbished customer premises equipment among installed devices, more than 2,300 kg of e-waste recovered, and more than 1,500 smartphones recovered through customer take-back programs (https://united.group/united-group-releases-2024-sustainability-report-highlighting-tangible-progress-across-esg-priorities/).

ESG context. United Group says it is building three solar plants and one wind farm in Bulgaria; by 2027 these assets are planned to supply 160% of electricity needed for the Group’s Bulgarian operations, cover 65% of total Group electricity use, remove about 120,000 tonnes of CO2 from Bulgaria’s grid each year, reach 124 MW combined capacity, and produce 310,000 MWh a year (https://united.group/united-group-enters-renewable-energy-production/).

ESG context. A Vivacom careers page says United Group Energy develops renewable power plants to supply United Group telecom and media operations with 100% green electricity, and says Bulgaria has more than 120 MW of renewable projects under development, construction and operation (https://www.vivacom.bg/bg/residential/za-nas/karieri/obiavi-za-rabota/31166/senior-electrical-engineer-high-voltage-substations-sofia).

ESG context. Vivacom says its management system is certified to ISO 9001:2015, ISO 14001:2015, ISO 45001:2018, ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, and ISO/IEC 27018:2019; I did not find an independent certificate register for each standard in this pass, so this is a client claim awaiting document proof (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata).

Geopolitical context. United Group is Netherlands-based and majority owned by BC Partners; it completed Vivacom’s acquisition on 31 July 2020 after European Commission approval in April 2020 and a November 2019 agreement (https://united.group/united-group-welcomes-vivacom-the-largest-telecom-operator-in-bulgaria/).

Geopolitical context. BC Partners said Vivacom had over 1.8 million unique customers at the time of the 2019 acquisition agreement, and described the deal as part of United Group’s expansion from six Southeast European countries (https://www.bcpartners.com/news/bc-partners-owned-united-group-acquires-vivacom/).

Geopolitical context. United Group agreed in February 2025 to sell SBB Serbia to e& PPF Telecom and to sell NetTV Plus and Western Balkan sports rights to Telekom Srbija; the announced combined enterprise value was EUR 1.5 billion, and United Group said the move completed its aim of exiting non-EU telecom assets (https://united.group/united-group-agrees-to-sell-sbb-serbia-as-well-as-net-tv-plus-business-and-its-sports-broadcasting-rights-for-western-balkans/).

Geopolitical context. A May 2026 SeeNews report said United Group was considering selling some or all Bulgarian assets, including Vivacom’s fixed network and Nova Broadcasting Group; the article says the process was early and based on local media reporting, so this is a live ownership-watch item, not a completed event (https://seenews.com/news/see-focused-united-group-mulls-selling-bulgarian-assets-report-1294890).

Geopolitical context. Bulgaria, Kosovo and North Macedonia signed 5G security declarations with the United States on 23 October 2020 under the Clean Network initiative; RFE/RL reported the initiative was aimed at limiting equipment from companies such as Huawei in telecom networks (https://www.rferl.org/a/bulgaria-kosovo-north-macedonia-join-us-initiative-to-block-chinese-equipment-in-5g-network/30909512.html).

Geopolitical context. CRC reported that A1, Vivacom and Yettel provided annual reports in 2024 on their Multivendor Strategy; this makes supplier mix and network security a regulator-visible issue for Vivacom (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Category context. Bulgaria’s electronic communications market reached EUR 2.06 billion in 2024, up 5.7% on 2023, according to the ICLG Bulgaria telecoms chapter citing CRC data (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).

Category context. United Group said in July 2026 that Bulgaria’s telecom market grew close to 5% last year to EUR 2.16 billion, and said the growth came in fibre, 5G and television (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/).

Category context. CRC reported bundled-service revenue of BGN 2.064 billion in 2024, up 10.6% year on year; A1, Vivacom and Yettel accounted for 97.8% of bundled-service revenue and 98.3% of bundled-service subscribers (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Category context. Vivacom’s bundled-service subscriber share rose from 30.7% in 2023 to 32.9% in 2024, and its bundled-service revenue share rose from 27.6% to 30.2%; CRC says Bulsatcom was deleted from the CRC register and its activity was reported by Vivacom (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Category context. CRC reported retail fixed internet and data-transfer revenue of BGN 1.879791 billion in 2024; Vivacom led retail fixed internet access with 39.4% of subscribers and 37.1% of revenue, up 7.2 and 8.3 percentage points year on year (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Category context. CRC reported 2.02 million pay-TV subscribers at the end of 2024; Vivacom led pay TV with 59.6% of subscribers and 56.5% of revenue after the incorporation of Bulsatcom and TVN Distribution Bulgaria (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Category context. CRC reported IPTV subscribers grew 9.4% in 2024 and IPTV reached 47.8% of pay-TV subscribers; Vivacom, A1 and Yettel together made up 95.0% of IPTV subscribers (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Category context. CRC reported satellite TV subscribers fell 8.4% in 2024; after Bulsatcom was incorporated into Vivacom, Vivacom’s satellite-TV subscriber share exceeded 80.0% by the end of 2024 (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).

Self-claim verdict: 5G coverage. Vivacom says it has the "5G мрежата с най-голямо покритие в България" and that its 5G covers 92% of Bulgaria’s population; CMS confirms Vivacom has extensive 5G coverage but does not rank it first, so the ranking claim needs proof before use (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata; https://cms.law/en/int/expert-guides/cms-expert-guide-to-5g-regulation-and-law/bulgaria). (bears on: reputation problem / desired perception)

Self-claim verdict: fibre speed. Vivacom says it has the fastest fixed fibre network for home internet in Bulgaria as of 23 May 2025 based on CRC’s tariff comparison tool; nPerf’s public awards page confirms a 2024 Bulgaria fixed-line performance award page exists, but the page opened in this pass did not expose the winner text, so the claim needs the CRC comparison record or nPerf report before it is used as a fact (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata; https://www.nperf.com/en/awards/bg/2024/broadband/bulgaria). (bears on: reputation problem / desired perception)

Platform dependency. United Group selected Eutelsat as the single future satellite operator for its next Direct To Home platform; the move covers Telemach, NOVA, Bulsatcom, VIVACOM, SBB and Total TV across eight countries and is expected to finish by the end of 2025 (https://united.group/united-group-and-eutelsat-develop-next-gen-dth-platform/). (bears on: programme, narrative and channels)

Ownership history. Vivacom’s ownership history is a reputation asset and a risk: Viva Ventures bought 65% of BTC for EUR 230 million in 2004, AIG bought 90% of BTC for 2.8 billion levs in 2007, Spas Roussev bought Vivacom at auction for EUR 730 million in 2015 including EUR 400 million of debt, and United Group completed its acquisition in 2020 after agreeing the deal in 2019 (https://euobserver.com/88022/bulgarias-phone-company-from-state-to-private-monopoly; https://seenews.com/news/aig-closes-acquisiion-of-90-percent-of-bulgarian-telco-btc-for-2-8-bln-levs-904186; https://developingtelecoms.com/telecom-business/operator-news/6155-bulgarian-operator-vivacom-acquired-at-auction-for-730m.html; https://united.group/united-group-welcomes-vivacom-the-largest-telecom-operator-in-bulgaria/). (bears on: business and organizational context)

Acquired-customer handling. Vivacom’s customer-integration pages for Networx customers say service provision moves to Vivacom, existing prices and conditions continue during current contract terms, first Vivacom invoices would be issued after 8 March 2024, and support continues through current Networx numbers and acquired offices; this bears on customer anxiety after acquisitions (https://www.vivacom.bg/networx). (bears on: priority audiences & current state)

Regulatory context. The banked record shows a regulatory pattern: Vivacom is being treated both as a regulated infrastructure holder and as the main object of consolidation scrutiny. The banked record says CRC imposed access, non-discrimination, transparency, reference-offer and price-control duties on Vivacom for passive physical infrastructure; rivals objected to or appealed Vivacom-linked acquisitions; and the Supreme Administrative Court cleared United Group’s acquisition of Bulsatcom infrastructure assets as not notifiable under Bulgarian competition law (banked findings: CRC Decision No. 220 of 30 July 2024; A1 objection; Supreme Administrative Court Bulsatcom ruling).

Regulatory context. On 27 June 2025, the Commission on Protection of Competition, the Commission for Consumer Protection and CRC signed a cooperation agreement for consumer protection, market transparency and price-increase scrutiny before and after euro adoption. CRC said it had agreements with telecom undertakings on a working model. The consumer regulator said mobile-service prices would be included in the unified consumer portal, and that rules for consumer protection in electronic communications had already been revised with CRC. The competition authority said it was about to start a sector analysis of the telecommunications services market (https://crc.bg/en/news/1699/cpc-ccp-and-crc-join-forces-for-better-consumer-protection-and-market-transparency).

Regulatory context. Bulgaria’s amended Cybersecurity Act entered into force on 13 February 2026 and transposed NIS2, 16 months after the original deadline. Public electronic communications network providers are classed as essential entities. Regulated entities must give an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notice within 72 hours and a final report within one month. Essential-entity penalties can reach EUR 10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, with manager liability also introduced (https://www.schoenherr.eu/content/bulgaria-implements-nis-2-directive-key-changes-to-the-cybersecurity-act).

Regulatory context. The European Commission sent Bulgaria a reasoned opinion on 7 May 2025 for failing to notify full NIS2 transposition by the 17 October 2024 deadline. The Commission says NIS2 covers public electronic communications services and other critical sectors (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/nis2-directive-bulgaria; https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-calls-19-member-states-fully-transpose-nis2-directive).

Regulatory context. The AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024 and became applicable on 2 August 2026, with earlier rules for prohibited practices, AI literacy and general-purpose AI. From 2 August 2026, the AI Office and member-state authorities enforce the Act. High-risk systems in sensitive areas now apply from 2 December 2027, and high-risk systems embedded in regulated products apply from 2 August 2028 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai).

ESG context. The banked record shows a proof split: United Group has quantified group-level environmental proof, while Vivacom-specific certificates still need document proof. The Stara Zagora ground station has 18 antennas and a mini data centre linking low-Earth-orbit satellites to optical networks and data centres in Bulgaria and Europe (https://united.group/vivacom-and-eutelsat-group-are-launching-in-bulgaria-the-fourth-european-ground-station/). (bears on: programme, narrative and channels)

Satellite business standing. World Teleport Association’s 2024 rankings put Vivacom in the Independent Top 10 and in the Fast 10 for teleport operators; this independently supports the satellite-services part of Vivacom’s broader business story (https://www.worldteleport.org/?page=TopOperators; https://www.worldteleport.org/news/692727/World-Teleport-Association-Publishes-Top-Operator-Rankings-for-2024.htm). (bears on: business and organizational context)

Parent-group trading context. United Group reported Q1 2026 revenue of EUR 717.7 million, up 14% year on year, and adjusted EBITDA after leases of EUR 232.5 million, up 13%; it said growth came from subscriber growth, price increases, customer up-selling and ICT projects (https://united.group/united-group-b-v-delivers-double-digit-revenue-and-earnings-growth-in-q1-2026/). (bears on: business and organizational context)

Parent-group financing context. United Group completed a EUR 1.5 billion refinancing in January 2026, including more than EUR 1.1 billion of senior secured floating-rate notes and EUR 355 million of holding-company payment-in-kind notes, with proceeds used to refinance existing debt (https://www.paulweiss.com/insights/client-news/united-group-completes-refinancing). (bears on: business and organizational context)

final_pre_engagement_pack_content.hypothesis: Vivacom's reputation problem is that its public story does not yet turn its strongest assets into one trusted national role. The open space is a clear story about useful Bulgarian digital infrastructure, grounded in fixed internet, television, coverage, satellite capacity, public-service duties, skills programmes and local digital projects. The claim must stay inside the evidence: Vivacom can credibly support leadership in fixed internet, pay TV, coverage and satellite growth, but it cannot claim total telecom leadership across every mobile, internet or customer-experience measure. A1, Yettel, CETIN and Neterra all carry credible network, quality, infrastructure or specialist claims, so Vivacom should not compete with another broad technology claim. It should make defusing the market-power / former-incumbent read an explicit workstream, proving the national outcomes that only its mix of incumbent infrastructure, United Group scale, EON, Bulsatcom, satellite assets, public-sector work and skills programmes can connect. (rests on: The white space)(rests on: Vivacom self-claim verdict)(rests on: The narratives running about it)(rests on: Category context)(rests on: Each peer's narrative)

hypothesis_test.confirms: The hypothesis holds if client data and stakeholder interviews show that decision-makers, employees, public-sector customers, and media accept Vivacom's infrastructure scale as useful national progress when it is tied to named outcomes rather than broad leadership language.
hypothesis_test.overturns: The hypothesis fails if audience research shows that Vivacom's scale mainly triggers former-incumbent, market-power, pricing, or service-friction associations that cannot be offset by fixed internet, television, satellite, public-sector, and skills proof.

style_note.tone: Vivacom's own voice is direct, service-led, confident, warmer, benefit-first, and anchored in first-person plural as the spine. It should avoid a cold formal-scale register, because that reinforces the incumbent perception the work is trying to shift.
style_note.sentence_length: The client uses mostly short to medium sentences in public-facing copy, with longer sentences when it lists service features, coverage figures, or programme details.
style_note.vocabulary: The client's vocabulary centres on connectivity, customers, digital services, innovation, technology, coverage, speed, education, skills, entertainment, support, and Bulgaria's digital development.
style_note.self_reference: Vivacom refers to itself by the brand name, by the company name, and through first-person plural forms in Bulgarian when it wants a warmer social or employer tone. Client-facing delivery should be Bulgarian; internal delivery should be English.

questions.question: Vivacom now has fixed, mobile, television, satellite, smart-city, cloud, and digital-education proof in the public record; which of these businesses must sit at the centre of the corporate story, and which should stay as supporting proof? (builds on: What the company does)

The public record shows strong fixed internet and pay-TV positions, Bulsatcom integration, and United Group backing, but it does not give a current Vivacom-only revenue split by consumer, enterprise, public sector, mobile, broadband, television, and information and communications technology services; what internal split can we use to keep the strategy tied to the business model? (builds on: Its business model)

Asen Velikov became the public chief executive officer after the 2025 leadership change, and a new chief financial officer was named in July 2026; what leadership story should the corporate platform help the new team tell in its first year? (builds on: Its leadership)

Pikasa counted 198 Vivacom media articles in Q1 2026, but described much of that volume as public-relations announcements with weak audience response; what would make earned coverage count as reputation progress rather than output volume? (builds on: How much media coverage it gets)
questions.builds_on: How much media coverage it gets

questions.question: The record shows positive proof in coverage, fixed internet, satellite, and employer signals, but customer reviews, outages, data-protection cases, consumer-law rulings, and competition concerns pull the other way; which risk line must the strategy address openly? (builds on: The sentiment of that coverage)

Vivacom's strongest defensible story is infrastructure scale, while that same scale feeds former-incumbent and market-power concern; how far can we lean into scale before it starts to hurt the desired perception? (builds on: The narratives running about it)

Vivacom's digital presence spans My Vivacom, EON, Vivacom Support on Viber, Pay by Vivacom, Happy Call, GAME ON, and social channels; which digital services should prove the corporate story, and which are mainly sales or service channels? (builds on: Channels)
Pikasa found Vivacom strongest on Instagram but weak at turning YouTube reach into response; what audience behaviour should the new corporate platform change on each channel? (builds on: Presence)

Vivacom's public tone moves from formal scale claims on corporate pages to warmer first-person plural language on LinkedIn and youth programmes; which version feels most like the voice the company wants in corporate reputation work? (builds on: Tone of voice)

The peer map shows A1 and Yettel as national retail rivals, Neterra as an enterprise and infrastructure specialist, and CETIN as a wholesale network-infrastructure peer; which competitor set should the corporate platform be built to beat? (builds on: Three to five peers)

A1 can claim breadth and speed, Yettel can claim certified mobile quality and employer trust, Vivacom can claim fixed internet, pay TV, coverage, and satellite proof, and Neterra can claim specialist infrastructure; which leadership claims are worth making, and which should we avoid? (builds on: The white space)

A1 and Yettel have both challenged Vivacom-linked consolidation, while the Supreme Administrative Court cleared the Bulsatcom infrastructure-assets transaction; how should the corporate story handle market-power scrutiny without repeating competitor framing? (builds on: Competition clearance development)

The stakeholder map includes United Group and BC Partners, the Communications Regulation Commission, competition and consumer authorities, employees, media, municipalities, schools, public-sector customers, business customers, and civic organisations; which groups must approve, which must believe, and which must only not object? (builds on: Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations)

interview_question_set.question_set:
# CD-S-002 Client Leadership Interview — Canonical Question Set

Canonical, harness-owned client-leadership interview question set for CD-S-002 corporate
communications strategy. Organized on the Purpose -> Proof -> Positioning -> Priorities ->
Risks -> Future arc. The interview-ingestion phase maps each respondent answer to one of
these questions by its exact text; the deterministic gate validates every extracted prompt
against this set. Override per engagement via inputs["interview_question_set_path"] or inline
inputs["interview_question_set"].

## Part 1 — Purpose
1. Beyond the products and services we sell… Why does the company matter? Where did the company come from, and what were its founders trying to change?
2. Imagine the company disappeared tomorrow. What would genuinely be missed?
3. What contribution over the last few years makes you personally proud?
4. If you had to describe the company in one sentence to someone who knows nothing about it, what would you say?
5. What do people still not understand about the company?
6. As the company enters a new leadership chapter… What should stay exactly the same? What should change?

## Part 2 — Proof
7. Which achievement best proves what the company stands for?
8. How would you prove it? What facts, numbers or examples give you confidence?
9. If someone challenged that achievement tomorrow, would the evidence be strong enough? Why?
10. Where do we already have strong proof? Where are we still ahead of the evidence?
11. What's one success story that deserves far more attention than it gets today?

## Part 3 — Positioning
12. Lots of companies say they're innovative, trusted and customer-focused. What makes this company genuinely different?
13. What's something only this company can honestly say?
14. What should the company stop saying about itself?
15. What should the company never become?
16. When people hear the company's name… What do you hope comes to mind first?

## Part 4 — Priorities
17. If only one group had to believe our story first… Who would it be? Why?
18. Which audience is hardest to convince today? Why?
19. Inside the company… Where do leaders see the future differently?
20. What would help everyone inside the company tell the same story?

## Part 5 — Risks
21. Which claims make you uncomfortable because we haven't fully earned them yet?
22. What topics require extra care before speaking publicly?
23. If you worked for a competitor… What weakness would you attack first?
24. Where do our actions still fall short of our ambitions?
25. What issue from the past could still shape how people see us today?

## Part 6 — The Future
26. Three years from now… What do you hope people say about the company?
27. What decisions do we need to make this year to earn that reputation?
28. How bold should our story be? Too cautious has risks. Too ambitious has risks. Where is the right balance?
29. Beyond reputation… How will we know we've succeeded?
30. If you could change just one thing about how the company is perceived tomorrow morning… What would it be?

## Closer
31. What question should I have asked — but didn't?

Carry this line and "Vivacom, that's my telecom" into Step 4 as hypotheses to test; treat the Step 1 notes as inputs, not verdicts.
- **The first ladder-ranked proof point:** Keep the proof as a verification bundle until Step 4: first commercial 5G network in Bulgaria, first 10-gigabit network in Bulgaria, wide high-speed city footprint, first unlimited consumer plans, EON, independent rankings and employer recognition.

# Client Intake Brief

Vivacom · Step 3 Final Brief. This brief defines the task the strategy is built from. It takes effect only when the named decision-maker approves it in writing, and no work begins before that.

## Client & context

_Who they are, business model, markets, moment._

Vivacom is a Bulgarian national telecommunications company serving consumer, business, enterprise and public-sector customers across fixed and mobile services, broadband, television, satellite, and smart-city, cloud and digital-education offers. The engagement is triggered by a leadership transition and the decision to build a corporate brand and communications strategy from a blank slate, while a live sale and divestment process keeps leadership cautious.

## Organisational objective

_The business change and by when; the story change that delivers it._

Business objective (Vivacom’s, sits above this work). Growth through preference and value in a mature, price-pressured market, supporting the owners’ goal of a strong eventual sale. This outcome depends on pricing, investment, competition and regulation beyond communications; it is context here, not our measure. Communications objective (what we own and are measured on). Build one warmer, proof-led corporate story that moves Vivacom from an activity-led presence to a trusted national role — lifting reputation, affinity and preference, and closing the “former BTK / activity-led” perception. Measured on the brand tracker, with NPS as a secondary signal.

## Assignment — the deliverable

_What the strategy work produces, which discipline leads, and how far the scope runs._

Deliverable. A complete corporate communications strategy document. Lead discipline. Corporate-led — corporate reputation is the frame; the brand and preference work, and the crisis-and-issues component, are contained inside it and serve it. Scope. Strategy is the Step 3 deliverable — research and diagnosis, positioning and corporate narrative, message architecture, channel approach, the issues-and-crisis approach, and measurement. Creative platform and activation are a named later phase, costed separately.

## Reputation problem / opportunity

_Current perception versus desired; the misperception to close._

Vivacom’s strongest assets do not yet add up to one trusted role in Bulgaria’s digital progress. The old BTK association, customer friction, market-power scrutiny and generic technology claims can overpower the story it wants to own — a stable telecom that became an innovator. The brand tracker shows the shape of this: Vivacom leads on functional and reliability attributes but under-indexes on warmth relative to that strength, and its lead disappears among Gen Z.

## Priority audiences

_Segments and their current state: what they know, feel and do today._

Existing customers are the primary, first-believer audience - and one of the hardest, after integrations and service changes. The critical urban audience is the influence multiplier, powerful for both praise and criticism. Beyond these sit Gen Z (a named repair priority), employees and future talent, business and public-sector customers, municipalities, regulators, media, government and parent-group stakeholders.

## Desired change

_What each audience must know, feel or do differently._

Existing customers should re-see Vivacom as useful, positive and part of daily life. The three-year hope, in Elitza Georgieva’s words, is that people say “Vivacom, that’s my telecom.” That belonging line leads into the research as the hypothesis to test; “You can’t do without it” is carried as the challenger. Both are expressions of desired feeling, not the platform — the platform is discovered in the next stages.

## Stakeholders & internal alignment

_Key internal players, their wants and fears, and the conflicts between them._

Elitza Georgieva, Communications Director, wants one warm, useful, emotionally positive story, and wants leaders to open up through company and industry events and social-responsibility topics. The Alignment Map records real tension: leaders are cautious under sale uncertainty, Legal and Regulatory Affairs require narrow proof-led claims, and employees need clearer direction while the company “hangs in the air.” One honest limit: only Elitza has been interviewed, so the Alignment Map is one person’s account of these conflicts, not yet corroborated by a second voice.

## Constraints & guardrails

_Commercial, regulatory, legal, do-not-say, AI and confidential-information limits._

Avoid the old BTK frame, broad market-leader boasting, unsupported superlatives and political framing. Keep internal, pending Legal: vendor migration, sale-process detail, ownership history, duct-access detail, Recovery and Resilience Plan work, customer disruptions, state-security specifics and unverified figures. Every superlative needs a legal-proof pair; “first,” not “the only,” on the 10-gig claim; no market-leader claim across all segments. These sensitive topics are also the seed of the potential-issues-and-crisis register that Step 4 research builds — a quarantined topic and a managed issue are two sides of one coin, and the sale process is both.

## Assets & access

_Research, tracking, past work, data, spokespeople, analytics for baselines._

Available now: public desk-audit evidence, CRC market data, competitor audits, media and social signals, Vivacom owned-channel examples, public proof pools, Elitza's debrief, and Vivacom's quarterly Kantar brand tracker and NPS wave (perception, image and functional attributes, the affinity funnel, and regression linking attributes to first choice). Still to confirm: the named Marketing / customer-insight owner who opens tracker access, the latest wave, and whether an employee-engagement or eNPS tracker exists in the Human Capital function.

## Success & measurement

_How success is defined; the scorecard sits in the measurement brief._

Share of voice alone is not enough - Elitza's standard. The primary instrument is the brand tracker (perception, affinity, preference); NPS is a secondary signal. The measurement standard is AMEC Barcelona Principles 4.0 and the Integrated Evaluation Framework; advertising value equivalents are not used unless the client specifically asks for them. The full scorecard - baseline, target, source, frequency and owner for each measure - is held in the measurement brief, which this brief governs.

## Scope & logistics

_Tier, budget, timeline, markets, decision-maker._

Enterprise tier, national in Bulgaria. The rollout shape and recommended annual investment are United Partners' to propose, not to elicit - authored in the proposal, phased across discovery, platform, activation and measurement. Two client parameters shape that proposal and are still to confirm: any budget band Vivacom is working within, and the divestment-calendar dates and no-go windows the timeline must respect.

_Who signs, and where a second confirmation is required._

Local strategic approval runs Elitza Georgieva (Communications Director) → Malina Chavdarova (Chief Human Capital Officer) → Asen Velikov (CEO), who holds final sign-off for Vivacom. # Final-brief board -- report

**Outcome: CLEARS the Board.** only low concerns stand.

Rule applied: Proceeds to the human ship gate with the Board report attached.

Two personas, convened on the Step 3 pair before the final-brief hard stop. The CFO asks where the business and the number are behind every measure; the Journalist asks which claim outruns the evidence the material actually supplies. The pair is adjudicated, not advised: a critical finding or a block from either stops the run before approval is even requested.

Convened on the Step 3 pair: The CFO / Board · The Journalist

## The verdicts

| persona | position | verdict | findings that survived the referee |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The CFO / Board | So what — where's the business and the number? | PASS | 0 |
| The Journalist | Where's the substance? I'm going to check. | PASS | 0 |

## The findings

No finding survived the referee pass.
## Struck by the referee

No attack counts unless it quotes the exact target. 0 were discarded before triage.


## How the findings were triaged

The system — not the operator — triages by these fixed rules. The one that fired is marked; the rest are shown so the outcome can be read against what did not happen.

| condition | outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Any CRITICAL finding (legal red line, factual falsehood, greenwashing, reputational landmine) | HARD BLOCK — fix before anything else, regardless of all other verdicts |
| Competitor returns BLOCK on distinctiveness | RETURN to Insight/Strategy — a table-stakes strategy cannot ship |
| Target Audience returns BLOCK (insight not held / unvalidated) | RETURN to Insight — trigger M7 validation |
| ≥ 2 High concerns, or ≥ 4 Medium | MUST REVISE — auto-revise loop |
| **Only Low concerns, or all PASS** | CLEARS the Board → proceeds to the human ship gate with the Board report attached |

## The review loop

1. Draft
2. Attack
3. Referee
4. Triage
5. Fix
6. Re-review
7. Clear

Bounded to 3 rounds. Round 1 of 3 ran here. If it still cannot clear, it escalates to a human — the one place seniority is invoked, and only on genuinely hard deadlocks.

## Keeping the Board honest

It is AI, so it can flatter or hallucinate.

- **Grounding.** Each persona is fed real data, not imagination — the competitor's real positioning, the client's real record, actual audience evidence.
- **Specificity requirement.** No attack counts unless it quotes the exact target; the referee discards the rest.
- **Severity calibration.** Anchored to worked examples so verdicts are consistent run to run — no drifting standards.
- **Validate the validators.** Periodically check the Board's findings against real senior reviews: does it catch what seniors catch, without crying wolf?

## Operator-independence

The operator never scores the Board and never adjudicates a finding. The triage above is a fixed rule, not a judgement, so a novice and a veteran get the same scrutiny and the same fix set.

research_pack.client_style_note:
## Client Style Note

Captured from the client's own published communications. Every client-facing deliverable is written to this voice -- its tone, typical sentence length, vocabulary, self-reference, and signature do/don't words.

- **tone:** Vivacom's own voice is direct, service-led, and confident. It often opens with the customer benefit, then supports it with network scale, product detail, or programme proof.
- **sentence length:** The client uses mostly short to medium sentences in public-facing copy, with longer sentences when it lists service features, coverage figures, or programme details.
- **vocabulary:** The client's vocabulary centres on connectivity, customers, digital services, innovation, technology, coverage, speed, education, skills, entertainment, support, and Bulgaria's digital development.
- **self reference:** Vivacom refers to itself by the brand name, by the company name, and through first-person plural forms in Bulgarian when it wants a warmer social or employer tone.
- **signature do words:** customers, digital services, connectivity, coverage, technology, innovation, education, skills, support, Bulgaria
- **signature dont words:** world-class, best-in-class, game-changing, state utility, former monopoly, price war, political positioning
- **sources:** https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata, https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini, https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/sotsialna-otgovornost, https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/karieri, https://www.vivacom.bg/pomosht/kontakti, https://www.vivacom.bg/business/satelitni-uslugi
- **long form voice:** Not yet calibrated: no long-form writing of the client's own has been read.
- **voice evidence read:** short-form copy only — long-form voice not yet calibrated
research_pack.up_house_style:
## Clear, professional communication language

Every Research document meets the clear, professional communication language standard. The wording is checked sentence by sentence and the whole text is checked end to end, against the rules named in the language standard.

**Wording rules**
- **Plain words:** Use the everyday word, not the impressive one. No jargon. No acronym without its meaning at first use. No filler.
- **Short sentences:** One idea per sentence. Active voice. If a sentence needs a second read, rewrite it.
- **Concrete, not abstract:** Say what happens, who does it, and by when. Replace vague claims with facts.
- **Proof, not adjectives:** Every claim carries evidence. Delete superlatives that carry none.
- **Confident, not inflated:** Assured, warm but not casual, direct. No hedging that hides a decision; no claim that outruns its proof.
- **One name per thing:** Call the same thing by the same name in every document. Never rename a concept midway.
- **Reader's language, not the method's:** Client-facing documents are written in the reader's language, not the method's. No process term reaches a client page unexplained.

**Whole-text rules**
- **One clear purpose:** The reader knows in the first paragraph what this document is and what it is for.
- **Headline first:** Every section starts with its point, then the support beneath it. A busy reader who reads only the headings still gets the story.
- **Logical flow:** Sections follow one order of thought. Each builds on the one before. No jumps, no repeats.
- **Right length:** As short as the content allows. Anything that supports but does not advance the argument goes to an appendix.
- **Short paragraphs:** One idea per paragraph. If a paragraph runs long, split it. A wall of text goes back.
- **Visual clarity:** Tables for comparisons, short lists for sequences, bold sparingly. White space is part of the writing.
- **Self-contained:** A new reader can use the document without a briefing. Terms, context and next steps are inside it.

do_not_say.why: Research works only from the material it was handed; a client relationship, quote or reference the material does not carry cannot be attributed to a client.
No number, percentage, ranking or share of voice enters the pack unless a source in the supplied material carries it. No invented figures, at all, for any reason.

A statement about the market, the audience or the client is only Research when a source in the supplied material grounds it. A finding Research could not source says so in its own row rather than being presented as a claim.

strategy_appendix.question: Can Vivacom turn infrastructure scale into a trusted role in Bulgaria's daily digital progress?
strategy_appendix.so_what: The strategy should make national usefulness the centre of the story, with named proof by place, service or audience.

findings.finding: Vivacom serves consumer, business, enterprise and public-sector customers across fixed, mobile, broadband, television, satellite, smart-city, cloud and digital-education offers.
Vivacom says it works with Bulgarian municipalities through smart-city services.
Bulgaria signed digital-network contracts with A1, Vivacom and CETIN for underbuilt areas, with more than half of target areas rural, remote or sparsely populated.

strategy_appendix.question: Where can Vivacom safely claim strength, and where must it use narrower language?
strategy_appendix.so_what: Vivacom should claim specific strengths and avoid any line that sounds like total telecom leadership.

findings.finding: ICLG reports that Vivacom served 39.4% of fixed internet subscribers and about 60% of pay-TV subscribers in 2024, while mobile shares across A1, Yettel and Vivacom sat in the 30% to 37% range.
Opensignal's January 2026 Bulgaria report says Vivacom dominated coverage experience while A1 was fastest and Yettel led reliability and time on network.
SpeedGeo ranked Vivacom first for broadband speed from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026, while A1 led mobile download speed.

strategy_appendix.question: What stops existing customers from feeling that Vivacom is useful, positive and part of daily life?
strategy_appendix.so_what: Warmth must be earned through customer-use proof and service experience, not added as tone alone.

findings.finding: The approved brief says Vivacom leads on functional and reliability attributes but under-indexes on warmth, and its lead disappears among Gen Z.
Trustpilot shows a weak public review signal for Vivacom and says the profile has not invited reviews.
Google Play and Apple App Store reviews show My Vivacom as a major customer-service touchpoint, with visible complaints about login, payment, passcode and service management.

strategy_appendix.question: Can Vivacom leaders speak clearly while sale uncertainty and legal caution remain active?
strategy_appendix.so_what: The strategy needs an internal leadership story that is safe, specific and usable before the external platform is approved.

findings.finding: Elitza Georgieva says leaders are cautious because the company is waiting for a sale and due diligence keeps restarting.

findings.finding: A1 communicates breadth, speed and market scale, and reports strong Bulgaria revenue through A1 Group.

cd_s_002.research_pack_markdown:
# Research & Insight Pack

One pack, not five disconnected audits. Every finding shows where it came from -- for a web finding, a URL (uniform resource locator); for supplied material, the place in the pack it came from. A finding this engine could not source from the material it was given says so in its own row rather than being presented as research. The AI (artificial intelligence) drafts each audit and a strategist validates and interprets it. The Sweet Spot the pack ends on names the client's USP (unique selling proposition) at the intersection with the insight nobody else has leveraged yet.

## Client Style Note

Captured from the client's own published communications. Every client-facing deliverable is written to this voice -- its tone, typical sentence length, vocabulary, self-reference, and signature do/don't words.

- **tone:** Vivacom's own voice is direct, service-led, and confident. It often opens with the customer benefit, then supports it with network scale, product detail, or programme proof.
- **sentence length:** The client uses mostly short to medium sentences in public-facing copy, with longer sentences when it lists service features, coverage figures, or programme details.
- **vocabulary:** The client's vocabulary centres on connectivity, customers, digital services, innovation, technology, coverage, speed, education, skills, entertainment, support, and Bulgaria's digital development.
- **self reference:** Vivacom refers to itself by the brand name, by the company name, and through first-person plural forms in Bulgarian when it wants a warmer social or employer tone.
- **signature do words:** customers, digital services, connectivity, coverage, technology, innovation, education, skills, support, Bulgaria
- **signature dont words:**,,, state utility, former monopoly, price war, political positioning
- **sources:** https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata, https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini, https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/sotsialna-otgovornost, https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/karieri, https://www.vivacom.bg/pomosht/kontakti, https://www.vivacom.bg/business/satelitni-uslugi
- **long form voice:** Not yet calibrated: no long-form writing of the client's own has been read.
- **voice evidence read:** short-form copy only — long-form voice not yet calibrated

## Clear, professional communication language

Every Research document meets the clear, professional communication language standard. The wording is checked sentence by sentence and the whole text is checked end to end, against the rules named in the language standard.

**Wording rules**
- **Plain words:** Use the everyday word, not the impressive one. No jargon. No acronym without its meaning at first use. No filler.
- **Short sentences:** One idea per sentence. Active voice. If a sentence needs a second read, rewrite it.
- **Concrete, not abstract:** Say what happens, who does it, and by when. Replace vague claims with facts.
- **Proof, not adjectives:** Every claim carries evidence. Delete superlatives that carry none.
- **Confident, not inflated:** Assured, warm but not casual, direct. No hedging that hides a decision; no claim that outruns its proof.
- **One name per thing:** Call the same thing by the same name in every document. Never rename a concept midway.
- **Reader's language, not the method's:** Client-facing documents are written in the reader's language, not the method's. No process term reaches a client page unexplained.

**Whole-text rules**
- **One clear purpose:** The reader knows in the first paragraph what this document is and what it is for.
- **Headline first:** Every section starts with its point, then the support beneath it. A busy reader who reads only the headings still gets the story.
- **Logical flow:** Sections follow one order of thought. Each builds on the one before. No jumps, no repeats.
- **Right length:** As short as the content allows. Anything that supports but does not advance the argument goes to an appendix.
- **Short paragraphs:** One idea per paragraph. If a paragraph runs long, split it. A wall of text goes back.
- **Visual clarity:** Tables for comparisons, short lists for sequences, bold sparingly. White space is part of the writing.
- **Self-contained:** A new reader can use the document without a briefing. Terms, context and next steps are inside it.

## Accountable review gates

Research writes the assignment on every pack so the discipline check reads a real owner next to every gate that reviews its output.

| review gate | accountable owner |
| --- | --- |
| Research pack review | United Partners strategy lead |
| Sourcing & figures audit | United Partners quality lead |
| Insight review board | United Partners head of insight |

## Primary reputation risks

Research names the primary reputation risks on every pack so the discipline check reads them against the work rather than inferring them from adjacent context.

- overclaim
- inconsistency
- ambiguity

## Do not say

Research works only from the material it was handed. The three shapes of invention the pack refuses are named here, each with why the pack refuses it.

| do not say | why |
| --- | --- |
| invented clients | Research works only from the material it was handed; a client relationship, quote or reference the material does not carry cannot be attributed to a client. |

The Sweet Spot the Synthesize phase finds at the intersection of client priorities/USP and unleveraged insight, and hands to strategist-owned Discovery for the Killer Insight. The patterns and benchmarks above feed the two ingredients named here; a strategist, not the engine, crosses them into the Killer Insight in Discovery.

cards.insight: Existing customers will not warm to Vivacom because it is large. They may warm to Vivacom if it proves one household relationship works across fixed internet, pay TV, coverage and customer help.
cards.evidence: The approved brief names existing customers as the primary first-believer audience and says Vivacom under-indexes on warmth. ICLG reports Vivacom at 39.4% of fixed internet subscribers and about 60% of pay-TV subscribers in 2024. Opensignal says Vivacom dominated coverage experience in January 2026, while A1 was fastest and Yettel led reliability and time on network. The pack also records visible friction in app reviews, Trustpilot criticism, contract penalties, outages and data-protection pressure, so service proof must sit inside the story rather than outside it.
cards.tension: Vivacom has the proof to matter in the household, but the same household judges it through bills, app payments, outages, contract clarity and support.
cards.so_what: The strategy should open with verified household usefulness, not national scale. A1 can answer with speed and scale, and Yettel can answer with reliability and certified quality, but Vivacom defends a narrower space: fixed internet, pay TV, coverage and customer-service proof in one paid relationship.
cards.audience: Existing customers who judge Vivacom through home internet, television, mobile coverage, bills, app payments, outages, support and contract clarity.
cards.opportunity: Turn the corporate story into a proof-led household relationship: fixed internet that carries the home, pay TV that is part of daily entertainment, coverage that reaches the customer, and visible service fixes that make the relationship easier to manage.
cards.audience_truth: Maya wants reliable service, clear billing, simple help and fewer surprises.
cards.ownable_truth: Vivacom can defend the combination of fixed internet strength, pay-TV strength, coverage-experience proof and customer-service touchpoints in one household relationship. A1 can counter with speed and scale, and Yettel can counter with reliability and trust, but neither has the same proof combination across the household services where Vivacom is strongest.
cards.how_contrarian: This contradicts the instinct to make the corporate story start with size, innovation or national importance. It also rejects a generic fairness claim that A1 or Yettel could copy, because the defended base is the narrower Vivacom proof combination in the household.
cards.what_would_validate_it: Ask current Vivacom customers who used billing, My Vivacom or support in the last six months to compare three story routes: national digital progress, best-network proof, and verified household usefulness. The insight is confirmed if they find the household route more believable and use their own words to describe less hassle, clearer control or fewer surprises. It is refined if they accept the household route but name a different tension than bills, app payments, outages, support or contract clarity. It is rejected if they trust the national-progress or best-network route more without needing household-service proof.

extraction_steps: Immerse — absorb the research pack, the filled buckets, the audits, the reputation read
Generate volume — write many candidates, empirical and intuitive; do not edit yet
So-What ladder — push each promising candidate up the pyramid with repeated 'so what?'
Screen — test each against the five T's and discard what fails any of them
Find the Sweet Spot — the ownable truth, an insight not yet leveraged, what the audience truly cares about
Distinctiveness Gate — reject anything a competitor could also claim, or the obvious white space everyone sees
Distil — land one to three Killer Insights, no more

# Killer Insight Cards

20 candidates were written and screened; 7 survived; 1 are put forward as cards. Volume first, then judgment.

**Nobody has selected the insight yet.** The volume reserves that for a person: the final insight is chosen, defined and defended by a human, and this engine does not author it on autopilot.

## Card 1

**Existing customers will not warm to Vivacom because it is large. They may warm to Vivacom if it proves one household relationship works across fixed internet, pay TV, coverage and customer help.**

**Type.** empirical

**The 5 T's.** True: pass — The pack supports a split market where A1 leads speed, Yettel leads reliability and Vivacom holds fixed internet, pay TV and coverage strengths. · Tacit: pass — It states the defended boundary Vivacom can hold when peers respond. · Touches the heart: partial — The phrase is strategically clear, but it still needs customer-language testing before public use. · Tension: pass — It turns competitor limits into Vivacom's useful household space. · Triggers action: pass — It creates a claim test for every message: prove the household use or cut it.

**The tension.** Vivacom has the proof to matter in the household, but the same household judges it through bills, app payments, outages, contract clarity and support.

**The audience it is about.** Existing customers who judge Vivacom through home internet, television, mobile coverage, bills, app payments, outages, support and contract clarity.
**Audience personas.** Maya

**The opportunity it opens.** Turn the corporate story into a proof-led household relationship: fixed internet that carries the home, pay TV that is part of daily entertainment, coverage that reaches the customer, and visible service fixes that make the relationship easier to manage.

**What the audience truly cares about.** Maya wants reliable service, clear billing, simple help and fewer surprises.

**The company's ownable truth.** Vivacom can defend the combination of fixed internet strength, pay-TV strength, coverage-experience proof and customer-service touchpoints in one household relationship. A1 can counter with speed and scale, and Yettel can counter with reliability and trust, but neither has the same proof combination across the household services where Vivacom is strongest.

**Evidence.** The approved brief names existing customers as the primary first-believer audience and says Vivacom under-indexes on warmth. ICLG reports Vivacom at 39.4% of fixed internet subscribers and about 60% of pay-TV subscribers in 2024. Opensignal says Vivacom dominated coverage experience in January 2026, while A1 was fastest and Yettel led reliability and time on network. The pack also records visible friction in app reviews, Trustpilot criticism, contract penalties, outages and data-protection pressure, so service proof must sit inside the story rather than outside it.
#### The evidence beneath it

| what the evidence shows | source & standing |
| --- | --- |
| Existing customers are the primary first-believer audience and are hard to win after integrations and service changes. | Approved Brief, Priority audiences · dated · high |
| Vivacom leads on functional and reliability attributes but under-indexes on warmth. | Approved Brief, Reputation problem / opportunity · dated · high |
| Vivacom served 39.4% of fixed internet subscribers and about 60% of pay-TV subscribers in 2024. | https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/ · dated · high |
| Vivacom dominated coverage experience, while A1 was fastest and Yettel led reliability and time on network. | https://insights.opensignal.com/reports/2026/01/bulgaria/mobile-network-experience · dated · high |
| Customer friction appears in app reviews, Trustpilot criticism, contract and pricing disputes, outages and data-protection enforcement. | Research & Insight Pack, Executive summary; Customer Warmth Gap; Regulatory And Issues Pressure · dated · high |


**So what.** The strategy should open with verified household usefulness, not national scale. A1 can answer with speed and scale, and Yettel can answer with reliability and certified quality, but Vivacom defends a narrower space: fixed internet, pay TV, coverage and customer-service proof in one paid relationship.

# The screening

Every candidate against the five T's and the distinctiveness check. A candidate is kept only when all five hold and no competitor could equally claim it.

| Vivacom can make Bulgarian digital life credible by showing where one service relationship works across the home, not by claiming total technology leadership. | intuitive | pass | pass | conditional | pass | pass | yes | kept |
| Vivacom's proof is strongest when it shows a home working: broadband that carries the household, television people use, coverage that reaches them and service that solves the practical issue. | empirical | pass | partial | conditional | pass | pass | yes | kept |

# The extraction process — seven steps

1. Immerse — absorb the research pack, the filled buckets, the audits, the reputation read
2. Generate volume — write many candidates, empirical and intuitive; do not edit yet
3. So-What ladder — push each promising candidate up the pyramid with repeated 'so what?'
4. Screen — test each against the five T's and discard what fails any of them
5. Find the Sweet Spot — the ownable truth, an insight not yet leveraged, what the audience truly cares about
6. Distinctiveness Gate — reject anything a competitor could also claim, or the obvious white space everyone sees
7. Distil — land one to three Killer Insights, no more

# Two kinds of insight — and why you need both

| | what it is | proven by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Empirical insight | Grounded in data acquired through research methods | The data itself |
| Intuitive insight | Grounded in knowing or sensing, without a rational process | Observation and qualitative evidence — it still needs backup |

**The UP principle.** It is through science that we prove, but through intuition that we discover. The strongest Killer Insights pair an intuitive human truth with empirical proof — the discovery and the evidence together.

# The climb — from data to insight

Insight is a level on a ladder, reached by disciplined questioning — not a lucky thought.

| level | what it is |
| --- | --- |
| Data | Raw, uncontextualised facts ("sales rose 23%") |
| Information | Data organised & compared ("23% — 5 points above target, 8 below history") |
| Insight | What it means, strategically ("the growth is masking a loyalty problem") |
| Foresight | What it signals for the future ("expect margin pressure in 12 months") |

**The tool that climbs it: the So What? test.** For every finding ask "so what?" and keep asking until you reach genuine meaning. Guard against the five traps:

- correlation mistaken for causation
- confirmation bias
- volume mistaken for significance
- the missing counterfactual
- outliers mistaken for trends

# The Sweet Spot

An insight sits where all three meet:

- the company's ownable truth
- an insight not yet leveraged
- what the audience truly cares about

# Step 5B · Validate the insight

A distinctive, contrarian insight cannot lock until it is tested against the real audience. Distinctiveness and wrongness look identical until tested.

## Validating card 1

**How contrarian.** This contradicts the instinct to make the corporate story start with size, innovation or national importance. It also rejects a generic fairness claim that A1 or Yettel could copy, because the defended base is the narrower Vivacom proof combination in the household.

**What would validate it.** Ask current Vivacom customers who used billing, My Vivacom or support in the last six months to compare three story routes: national digital progress, best-network proof, and verified household usefulness. The insight is confirmed if they find the household route more believable and use their own words to describe less hassle, clearer control or fewer surprises. It is refined if they accept the household route but name a different tension than bills, app payments, outages, support or contract clarity. It is rejected if they trust the national-progress or best-network route more without needing household-service proof.

**Verdict.** Confirm · Refine · Reject — none recorded. The test has not been run.


# Open — waiting on a person

- **Which of these is the insight?** — not yet decided; no owner recorded.
- **What did the audience say?** — the validation test has not been run, so no verdict is recorded.

cd_s_002.insight_mini_board_markdown:
# Insight mini-board — report

**Outcome: CLEARS the Board.** only low concerns stand.

Rule applied: Proceeds to the human ship gate with the Board report attached.

Three personas, convened at step 5B against the insight alone, to kill a weak insight before a whole strategy is built on it. The Competitor asks whether they could claim it word for word, the Target Audience whether they recognise themselves in it, the Activist what it looks like turned over. It is not the pre-ship board and it does not clear the work; it stops one thing from being built on.

Convened at step 5B: The Competitor · The Target Audience · The Hostile Stakeholder / Activist

## The verdicts

| persona | position | verdict | findings that survived the referee |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The Competitor | I can say that too. | PASS | 0 |
| The Target Audience | Why do I care? I don't believe you. | CONCERN | 2 |
| The Hostile Stakeholder / Activist | Here's how this blows up. | PASS | 0 |

## The findings

### 1. The Target Audience — Medium

**Finding.** Card 1 states the warmth barrier as a settled audience truth rather than a hypothesis still awaiting customer validation.

**Quoted target.** "Existing customers will not warm to Vivacom because it is large."

**Suggested fix.** Rewrite as a testable hypothesis: existing customers may not warm to Vivacom through scale alone; validate whether household-service proof changes belief.

### 2. The Target Audience — Medium

**Finding.** The card names what Maya cares about as established, but the pack says direct audience research has not yet been run.

**Quoted target.** "Maya wants reliable service, clear billing, simple help and fewer surprises."

**Suggested fix.** Keep this as the proposed validation language for customer interviews, then replace it with the audience's own words after testing.

## Struck by the referee

No attack counts unless it quotes the exact target. 0 were discarded before triage.


## How the findings were triaged

The system — not the operator — triages by these fixed rules. The one that fired is marked; the rest are shown so the outcome can be read against what did not happen.

| condition | outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Any CRITICAL finding (legal red line, factual falsehood, greenwashing, reputational landmine) | HARD BLOCK — fix before anything else, regardless of all other verdicts |
| Competitor returns BLOCK on distinctiveness | RETURN to Insight/Strategy — a table-stakes strategy cannot ship |
| Target Audience returns BLOCK (insight not held / unvalidated) | RETURN to Insight — trigger M7 validation |
| ≥ 2 High concerns, or ≥ 4 Medium | MUST REVISE — auto-revise loop |
| **Only Low concerns, or all PASS** | CLEARS the Board → proceeds to the human ship gate with the Board report attached |

## The review loop

1. Draft
2. Attack
3. Referee
4. Triage
5. Fix
6. Re-review
7. Clear

Bounded to 3 rounds. Round 1 of 3 ran here. If it still cannot clear, it escalates to a human — the one place seniority is invoked, and only on genuinely hard deadlocks.

## Keeping the Board honest

It is AI, so it can flatter or hallucinate.

- **Grounding.** Each persona is fed real data, not imagination — the competitor's real positioning, the client's real record, actual audience evidence.
- **Specificity requirement.** No attack counts unless it quotes the exact target; the referee discards the rest.
- **Severity calibration.** Anchored to worked examples so verdicts are consistent run to run — no drifting standards.
- **Validate the validators.** Periodically check the Board's findings against real senior reviews: does it catch what seniors catch, without crying wolf?

## Operator-independence

The operator never scores the Board and never adjudicates a finding. The triage above is a fixed rule, not a judgement, so a novice and a veteran get the same scrutiny and the same fix set.

Core narrative: Vivacom should not ask people to admire its size. It should show how one useful relationship keeps the home connected, entertainment working, reach visible through OpenSignal coverage-experience proof, and help easier to manage.
Key message 1: Vivacom is strongest when it proves what customers use every day.
Key message 2: Fixed internet and television make the home the first proof point.
Key message 3: Coverage-experience proof means reach, not speed, reliability or quality.
Key message 4: Service moments decide whether the warmer story is believed.

ICLG reports Vivacom at 39.4% of fixed internet subscribers and about 60% of pay-TV subscribers in 2024. The Research & Insight Pack records app reviews, Trustpilot criticism, contract penalties, outages and data-protection pressure as visible friction.
one_pager.channels: PESO means paid, earned, shared and owned media. The approach should lead with earned media because corporate reputation needs third-party proof, then use owned service channels, shared customer proof and selective paid support to repeat the same story.

The main risks are overclaim, customer friction, sale sensitivity, legal clearance, data and cyber pressure, and the old BTK frame. Crisis-and-issues management runs through the strategy, so every public claim needs proof and a cleared response line.
