# Measurement & Evaluation Framework

Start from the business change and work backwards. A metric that cannot be connected upward to an audience change or an organizational objective does not belong here.

**Not approved.** The organizational objective is a person's to approve, and no owner is recorded.

Acronyms used below: AMEC (Association for Measurement and Evaluation of Communication), KPI (key performance indicator), IEF (Integrated Evaluation Framework), and AVE (Advertising Value Equivalent).

## The AMEC (Association for Measurement and Evaluation of Communication) chain

Organizational objectives → Communication objectives → Inputs → Activities → Outputs → Outtakes → Outcomes → Impact.

## Objectives

### Organizational (at most 1)

- By 30 June 2027, increase preference-led support for Vivacom's value growth among existing and prospective Bulgarian customers from baseline not established; the baseline will be read from the latest Kantar brand tracker before launch to a target agreed with Vivacom once that reading is confirmed.

### Communication (at most 3)

- By 30 June 2027, increase recognition of Vivacom as a warmer, proof-led national role among existing customers from baseline not established; the baseline will be read from the latest Kantar brand tracker before launch to a target agreed with Vivacom once that reading is confirmed.
- By 30 June 2027, increase recall of So You Can and The Invisible Thread among existing customers and the critical urban audience from baseline not established; the baseline will be set in the pre-launch message-recall read to a target agreed before launch.
- By 30 June 2027, decrease priority customer-friction themes among existing customers from baseline not established; the baseline will be read from current customer-service, app-review, regulator and social-service records before launch to a target agreed after that read.

### Executive KPIs (at most 5)

- By 30 June 2027, increase reputation, affinity and preference among existing customers from the latest Kantar brand tracker baseline to a target agreed with Vivacom once the latest wave is confirmed.
- By 30 June 2027, increase message recall tied to So You Can, The Invisible Thread and named proof among existing customers and the critical urban audience from baseline not established; the baseline will be set in the pre-launch message-recall read to a target agreed before launch.
- By 30 June 2027, increase quality earned attention for So You Can and The Invisible Thread among media, regulators and parent-group stakeholders from baseline not established; the baseline will be captured at campaign start to a target agreed after that review.
- By 30 June 2027, decrease priority customer-friction themes among existing customers from baseline not established; the baseline will be read before launch to a target agreed after that read.
- By 30 June 2027, increase employee understanding of the Vivacom corporate story among employees from baseline not established; the baseline will be read from an employee pulse or existing Human Capital source before launch to a target agreed after that read.

## Shared measurement concepts

The words below are shared with the other engagement document that names them, and every document that carries one of them must preserve the same one-line definition beside it, so the reader finds the same meaning under the same word wherever they read:

- **definition** — what is being measured, and how the number is worked out
- **baseline** — the number a target is checked against
- **target** — the number this engagement aims at
- **source** — where the number is read from
- **collection_frequency** — how often the number is read
- **owner** — the person responsible for the number

## The KPI ladder

Each KPI on its level, with what it climbs to and how strongly it can be attributed.

| KPI | level | climbs to | attribution | baseline | target | source | owner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Brand tracker movement on reputation, affinity and preference | Impact | Increase recognition of Vivacom as a warmer, proof-led national role among existing customers. | medium — say 'contributed to', or anything weaker: 'coincided with' | Latest Kantar brand tracker wave before launch; the current material names top-of-mind Vivacom at 37.6 versus A1 at 38.9 and confirms a warmth gap, but the full launch baseline is not yet established. | Close the top-of-mind gap, lift warmth attributes and repair the Gen Z gap; exact target to be set with Vivacom after the latest wave is confirmed. | Kantar brand tracker. | United Partners account lead with Vivacom Marketing or insight owner. |
| Message recall tied to So You Can and The Invisible Thread | Outtake | Increase recall of So You Can and The Invisible Thread among existing customers and the critical urban audience. | medium — say 'contributed to', or anything weaker: 'coincided with' | Baseline not established; it will be set in the pre-launch message-recall survey or structured stakeholder interview read. | Target to be agreed before launch once the baseline read is complete. | Message-recall survey or structured stakeholder interviews. | United Partners account lead. |
| Quality earned attention for the platform | Output | Increase recognition of Vivacom as a warmer, proof-led national role among media, regulators and parent-group stakeholders. | low — say 'coincided with' | Baseline not established; the media baseline will be captured at campaign start. | Target to be set after the baseline quality review. | Media monitoring, social listening and coverage-quality review. | United Partners account lead. |
| Owned proof-page engagement | Outtake | Increase recall of So You Can and The Invisible Thread among existing customers and the critical urban audience. | low — say 'coincided with' | Baseline not established; it will be read from owned analytics when proof pages go live. | Target to be set after the first live analytics read. | Vivacom owned-channel analytics. | United Partners account lead with Vivacom digital owner. |
| Priority customer-friction themes | Outcome | Decrease priority customer-friction themes among existing customers. | low — say 'coincided with' | Baseline not established; the first read will come from current customer-service, app-store, regulator and social-service records before launch. | Target reduction to be set after the baseline read and confirmed service-operation context. | Customer-service records, app-store audit, Communications Regulation Commission complaints and social-service logs. | United Partners account lead with Vivacom customer-service and digital owners. |
| Employee understanding of the corporate story | Outcome | Increase employee understanding of the Vivacom corporate story. | medium — say 'contributed to', or anything weaker: 'coincided with' | Baseline not established; Human Capital will confirm whether an employee pulse or employee Net Promoter Score source exists before launch. | Target to be set once the employee baseline is confirmed. | Employee pulse, internal-channel analytics and leadership-communication review. | United Partners account lead with Vivacom Human Capital. |

### How each KPI is measured

#### Brand tracker movement on reputation, affinity and preference

**Definition.** Quarterly movement in Kantar brand tracker measures for reputation, affinity and preference, read by audience segment and interpreted against the So You Can and The Invisible Thread campaign period.

**Collection.** Quarterly, with a strategy review after each tracker wave.  ·  **Breakdown.** Existing customers, critical urban audience, Gen Z and other segments available in the tracker.

**Target grounded in resources.** The target assumes United Partners strategy, campaign management, measurement support and a client-approved annual investment for earned, owned, shared and selective paid activity.

**Target grounded in execution control.** United Partners controls the communications strategy, messaging and reporting, while tracker movement also depends on service performance, pricing, competition, regulation and market conditions.

**Attribution method.** Compare tracker movement with campaign exposure, message recall and issue context; state that the campaign contributed to movement only where the evidence supports that link.  —  correlation with some controls — say 'contributed to'

**Known limitations.** The tracker cannot isolate communications from product, service, price, competitor and market effects without a controlled model or matched comparison.

#### Message recall tied to So You Can and The Invisible Thread

**Definition.** Share of priority-audience respondents who recall So You Can or The Invisible Thread and connect it to named Vivacom proof rather than to a generic telecom claim.

**Collection.** Before launch, then quarterly.  ·  **Breakdown.** Existing customers, critical urban audience, Gen Z where sample size allows and stakeholder groups where interviews are used.

**Target grounded in resources.** The target assumes a message-recall survey or interview budget, United Partners analysis time and client access to agreed audience samples.

**Target grounded in execution control.** United Partners controls the question design and analysis, while sample access and audience response depend on Vivacom and the research supplier.

**Attribution method.** Read recall against confirmed campaign exposure and message assets, then describe the campaign as contributing to recall where respondents name the platform and proof.  —  correlation with some controls — say 'contributed to'

**Known limitations.** Recall does not prove preference or behaviour change on its own.

#### Quality earned attention for the platform

**Definition.** Number and quality of earned items that mention So You Can or The Invisible Thread, carry named proof, use cleared reach language and avoid unsupported speed, reliability or total-leadership claims.

**Collection.** Monthly, with weekly reads during launch.  ·  **Breakdown.** By outlet type, market relevance, message presence, proof presence, prominence and audience relevance.

**Target grounded in resources.** The target assumes United Partners media relations time, spokesperson availability, claim-cleared proof points and media-monitoring access.

**Target grounded in execution control.** United Partners controls story development and outreach, while publication volume, prominence and editorial wording depend on journalists and the news environment.

**Attribution method.** Assess whether earned attention coincided with outreach, briefings and released assets; do not claim it produced business movement without a controlled model.  —  directional evidence without controls — say 'coincided with', never 'caused'

**Known limitations.** Earned attention shows visibility and message quality, not reach to individuals or business impact.

#### Owned proof-page engagement

**Definition.** Visits, engaged sessions and completion actions on owned pages that explain The Invisible Thread through household, reach and service proof.

**Collection.** Weekly during launch, then monthly.  ·  **Breakdown.** By page, source, audience segment where available, device and content theme.

**Target grounded in resources.** The target assumes working owned pages, analytics tagging, content production time and selective paid support where approved.

**Target grounded in execution control.** United Partners controls content planning and measurement design, while site build, tagging access and traffic sources depend on Vivacom and its partners.

**Attribution method.** Compare traffic and engagement with live content, paid support and earned links; describe movement as coinciding with activity unless a controlled traffic test is used.  —  directional evidence without controls — say 'coincided with', never 'caused'

**Known limitations.** Engagement with a page does not prove attitude, behaviour or business impact.

#### Priority customer-friction themes

**Definition.** Monthly count and theme mix of customer complaints, app-review issues, regulator complaints and social-service logs linked to pricing, migration, outages, contracts and digital experience.

**Collection.** Monthly, with weekly issue checks during launch.  ·  **Breakdown.** By theme, channel, severity, audience segment where available and service area.

**Target grounded in resources.** The target assumes access to customer-service records, app-review data, regulator complaint themes, social-service logs and client service-team capacity.

**Target grounded in execution control.** United Partners controls reporting and response-line guidance, while friction reduction depends mainly on Vivacom service operations, product decisions and customer-care execution.

**Attribution method.** Track whether friction themes changed during the campaign and compare them with service actions and communications activity; describe communications as contributing only where response changes are documented.  —  directional evidence without controls — say 'coincided with', never 'caused'

**Known limitations.** A reduction in complaints cannot be assigned to communications alone without service-operation evidence and a matched comparison.

#### Employee understanding of the corporate story

**Definition.** Share of employees who can explain the Vivacom corporate story in plain language and connect So You Can and The Invisible Thread to named proof.

**Collection.** Quarterly.  ·  **Breakdown.** By function, location, seniority and employee group where data privacy and sample size allow.

**Target grounded in resources.** The target assumes Human Capital access, internal-channel support, leadership visibility and United Partners internal-communications planning time.

**Target grounded in execution control.** United Partners controls the story architecture and internal content plan, while employee participation and leadership delivery depend on Vivacom.

**Attribution method.** Compare employee understanding with internal communication exposure and leadership moments, then state that internal communications contributed where the evidence supports it.  —  correlation with some controls — say 'contributed to'

**Known limitations.** Employee understanding does not prove advocacy, retention or business performance on its own.

## Reporting

**Baseline before launch.** The baseline report is produced before launch. It records the latest Kantar tracker wave, message-recall starting point, earned-quality starting point, owned-channel starting point, customer-friction themes and employee-understanding baseline, then ends with target decisions and next actions.

**During the campaign.** During the campaign, reporting tracks whether So You Can and The Invisible Thread are being seen, understood and proved through the agreed channels. Each report ends with the decision to scale, change or stop activity, and with the next owner and date.

**One-page executive scorecard.** The one-page after-campaign executive scorecard is produced after the first full post-campaign Kantar tracker wave and the matching campaign performance data are available.

**Cadence.** Weekly reporting runs during launch and active campaign periods, monthly reporting reviews earned, owned and friction signals, and quarterly reporting reviews tracker movement and executive implications.

## The three checkpoints

- Measurement gate
- Optimization gate
- Learning gate

## Impact evaluation

Impact evaluation records the following as possible alternative explanations for any impact-level result, so the reading names what else could have moved the number before it credits the campaign:

- product changes
- price promotions
- competitor activity
- seasonality
- major news events

## Governance

| role | assigned to |
| --- | --- |
| Client lead | approvals |
| Account director | the brief and alignment |
| Strategy lead | baseline and methodology |
| Channel leads | tagging and collection |
| Analyst | data quality, dashboards and evaluation |
| Campaign lead | execution decisions |

## The non-negotiables

These are enforced, not recited.

- Do not use Advertising Value Equivalents
- Do not present impressions as actual reach unless the data supports deduplication
- Do not equate positive sentiment with behaviour or business impact
- Do not aggregate markets without showing material local differences
- Do not optimize solely for the easiest metric to collect
- Always show baseline, target, result and trend together
- Always distinguish what UP (United Partners) delivered, what audiences did, and what changed for the client
- Preserve definitions, query logic and tagging conventions so results are repeatable
- End every report with decisions and next actions, not merely observations

## How an objective is written

`By [date], increase/decrease [audience change] among [specific audience] from [baseline] to [target], contributing to [organizational objective]`

An objective not written this way cannot be measured, because at least one of the date, the change, the audience, the baseline, the target or the business goal is missing.

## The KPI ladder — the template to select from

A fill-in template, not a menu: the operator selects the right KPIs for this campaign. Every campaign carries measures on at least three levels, including one outtake or outcome.

| level | recommended core KPIs | supporting diagnostics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outputs | Quality coverage rate; key-message penetration | Volume, impressions, publication count, content produced, relevant audience reach |
| Outtakes | Message recall; understanding; positive consideration; trust/sentiment shift | Engagement rate, video completion, dwell time, comment themes |
| Outcomes | Qualified visits; enquiries; registrations; applications; stakeholder action | CTR (click-through rate), branded search, landing-page behaviour, downloads |
| Impact | Pipeline/revenue contribution; reputation shift; recruitment result; policy/societal progress | Cost per result, efficiency trend, client operational data |

### Quality coverage rate (replaces raw clipping totals)

Score each item against:

- priority outlet/influencer
- priority-audience relevance
- key-message inclusion
- positive or neutral tone
- brand/spokesperson prominence
- desired call to action
- original reporting vs syndication

Report both the percentage meeting the agreed threshold and the underlying criteria. Collapsing them into one unexplained proprietary score is the thing this replaces.

## KPI modules by campaign type

| campaign type | outtake | outcome | impact |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Brand / product | Awareness, recall, message understanding, preference | Branded search, qualified traffic, trials, enquiries, purchases | Sales, market share, customer acquisition, brand-equity change |
| Corporate reputation | Trust, perceived leadership, association with desired attributes | Stakeholder engagement, advocacy, meeting requests, partner interest | Reputation score, licence to operate, risk reduction, investor/partner confidence |
| B2B (business-to-business) thought leadership | Recognition of expertise & issue understanding | Senior engagement, content consumption, qualified leads, sales conversations | Influenced pipeline and revenue |
| Employer branding | Employer awareness, understanding of EVP (employer value proposition), consideration | Career-page visits, qualified applications, offer acceptance | Time-to-hire, cost-per-hire, retention / quality-of-hire |
| Public affairs / public sector | Awareness, understanding, confidence, stakeholder sentiment | Consultation participation, adoption, citizen action, stakeholder support | Policy progress, service uptake, compliance, societal benefit |
| Crisis communications | Response speed, message consistency, stakeholder coverage. Understanding, reassurance, misinformation penetration | Complaint behaviour, stakeholder support, recovery of positive/neutral conversation | Trust recovery, reduced customer loss, risk avoided |

## Reporting cadence

The weekly report must drive action, not simply document activity.

| cadence | what it carries |
| --- | --- |
| Weekly | Five headline KPIs against target, and the action required for each |
| Monthly | The one-page scorecard: objective/KPI, baseline, target, result, status, insight, decision |
| Quarterly | The eight-part evaluation narrative, read against the objectives |

## Open — waiting on a person

- **Is this the organizational objective we are held to?** — not yet approved; no owner recorded.

## The evaluation narrative

### Objective status — on, at risk or off, and why it happened

The objectives are measurable, but they are not yet ready for launch because several baselines are not established.

### Organizational contribution

The campaign can contribute to preference-led value growth, but it cannot claim to create business growth without a controlled model or matched comparison.

### Outputs, outtakes and outcomes evidence across PESO (Paid, Earned, Shared, Owned)

The framework covers outputs, outtakes, outcomes and impact through earned quality, recall, owned engagement, friction themes, employee understanding and tracker movement.

### Audience and market differences

The first readings must separate existing customers, the critical urban audience, Gen Z, employees and stakeholders because each group starts from a different position.

### What worked, and why

No live result exists yet, but the measurement design works because every metric connects back to So You Can, The Invisible Thread and a named audience change.

### What did not, and why

The pack is not launch-ready until Vivacom opens tracker access, message-recall baseline access, media monitoring, friction data and the employee source.

### Decisions and next actions

The next decision is to hold launch reporting until baselines and targets are set from real readings; the next actions are to confirm owners, sources and dates.

### Limitations and confidence, with three recommendations

Confidence is medium before launch because the logic is clear but the readings are missing. Next time, set the measurement owner before strategy approval, field the message baseline before platform approval and agree any matched comparison before claiming business contribution.

## Decisions and next actions

- **Increase recognition of Vivacom as a warmer, proof-led national role among existing customers.** Change the launch gate by making tracker access and target-setting a pre-launch requirement.
- **Message recall tied to So You Can and The Invisible Thread.** Scale measurement readiness by approving and fielding the recall baseline before launch.
- **Quality earned attention for the platform.** Change the monitoring setup so it records message quality, not volume alone.
- **Priority customer-friction themes.** Change the reporting pack so friction themes sit on the executive scorecard.
- **Employee understanding of the corporate story.** Change the internal plan by adding an employee baseline before leadership rollout.

## The re-tests

### The reputation & trust audit, re-run

**Still holds.** The original reputation tension still holds before launch. So You Can and The Invisible Thread answer a real gap because Vivacom has strong proof in fixed internet, pay TV, coverage, satellite, public-sector work and skills, but the record does not yet show one trusted national role.

### The say-do gap, re-tested

**Still holds.** The say-do gap still holds. The narrative wants Vivacom to feel warmer and more useful, but the record still shows customer friction in service, billing, app use, contracts, data and outages. So You Can can only work if The Invisible Thread is backed by visible service proof.

### The insight's tension, still holding or not

**Still holds.** The insight still holds. Vivacom has proof of usefulness, but the proof remains scattered across products, infrastructure and programmes. So You Can and The Invisible Thread remain the right strategic test because they turn that scattered proof into everyday Bulgarian outcomes.

### The strategic approach's continued distinctiveness

**Still holds.** The approach remains distinctive if it stays narrow. A1 can claim breadth and speed, Yettel can claim certified network quality and trust, and Neterra can claim specialist business continuity. Vivacom's safer lane remains useful daily digital life, proven from the household outward.

## The Learning Library

What the year taught, with what showed it.

| learning | evidence |
| --- | --- |
| So You Can must lead with useful customer proof, not with Vivacom's scale. | The Strategy One-Pager says the decision rule is that every message must show how Vivacom makes a real customer, household, workplace or public-service relationship work with named proof. |
| The Invisible Thread needs narrow claim language. | The Research & Insight Pack records that Opensignal supports coverage experience, while A1 leads speed and Yettel leads reliability and time on network. |
| Warmth cannot be solved by tone alone. | The Customer Warmth Gap records app, support, billing and contract friction beside the approved brief's warmth gap. |
| The platform can travel beyond existing customers only if it starts with the household relationship. | The Strategy One-Pager names Maya as the first believer and says the proof logic then extends to employees, business buyers, municipalities, regulators, media and parent-group stakeholders. |
| The annual review cannot yet judge performance movement. | The Measurement & Evaluation Framework says the launch baseline report, message-recall read, owned analytics read, friction read and employee-understanding baseline are still pending. |

## The say-do gap

Where the narrative outran what the evidence demonstrably shows.

**Last year said.** The strategy said Vivacom could use So You Can and The Invisible Thread to become a warmer, proof-led national role in Bulgaria's daily digital life.

**The evidence shows.** The record shows strong service, infrastructure and programme proof, but it also shows unresolved warmth, customer-friction, claim-clearance and baseline gaps before launch.

**The gap.** The idea is strategically sound, but the engagement has not yet proved that audiences believe it or that customer friction has changed.

**The action that closes it.** Before launch, Vivacom and United Partners must set the Kantar, message-recall, earned-quality, owned-channel, customer-friction and employee-understanding baselines, then clear every So You Can and The Invisible Thread claim against named proof.

## What worked, and what did not

- **Worked.** The Big Idea you approved in writing gives the work one clear platform: So You Can, launched through The Invisible Thread.
- **Worked.** The approach starts with the existing customer, which matches the approved brief's warmth gap and the daily service evidence.
- **Worked.** The proof boundary is clear: coverage means reach under the Opensignal coverage-experience measure, not speed, reliability or quality.
- **Worked.** The measurement framework connects reputation, recall, earned attention, service friction and employee understanding back to the business change.
- **Worked.** The research pack names the main risks before launch: overclaim, inconsistency and ambiguity.
- **Did not.** No full launch baseline exists yet, so the annual review cannot state movement on reputation, trust, awareness, stakeholder relationships or employer-brand signals.
- **Did not.** Primary audience validation is incomplete because the only recorded stakeholder interview voice is Elitza Georgieva.
- **Did not.** The organizational objective is not approved, and no owner is recorded.
- **Did not.** Several named stakeholders are not verified as current, so the stakeholder map cannot yet be used operationally without checks.
- **Did not.** The client long-form voice is not calibrated, so longer narrative documents still need extra style control before they ship.

## Keep, evolve or retire — drafted for the owner's judgement

The engine drafts these recommendations; a person decides them.

| element | recommendation | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| So You Can | Keep | It gives the work a simple customer-benefit platform and fits the evidence that Vivacom must show useful daily digital life. |
| The Invisible Thread | Keep | It joins fixed internet, television, coverage, service and public-use proof without forcing a broad leadership claim. |
| Household-outward strategy | Keep | It starts with Maya, the existing customer, and then extends the same proof logic to wider audiences. |
| Coverage-experience claim | Evolve | It is useful proof, but every use must state that coverage means reach and does not claim speed, reliability or total network quality. |
| Warm corporate tone without service proof | Retire | The record shows that warmth will fail if customers can disprove it through bills, app payments, outages, contracts or support. |
| Activity-led media volume | Retire | The Q1 2026 record shows Vivacom led article volume, but that did not prove trust, recall or audience response. |

## Refreshed objectives for the coming year

Drafted for written re-approval — nothing below is approved yet.

- By 30 June 2027, increase recognition of Vivacom as a warmer, proof-led national role among existing customers from the latest Kantar brand tracker baseline before launch to a target agreed with Vivacom after that reading, contributing to preference-led support for Vivacom's value growth among existing and prospective Bulgarian customers.
- By 30 June 2027, increase recall of So You Can and The Invisible Thread among existing customers and the critical urban audience from the pre-launch message-recall baseline to a target agreed before launch, contributing to preference-led support for Vivacom's value growth among existing and prospective Bulgarian customers.

- By 30 June 2027, increase employee understanding of the Vivacom corporate story among employees from the employee pulse or Human Capital baseline to a target agreed after that read, contributing to preference-led support for Vivacom's value growth among existing and prospective Bulgarian customers.

## The next cycle's brief, re-based

The next cycle brief is re-based on proof, not assumption. It takes the pre-launch Kantar brand tracker, message-recall read, earned-quality review, owned-channel analytics, customer-friction read, employee-understanding baseline, stakeholder verification and claim-clearance decisions, then uses them to test whether So You Can and The Invisible Thread are being seen, understood and believed.

# Tactical Roadmap

The phased twelve-month sequence of the approved platform: signature moments balanced against an always-on presence, every tactic an Activation Card placed by date, channel, audience, message, phase and KPI (key performance indicator).

**The platform is approved: So You Can, decided by Maria Bengtsson.**
**The owners and the calendar below are not yet approved; no owner is recorded.**

**Period and markets.** The campaign period is a 12-month Vivacom Bulgaria roadmap from Month 1 proof lock to Month 12 recalibration, with local-market adaptation available only where United Group deploys the So You Can toolkit.

## The phases

| phase | objective | months |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-Seed | Lock the So You Can proof, claim boundaries, service response lines and internal readiness before public launch activity. | 1 · 2 |
| Launch | Introduce So You Can through The Invisible Thread with an earned-led household story and owned proof behind it. | 3 · 4 |
| Sustain | Keep the platform visible through recurring household proof, service answers, reach explainers and trained advocates. | 5 · 6 · 7 · 8 · 9 |
| Amplify | Extend the proof from homes to workplaces, municipalities, public services and credible third parties once evidence is cleared. | 10 · 11 · 12 |

The four phases are the year. Inside a phase, each major moment runs Tease → Launch → Sustain → Amplify; across the year the corporate rollout widens the audience Engage → Enhance → Advocate → Amplify.

## The activation map

Built before the calendar: every tactic placed against an audience, a message and a channel.

| audience | message / pillar | channel | tactic | tier | phase |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Legal and Regulatory Affairs, leaders, communications teams, service teams and priority stakeholder handlers. | Reach is proved carefully, not claimed broadly. | Owned and internal | Proof and Claim Lock | Hygiene | Pre-Seed |
| Existing customers, employees, service teams and leaders. | Service moments prove the idea in public. | Owned, shared and earned response | Service Moment Response Lines | Hygiene | all phases |
| Existing customers, service teams, communications teams and trained advocates. | Vivacom keeps The Invisible Thread working from the home outward. | Owned, shared and earned monitoring | Conversation Management Loop | Hygiene | all phases |
| Media contacts, stakeholders, communications teams and leaders. | The Invisible Thread works when proof is visible. | Earned, owned and shared | The Observatory Newsroom | Hygiene | all phases |
| Employees, service teams, leaders and spokespeople. | Every service moment is where The Invisible Thread is either proved or broken in public. | Owned and internal | Internal Alignment and Spokesperson Pack | Hub | Pre-Seed |
| Existing customers, with Maya as the first believer, plus media and consumer audiences. | Vivacom keeps The Invisible Thread working, So You Can get on with daily life. | Earned, owned, shared and selective paid | The Invisible Thread at Home | Hero | Launch |
| Existing customers and consumer audiences. | The Invisible Thread starts at home. | Owned, shared and paid | Household Launch Reinforcement | Hub | Launch |
| Consumer customers and the critical urban audience. | The household relationship is Vivacom's first proof. | Owned, shared, earned and paid | Household Proof Series | Hub | Sustain → Amplify |
| Regulators, media, government and parent-group stakeholders. | Coverage-experience proof means reach, not speed, reliability or quality. | Earned, owned and paid amplification | Reach, Clearly Explained | Hub | Sustain → Amplify |
| Employee advocates, service-team champions, credible alumni and partner advocates. | Useful relationships are stronger than broad claims about size. | Shared, earned and stakeholder briefings | Expert and Advocacy Proof Kit | Hub | Sustain → Amplify |
| Business buyers, public-sector customers, municipalities, employees and parent-group stakeholders. | The same proof logic carries from the home to workplaces, municipalities and public services. | Earned, owned, events and stakeholder briefings | Beyond the Home Case Stories | Hero | Amplify |
| Parent-group stakeholders, media and professional influencers. | Useful relationships are stronger than broad claims about size. | Earned, stakeholder briefings and shared | Credible Third-Party Visibility Push | Hero | Amplify |
| Executive, communications, service and stakeholder teams. | The Invisible Thread works when proof is visible. | Owned and executive reporting | Year-Close Scorecard and Recalibration | Hygiene | Amplify |

## The Hero / Hub / Hygiene balance

**Hero — signature moments, about a fifth.** Hero effort is concentrated in The Invisible Thread at Home, Beyond the Home Case Stories and the Credible Third-Party Visibility Push, giving the year a small set of signature So You Can moments.

**Hub — sustained programmes, about three fifths.** Hub effort carries most of the work through internal alignment, launch reinforcement, the Household Proof Series, Reach Clearly Explained and the Advocacy Proof Kit.

**Hygiene — always-on maintenance, about a fifth.** Hygiene effort protects the platform through proof lock, service response lines, the Conversation Management Loop, The Observatory Newsroom and the year-close scorecard.

## The Activation Cards

No tactic goes on the calendar until it is a card.

### Proof and Claim Lock

**Insight.** The So You Can platform fails if reach, service or household proof outruns the evidence customers and stakeholders can check.

**Idea.** Lock the approved proof, do-not-say lines and The Invisible Thread claim boundaries before anything public runs.

**Engagement — the mechanic.** Use internal working sessions and written clearance to align Legal and Regulatory Affairs, leaders and communications teams before launch.

**Desired outcome.** Vivacom enters launch with one cleared proof base for So You Can and no broad network or size claim in market.  ·  **Targets.** By the end of Month 1, the claim register is read for every household, service and reach claim, with source, clearance status and do-not-say risk visible.  ·  **Approver.** Elitza Georgieva

**Signature.** So You Can / The Invisible Thread proof lock  ·  **KPI.** Priority claims with named proof source — percentage of claims in the register, So You Can claim register · Do-not-say risk resolved before release — integer count of unresolved risks, pre-publish governance checklist  ·  **Month.** 1

### Service Moment Response Lines

**Insight.** A service issue can prove or break The Invisible Thread in public.

**Idea.** Build plain-language updates for outages, bills, app payments, contract questions and help moments; live, unpromoted, until the Launch moment in Month 3.

**Engagement — the mechanic.** Publish first through owned service channels when needed, then support through shared updates and earned response lines if the issue becomes public.

**Desired outcome.** Customers see service friction answered as part of the So You Can promise, not treated as a side issue.  ·  **Targets.** From Month 1 through Month 12, the service response register is read weekly and after each visible service issue for approval speed, clarity and repeated question themes.  ·  **Approver.** Elitza Georgieva

**Signature.** The Invisible Thread in service  ·  **KPI.** Approved service response time — median hours from issue log to approved line, service response register · Customer understanding of service updates — 1-to-5 clarity score, plain-language service update rubric  ·  **Months.** 1 to 12

### Conversation Management Loop

**Insight.** The platform cannot hold reputation between bursts if nobody is listening, triaging, responding and escalating every day.

**Idea.** Run the daily listen-triage-respond-escalate loop under So You Can so service questions and proof opportunities are caught before they drift.

**Engagement — the mechanic.** Read social, service, app-review and earned-media signals daily, route them to the right owner and feed cleared language back into response teams.

**Desired outcome.** Vivacom keeps The Invisible Thread credible between campaign moments.  ·  **Targets.** Daily from Month 1 through Month 12, the conversation log is read for live issue themes, escalation status, approved response use and advocacy opportunities.  ·  **Approver.** Maria Bengtsson

**Signature.** So You Can response loop  ·  **KPI.** Escalated issues with owner and next action recorded — percentage of escalated issues, conversation management log · Recurring customer questions converted into approved answers — integer count of question themes closed, question-theme register  ·  **Months.** 1 to 12

### The Observatory Newsroom

**Insight.** Moments worth entering close quickly, and The Invisible Thread needs cleared proof before Vivacom speaks into them.

**Idea.** Run a newsroom watch that spots relevant household, service, reach and stakeholder moments for So You Can; live, unpromoted, until the Launch moment in Month 3.

**Engagement — the mechanic.** Read media, competitor, regulator, service and community signals, then prepare cleared owned, earned and shared lines for moments worth entering.

**Desired outcome.** Vivacom enters relevant moments with proof-led lines instead of late or broad claims.  ·  **Targets.** Weekly from Month 2 through Month 12, the newsroom watchlist is read for moment fit, proof readiness, channel route and whether the moment should be entered or left quiet.  ·  **Approver.** Maria Bengtsson

**Signature.** The Observatory for So You Can  ·  **KPI.** Relevant moments with cleared entry line before window closes — percentage of entered moments, Observatory watchlist · Moments rejected for weak proof before publishing — integer count of rejected moments, moment-fit decision log  ·  **Months.** 2 to 12

### Internal Alignment and Spokesperson Pack

**Insight.** Spokespeople can only protect the So You Can idea if they know the proof, the guardrails and the words not to use.

**Idea.** Brief leaders, service teams and spokespeople on The Invisible Thread, the proof base, audience messages and do-not-say lines before public launch; live, unpromoted, until the Launch moment in Month 3.

**Engagement — the mechanic.** Use internal briefings, a 30-second pitch, spokesperson materials and Q&A (questions and answers) rehearsal to test whether teams can use approved lines.

**Desired outcome.** The organisation can explain So You Can consistently before the first earned story lands.  ·  **Targets.** By the end of Month 2, the briefing record is read for attendance, approved-language use in rehearsal and unresolved spokesperson questions.  ·  **Approver.** Maria Bengtsson

**Signature.** So You Can spokesperson pack  ·  **KPI.** Briefed teams passing approved-language rehearsal — percentage of participating teams, spokesperson rehearsal rubric · Unresolved launch questions after briefing — integer count of open questions, internal Q&A register  ·  **Month.** 2

### The Invisible Thread at Home

**Insight.** Existing customers judge Vivacom first through ordinary household moments: internet, television, bills, app payments, outages and help.

**Idea.** Launch So You Can through one named household story that shows The Invisible Thread helping daily life continue without asking people to admire the system.

**Engagement — the mechanic.** Lead through earned media, then drive readers to owned proof pages and shared assets that explain the service and support behind the story.

**Desired outcome.** Existing customers begin to see Vivacom as useful, warmer and proof-led.  ·  **Targets.** In Month 3, the launch coverage report and owned proof-page analytics are read after the earned launch and again at month close.  ·  **Approver.** Maria Bengtsson

**Signature.** #SoYouCan / The Invisible Thread starts at home  ·  **KPI.** Earned stories carrying the household proof message — percentage of launch coverage, earned launch quality report · Proof-page visits from launch routes — integer count of tagged visits, owned proof-page analytics report  ·  **Month.** 3

### Household Launch Reinforcement

**Insight.** The first household story needs repetition in owned and shared channels before it becomes a usable platform memory.

**Idea.** Use the social pack and owned proof pages to repeat The Invisible Thread at home under So You Can after the earned launch.

**Engagement — the mechanic.** Publish approved posts, route paid support to proof pages and answer household questions through the response loop.

**Desired outcome.** The launch idea moves from one story into a recognisable household proof pattern.  ·  **Targets.** In Month 4, the social pack report and proof-page analytics are read weekly for approved post engagement, repeat visits and service-friction themes.  ·  **Approver.** Maria Bengtsson

**Signature.** #SoYouCan at home  ·  **KPI.** Approved household posts with proof-page route used — percentage of published posts, social pack publishing checklist · Repeat visits to household proof pages — integer count of tagged repeat visits, owned proof-page analytics report  ·  **Month.** 4

### Household Proof Series

**Insight.** Vivacom is most believable when it proves the relationship customers already use every day.

**Idea.** Publish a recurring owned hub series connecting fixed internet, television, coverage-experience reach and help as one household relationship under The Invisible Thread.

**Engagement — the mechanic.** Use owned stories as the proof home, feed selected stories to influencers and use paid and shared routes to bring readers back to the proof.

**Desired outcome.** The household relationship becomes the repeatable proof of So You Can, not a one-off launch story.  ·  **Targets.** Monthly from Month 5 through Month 12, the series dashboard is read for repeat visits, shared engagement, influencer proof use and affinity-tracker movement when the tracker is available.  ·  **Approver.** Maria Bengtsson

**Signature.** The Invisible Thread at home  ·  **KPI.** Returning readers to household proof stories — percentage of tagged story readers, household proof series dashboard · Influencer or creator references using approved proof — integer count of approved references, influencer proof-use register  ·  **Months.** 5 to 12

**Insight.** Coverage-experience proof can support reach, but it cannot support claims about speed, reliability or overall quality.

**Idea.** Create claim-cleared explainers and media lines that show how Vivacom proves reach while keeping The Invisible Thread inside approved evidence.

**Engagement — the mechanic.** Brief media and stakeholders with the source boundary visible, then amplify the cleared explanation through owned and selective paid channels.

**Desired outcome.** Regulators, media and parent-group stakeholders see a disciplined proof story instead of a broad network claim.  ·  **Targets.** Monthly from Month 6 through Month 12, the reach wording report is read for approved wording pull-through, unsupported network claims and clearance status.  ·  **Approver.** Elitza Georgieva

**Insight.** Advocacy asked for before people understand the proof becomes noise.

**Idea.** Equip employee advocates, service-team champions, credible alumni and partner advocates trained by the Conversation Management Loop with approved So You Can proof and disclosure guidance.

**Engagement — the mechanic.** Give advocates proof cards, draft lines, disclosure rules and escalation routes, then read their use before widening participation.

**Desired outcome.** The people closest to the proof can carry The Invisible Thread without drifting into unsupported claims.  ·  **Targets.** Monthly from Month 8 through Month 11, the advocacy register is read for approved proof use, disclosure status, questions raised and lines needing correction.  ·  **Approver.** Maria Bengtsson

**Signature.** So You Can advocacy kit  ·  **KPI.** Advocate posts or briefings using approved proof without correction — percentage of reviewed advocate outputs, advocacy proof-use register · Disclosure-compliant advocate outputs — percentage of reviewed advocate outputs, creator and advocate disclosure checklist  ·  **Months.** 8 to 11

**Insight.** The household proof logic can travel only when workplace, municipal and public-service examples are named, current and cleared.

**Idea.** Publish cleared case stories that show So You Can extending The Invisible Thread from homes to workplaces, municipalities and public services.

**Engagement — the mechanic.** Use earned stories, owned case pages, events and stakeholder briefings only after partner and claim clearance.

**Desired outcome.** The platform widens without becoming a broad leadership or scale claim.  ·  **Targets.** Monthly from Month 10 through Month 12, the case clearance tracker is read for named-party approval, claim clearance, stakeholder engagement and qualified interest.  ·  **Approver.** Iva Gajić

**Signature.** The Invisible Thread beyond the home  ·  **KPI.** Case stories cleared by named partner and claim owner — integer count of cleared case stories, case clearance tracker · Qualified business or public-sector interest from case routes — integer count of qualified enquiries, stakeholder engagement register  ·  **Months.** 10 to 12

### Credible Third-Party Visibility Push

**Insight.** For corporate reputation, third-party proof carries more trust than paid reach alone.

**Idea.** Use professional influencers, analysts, editors and respected partners to show that So You Can is proved through visible relationships, not size claims.

**Engagement — the mechanic.** Brief credible third parties with the approved 30-second pitch, proof notes and do-not-say lines, then amplify only compliant earned and shared outputs.

**Desired outcome.** The platform gains visible validation without losing claim discipline.  ·  **Targets.** In Month 11, the third-party visibility report is read for approved-language use, earned quality, disclosure compliance and do-not-say breaches.  ·  **Approver.** Iva Gajić

**Signature.** Proof you can see  ·  **KPI.** Third-party outputs using approved So You Can language — percentage of reviewed outputs, third-party language audit · Do-not-say breaches in amplified third-party material — integer count of breaches, visibility compliance log  ·  **Month.** 11

**Insight.** The platform only improves if reputation, service, proof and channel signals are read together.

**Idea.** Close the So You Can year with one executive scorecard across paid, earned, shared, owned, service and reputation signals.

**Engagement — the mechanic.** Read the year's tagged results, tracker movement, service themes, earned quality and proof performance, then set the next-cycle recalibration.

**Desired outcome.** Vivacom can see what The Invisible Thread proved, what weakened it and what should change next year.  ·  **Targets.** In Month 12, the executive scorecard is read with all tagged PESO (Paid, Earned, Shared, Owned), service and reputation measures available for annual review.  ·  **Approver.** Asen Velikov

## The always-on loop

Underneath the phases runs the Conversation Management loop — supported by the always-on newsroom running proactive stories and reactive issues management: establish goals → gather assets → develop proprietary content → deploy across owned, earned and paid → train advocates → deploy the trained advocates → measure → refine. **Then visibility** — Months 11 to 12: Credible Third-Party Visibility Push, Year-Close Scorecard and Recalibration. This stage proves that the platform has earned outside validation and can be measured before the next cycle is widened.

UNITED PARTNERS · AI TRANSFORMATION
The Corporate Reputation
Strategy System
THE COMPLETE DOCUMENT LIBRARY
Thirteen documents, one volume: the master runbook, the navigation map and language  
standard, the nine step guides, and the two system documents.
July 2026
Contents of this volume
In reading order. Each document begins on its own cover page.
# Document Role
1 CD-S-002 — Corporate Reputation Strategy (Integrated Master) The runbook the team follows — 11 steps, gates, 
deliverables
2 Guide Index & Navigation Map The front door — how it all fits, plus the language 
standard
3 Client Intake & Briefing Toolkit Step guide · Steps 1–3 (brief, debrief, final brief)
4 Research & Audit Guide Step guide · Step 4

UNITED PARTNERS · AI TRANSFORMATION
CD-S-002
Corporate Reputation Strategy, Built From Scratch
The 11-Step AI-Aligned Process · the master specification the AI transformation team follows
Integrated master — the CD-S-002 from-scratch workflow enriched with the AI-Aligned Process spec  
(deliverables, formats, gates, AI/human split).
Measurement standard: AMEC Barcelona Principles 4.0 + AMEC IEF
About this document
This is the master specification for building a corporate communications strategy the United Partners way — 
and the blueprint the AI automation must follow step for step. It integrates two source documents into one: the 
CD-S-002 from-scratch workflow (the reasoning spine and the Enterprise/SME and B2B/B2C forks) and the AI-
Aligned Process (the per-step purpose, frameworks, AI/human split, quality gate, deliverable and document 
format).
From-scratch premise. Nothing about positioning, narrative or pillars is pre-decided — the workflow reasons to 
them from evidence. The spine is identical for all clients; the branch blocks show where the path forks for 
Enterprise vs. SME and B2B vs. B2C.
Two principles the engine must never break
1 · AI raises the floor, the human sets the ceiling. Every step has an explicit AI-drafts / human-owns split. The 
engine generates volume, checks line-of-sight and enforces the gates; a person judges, interprets, chooses the 
ownable idea and signs. No insight, approach, narrative, platform or impact claim ships on autopilot.
2 · Nothing advances that cannot trace up the chain. Business objective → communication objective → 
strategic approach → narrative → messages → pillars → platform → tactics → KPIs. Every quality gate tests this 
line of sight; anything orphaned goes to the appendix, never the strategy.
Legend
Marker Meaning
Core spine Applies to all clients
Enterprise / SME Fork by client size
B2B / B2C Fork by market
GATE Review gate — must pass to advance
DECISION Client-owned call
HARD STOP No downstream work begins until passed
LOCK Scaffold converted into approved strategy
The flow at a glance
Eleven steps, grouped into four movements — Frame, Discover, Build, Activate & Evaluate. The reasoning 
stages of the original CD-S-002 (positioning options, recommend direction, founder elicitation, lock the 
platform, proof discipline) are folded into the matching steps.
Movement Steps
FRAME 1 · Brief from the client   2 · Debrief (Q&A) + founder/executive elicitation   3 · Final brief (locked — the task 
for AI)
DISCOVER 4 · Research & analysis   5 · Frame the problem → Insights defined   (optional) Creative Big Idea — Idea Haus
BUILD 6 · Strategic approach (positioning options → recommend → prioritise)   7 · Narrative, key messages & pillars 
→ LOCK the platform   8 · Communications platform architecture
ACTIVATE & EVALUATE 9 · Engagement plan & execution rollout   10 · Measurement & evaluation   11 · Annual review & update
Cross-cutting.  The Language & Style Standard and the Risks, Guardrails & Proof Discipline (below) apply to 
every step and are enforced at every gate.
Language & Style Standard
Applies to every document at every step. Two decisions govern how the work reads: which language it is 
delivered in, and which voice it is written in. Both are set early, locked in the final brief, and enforced at every 
drafting gate — so a corporate reputation strategy reads as one considered, consistent voice from the brief to 
the scorecard.
Decision 1 — Delivery language
Rule
Default Deliver client-facing documents in the language of the client's primary stakeholders and approval chain. Internal 
engine artifacts (research pack, insight cards, gap registers) are produced in the engine's working language, unless 
the client team works in a local language.
Multi-market Build one core set in the lead language, then localise per market — mirroring the global-toolkit → localised 
principle in Step 9. A small set of global terms stays fixed; local markets adapt language, hooks and proof.
Where it is locked The delivery language(s) is a locked field in the Step 3 final brief. No drafting begins until it is set.
Decision 2 — Voice & style: mirror the client where strong, default to house 
style where not
The strategy should feel native to the client. Where the client already communicates well, we mirror their voice; 
where they don't, we hold the line with the UP house style — and note that a weak or inflated corporate voice 
is often part of the reputation problem the strategy must solve.
Style calibration (Step 1, refined 
in Step 4)
Action
If strong enough Capture a one-page Client Style Note (tone, typical sentence length, vocabulary, how they refer to 
themselves, signature do/don't words) and mirror it across all client-facing deliverables so the strategy 
reads as their own voice.
If not strong enough Default to the UP house style below, and flag the gap — an unclear, jargon-heavy or inflated corporate 
voice is frequently a symptom of the reputation problem, not a neutral choice.
The UP house style (the floor every document meets)
Principle Rule
Plain language Write for a smart reader in a hurry. No jargon; no acronym without its first-use definition; no filler.
Short & active One idea per sentence; active voice; short paragraphs. Speak in headlines, then support them.
Evidence over adjectives Claims carry proof, not superlatives — the proof-first guardrail applies to language, not just content.
Confident, not boastful Warm, not casual; assured, not inflated. No hedging that hides a decision; no claim that outruns its evidence.
Consistent terminology The same thing is called the same name throughout — preserve definitions across every document (the AMEC 
discipline).
Reader-first structure Headline first, then the support beneath it — the Trident 1°→2°→3° logic applied to how every page is written.
How the standard applies by document type
Document type Standard
Internal analytical Research pack, insight cards, gap registers — precise, sourced, plain. Working language. Clarity over polish, 
but never jargon.
Client-facing strategic Brief, one-pager, narrative, message architecture, platform — the client's voice where strong, else UP house 
style. Polished and board-ready.
Execution collateral Releases, social, Q&A, spokesperson materials — the audience's language and the brand narrative voice. On-
template, on-brand, do-not-say lines enforced.
Measurement Scorecard and reports — plain and decision-led. Baseline/target/result/trend always shown; no jargon, no 
inflated attribution.
Enforcement.  The delivery language and the chosen voice (mirror vs house style) are locked in the Step 3 final 
brief; the Client Style Note travels with the engagement and every drafting step references it; the pre-publish 
quality gate in Step 9 and each step's own gate check for language and style compliance before anything 
advances.
Risks, Guardrails & Proof Discipline
A cross-cutting discipline that gives the workflow teeth. It applies from the first build and is checked at every 
gate.
1. Name the primary reputation risks (overclaim, inconsistency, ambiguity).
2. Set the proof-quality ladder: named ref > anon-verifiable > artifact > demo. Place validated proof on the 
ladder; drop what cannot be placed.
3. Assign accountable review gates with named owners GATE.
4. Write the “do-not-say” list — no invented clients, metrics or claims.
5. Set claim-tiering language rules (the attribution wording must match the evidence).
Enforced by the engine.  This discipline is operationalised by the Adversarial Review Board's Competitor, CFO, 
Journalist and GC personas and by the do-not-say lines carried in Steps 7–9 — so weak or unsubstantiated 
claims are caught before they reach a stakeholder.
The Process — eleven steps
Each step sets out its purpose, the frameworks the engine runs, the AI/human split, the quality gate, and the 
exact deliverable and document format. Where the original CD-S-002 adds reasoning detail or a client fork, it is 
folded into the matching step as Process steps and Forks.
FRAME   empty slate → a locked, approved brief
Step 1 —  Brief from the Client
Source guide: Client Intake & Briefing Toolkit (Pass 1 — Prepare). The engine's Frame phase begins here.
Purpose Receive and frame the client's request — but never take the brief at face value. A corporate reputation 
strategy is only as good as the brief beneath it; weak inputs produce a confident, well-structured, wrong 
strategy.
Frameworks & tools The desk-audit pass before any conversation: Business audit, Reputation audit, Social & digital audit, 
Competitive audit, Stakeholder scan, Context scan (regulatory/ESG/geopolitical). Arrive with a hypothesis — a 
provisional point of view on the reputation problem and the white space. Run the Style calibration (read the 
client's own published communications).
What the AI drafts Runs the six pre-conversation audits from public sources; assembles a briefing pack on the company, its 
reputation, its peers and the category; drafts a provisional problem hypothesis and a draft Client Style Note for 
the operator to challenge.
What the human owns Adds the point of view; decides which hypothesis to test; tailors the question bank so every question shows the 
client we already understand them.
Quality gate The desk audit is complete and a written hypothesis exists before any client conversation. “Tailor, don't recite” 
— the question bank is a starting point, not a script.
Deliverable Pre-Engagement Briefing Pack + Provisional Hypothesis (+ draft Client Style Note)
Document format Word document (6 short audit sections + one-paragraph hypothesis), 3–5 pages. Stored in the client folder on 
Google Drive.
Process steps (from CD-S-002 · Phase 1)
1. Capture client type: industry, market, B2B/B2C, size (Enterprise vs SME).
2. State the trigger event and the real business/reputation problem.
3. Set objectives as business outcomes (not positioning).
4. List candidate audiences — unranked at this stage.
5. Define must-say / must-avoid guardrails.
6. Log constraints: legal, regulatory, confidentiality, AI-use limits, anonymization.
7. Name expected outputs and “what good looks like”.
Fork — Brief emphasis forks by client size
Enterprise SME
Parent-group / board constraints captured Founder ambition & constraints captured
Regulatory & disclosure exposure logged Lean, execution-by-small-team framing
Multi-stakeholder approval chain mapped Name/search & discoverability noted early
Step 2 —  Debrief (Q&A) + Founder / Executive Elicitation
Source guide: Client Intake & Briefing Toolkit (Pass 2 — Ask). The structured client conversation(s).
Purpose Extract the maximum useful information from the client — and surface the conflicts between stakeholders — 
through structured, well-prepared conversation. The brief is a battlefield: the CEO wants boldness, the CFO 
wants value, the GC wants safety, HR wants internal-first. Elicit substance — never invent it.
Frameworks & tools The eight-set question bank: A essentials/the ask · B business & organizational context · C reputation & 
stakeholder context · D audience & insight · E programme, narrative & channels · F team, culture & ways of 
working · G constraints & guardrails (incl. AI-use / MNPI) · H logistics & decision process. Technique: open, then 
probe with “why?” and “so what?” until the real answer surfaces. Founder/executive elicitation prompts to 
surface the ownable line and the first ladder-ranked proof point.
What the AI drafts Tailors the question bank to this client from the Step 1 pack; tracks answers against the eight sets in real time; 
flags thin or evasive answers for follow-up; drafts the debrief write-up.
What the human owns Runs the conversation; interviews more than one stakeholder; listens for the unsaid (the tension, the 
hesitation, the downplayed misperception); reflects the problem back before leaving.
Quality gate More than one voice interviewed where possible; the stakeholder conflicts are captured as a Client Alignment

Step 5 —  Frame the Problem → Insights Defined
Source guide: Discovering & Defining Insights. The most important distinction in the whole engine — a strategy built on a 
fact is a strategy built on sand.
Purpose Turn research into the one previously-unspoken truth about people that, once said, feels obviously true — and 
reveals an opportunity. Data tells you WHAT; an insight tells you WHY it matters and WHAT it means, and 
always carries a tension the strategy can resolve.
Frameworks & tools Insight-or-not calibration; empirical + intuitive insight (prove and discover); the 5 T's (True, Tacit, Touches the 
heart, Tension, Triggers action); the So-What ladder (Data → Information → Insight → Foresight) and the five 
traps; the seven-step extraction process; the Sweet Spot; the Distinctiveness Gate; the Validation Gate (test 
contrarian insights with the real audience). Reputation lens: trust drivers, the say-do gap, the misperception, 
the stakeholder tension.
What the AI drafts Generates many candidate insights (empirical & intuitive) from the research; surfaces supporting evidence; 
runs the So-What ladder, the 5 T's, the traps and the Distinctiveness check; drafts the Killer Insight card.

candidate is the one. AI never authors the insight on autopilot.
Quality gate It is an insight, not a fact/statistic/observation; passes all 5 T's; survived the So-What ladder and avoids the five 
traps; sits in the Sweet Spot and passes the Distinctiveness Gate; validated with the audience where 
contrarian; human-owned, sourced, sharply written; no more than three — ideally one.

Step 6 —  Strategic Approach
Source guide: Building the Strategic Approach. Where the insight becomes a decision about how to win — the single 
organizing idea for how communications will change what stakeholders think, feel or do.

messages/channels/tactics → KPIs, all in line of sight). The SMART+I communication objective. The GET /

the insight; expressed as GET/WHO/TO/BY plus one-line positioning; chosen from options and passes the

Step 10 —  Measurement & Evaluation
Source guide: Campaign Measurement Framework (AMEC-based). Start with the business change, then work backwards to 
activities and metrics. Not advisory — adjudicated.
Purpose Demonstrate not just that a campaign was visible, but whether the intended audience noticed it, understood 
it, acted differently, and contributed to a meaningful client outcome — the same way, whoever ran it.
Frameworks & tools The AMEC chain (Organizational objectives → Communication objectives → Inputs → Activities → Outputs → 
Outtakes → Outcomes → Impact) with the vertical rule. The Measurement Brief (approved at Step 3). The KPI 
ladder (measures on ≥ 3 levels, incl. one outtake/outcome); Quality Coverage Rate (replaces clip counts); 
engagement quality; disciplined SOV. KPI modules by campaign type (corporate reputation, employer 
branding, crisis in scope). PESO measurement chain. Reporting cadence: baseline before launch; daily/weekly 
during; one-page executive scorecard after. Attribution wording auto-matched to confidence (generated / 
contributed to / coincided with).
What the AI drafts Selects KPIs from the vetted set per campaign type; wires tagging/UTM/CRM fields; assembles daily/weekly 
reports and the executive scorecard; matches attribution wording to the evidence confidence level; flags any 
KPI without a baseline/target.
What the human owns Approves the organizational objective and success criteria; establishes baseline, KPI definitions and 
interpretation; turns weekly findings into execution decisions; judges attribution and alternative explanations.
Quality gate (three 
checkpoints)
Measurement gate: no brief approved without baseline, target, source, owner. Optimization gate: weekly 
performance must produce a documented decision. Learning gate: closure adds ≥ 3 findings to the benchmark 
& learning library. Non-negotiables enforced: no AVEs; no impressions-as-reach; positive sentiment ≠ impact; 
show baseline/target/result/trend together; distinguish what UP delivered vs what audiences did vs what 
changed for the client.

5. Language requirements — every document, no exceptions
Every document we deliver must be simple, professional and understandable — in its wording and as a whole 
text. A strategy that cannot be understood at first reading is not finished. These requirements apply to all 
documents, internal and client-facing, and are checked at every gate.
5.1 The wording — sentence by sentence
Requirement Rule
Plain words Use the everyday word, not the impressive one. No jargon. No acronym without its meaning at first use. No filler.
Short sentences One idea per sentence. Active voice. If a sentence needs a second read, rewrite it.
Concrete, not abstract Say what happens, who does it, and by when. Replace vague claims with facts.
Proof, not adjectives Every claim carries evidence. Delete superlatives that carry none.
Confident, not inflated Assured, warm, direct. No hedging that hides a decision; no claim that outruns its proof.
One name per thing Call the same thing by the same name in every document. Never rename a concept midway.
Reader's language, not the 
method's
Client-facing documents are written in the reader's language, not the method's — the frameworks run the kitchen, but 
the menu is in plain words. No process term (lock, disposition, quarantine, proof pair) reaches a client page 
unexplained.
5.2 The whole text — how the document reads end to end
Requirement Rule
One clear purpose The reader knows in the first paragraph what this document is and what it is for.
Headline first Every section starts with its point, then the support beneath it. A busy reader who reads only the headings still gets the 
story.
Logical flow Sections follow one order of thought. Each builds on the one before. No jumps, no repeats.
Right length As short as the content allows. Anything that supports but does not advance the argument goes to an appendix.
Visual clarity Tables for comparisons, short lists for sequences, bold sparingly. White space is part of the writing.
Self-contained A new reader can use the document without a briefing. Terms, context and next steps are inside it.
5.3 The test before any document ships
The plain-language check — run at every gate
  ☐ Could a smart reader outside our industry understand every sentence at first reading?
  ☐ Does every section start with its point? Do the headings alone tell the story?
  ☐ Is there any jargon, unexplained acronym, filler or empty superlative left? Remove it.
  ☐ Does every claim carry its proof?
  ☐ Is the document as short as it can be while still complete?
  ☐ Is every client-facing page in the reader's language — no unexplained process terms?
  ☐ Would you be comfortable reading it aloud to the client's board?
Who enforces it.  The AI applies these rules in every draft. The human checks them at every gate. The Review 
Board's Journalist persona attacks unclear or inflated language. A document that fails the check goes back — it 
does not advance.
Relation to the master.  This section is the working summary of the Language & Style Standard in the CD-S-002 
master (delivery language, mirror-the-client vs house style, document-type rules). The master holds the full 
standard; this is the everyday test.

Haus (optional) · Strategic Approach · Narrative, Messages & Pillars · Communications Platform ·
