# Real Client Case For AI Workflow Demo

Selected case: Corporate brand strategy, built from scratch

Client: A real United Partners telecom client, sanitized. No client name is used.

Status: Sanitized, confidential, for AI workflow demo.

## Short Ask

This case is a corporate brand and corporate communications strategy built from a blank slate. The client has no approved corporate brand strategy, and positioning, narrative, and pillar architecture are not pre-decided. The workflow must reason from evidence to a defensible strategy and show what is fact, what is missing, and what is strategic judgment.

## Client Type

Industry/category: Telecommunications: fixed line, mobile, broadband internet, TV/entertainment, and B2B solutions such as IoT, smart cities, cloud, and digital education.

Market/country: A single mid-sized European national market. The client is a subsidiary of a larger regional telecoms-and-media group.

B2B or B2C: Both. Mass-market consumer is the revenue core. B2B, enterprise, and public-sector solutions are strategic growth areas.

Current business situation: Market leader by revenue and the incumbent operator. Operationally strong, with leading network, fixed infrastructure, and entertainment assets. Stable and profitable, but operating in a mature, saturated, price-pressured market where the three main operators have converged on near-identical positioning. The company operates beyond core connectivity, but is not yet recognized for that broader role.

## Real Challenge

Trigger: A leadership transition requiring a narrative reset. The specific transition details are excluded from AI use.

What the client wants to change: Move from reactive, campaign-by-campaign communications to one coherent corporate brand strategy. The client must decide on a corporate positioning and narrative that do not currently exist in approved form. Prior agency proposals were liked but never adopted, so the company is effectively starting fresh.

Business/reputation problem:

- Differentiation: the three main operators recycle technology leadership, ESG, and employer-brand claims.
- Affinity: the category is trusted but not loved.
- Contested leadership: share of voice has moved from clear dominance to a tight race.
- Latent strength: national scale, infrastructure, digital-economy role, CSR, and skills programmes exist, but are communicated as episodes rather than one corporate story.

## Objectives

- Re-establish corporate reputation and leadership trust after the transition.
- Build a differentiated corporate brand platform the market can recognize.
- Lift affinity and preference in a trusted-but-not-loved category.
- Strengthen employer brand for digital and engineering talent.
- Establish credible, ownable ESG and societal-contribution leadership.

## Audiences To Prioritize

These audiences are not pre-ranked. The strategy must prioritize them.

- Media: national news, business/financial press, tech media, consumer media.
- Regulators, policy stakeholders, and government stakeholders.
- Talent and future talent: students, STEM graduates, tech community.
- Business and enterprise customers and partners.
- General public and consumer base.
- Parent-group corporate stakeholders.

## Must-Say And Must-Avoid

Because positioning is open, these are guardrails, not the message itself.

Must-say guardrails:

- Use verifiable and ownable proof.
- Show a genuine role in the country’s digital progress.
- Build one company story rather than disconnected activity claims.

Must-avoid guardrails:

- Do not fall back into state-utility or former-monopoly framing.
- Do not recycle shared category claims around technology leadership, ESG, or employer branding as the central idea.
- Do not use competitive price-war messaging as corporate positioning.
- Do not introduce political framing.

## Decision Setup

Primary approval owner: client-side Corporate Communications lead.

Final sign-off: CEO and parent-group corporate communications function.

Consulted teams: Marketing, HR/People, Product, Regulatory Affairs, Legal, and parent-group communications.

Internal alignment tension: Marketing owns consumer brand and advertising budget. Corporate Communications owns reputation and PR. The corporate platform must sit above and feed consumer campaigns without colliding with them. Parent-group requirements add an approval layer. Because positioning is genuinely undecided, the strategy must force and document the positioning decision the client still owes itself.

## Competitive And Market Context

Main competitors: two strong rivals in a three-player market. One is positioned around technology/network leadership and social-impact programming. The other is positioned around customer experience and independently certified network quality. Both invest heavily in corporate narrative and are closing the share-of-voice gap.

Reference brands: major European incumbent operators that repositioned from utility to digital enabler. These are directional benchmarks only, not targets to copy.

Market pressure: mature, saturated, price-competitive market; streaming pressure on traditional TV consumption; convergence pressure from over-the-top players. Growth must come from preference and value, not volume.

Known audience-perception problem: the category is trusted but not admired. The client is respected for reliability and scale but is not associated with a distinctive idea. Competitors out-narrate it on innovation and customer experience, while the client’s relative strength appears more in corporate, sustainability, and CSR coverage than product buzz.

Open strategic question: Is incumbent scale and infrastructure a liability to move away from, or, retold in human and national terms, the one position rivals cannot match? The strategy must take a view; the brief must not assume one.

## Channels And Components

PESO direction:

- Earned: core driver for corporate reputation.
- Owned: newsroom, reports, internal channels, and thought-leadership content.
- Shared: professional social, executive social, consumer social where relevant.
- Paid: supporting role only.
- Partnerships, CSR, and ESG: high relevance.
- Crisis sensitivity: regulatory proceedings, outages, data security, and leadership-transition sensitivities.

## Constraints

Legal/regulatory:

- The client operates under a national communications regulator.
- Claims touching market share, pricing, or competitive position require Legal/Regulatory review.
- ESG claims must align with group-verified data.
- GDPR applies to audience targeting, campaign data, and influencer data handling.
- EU AI Act, DSA, and DMA awareness is required where relevant.

AI-use limits:

- Exclude leadership-transition specifics.
- Exclude real commercial or retainer terms.
- Exclude competitor-by-name intelligence.
- Exclude unannounced strategic plans.
- Use only publicly grounded facts plus this sanitized brief.
- Treat prior unadopted agency positioning ideas as tone reference only, never approved positioning.
- Replace client and individual names with generic stand-ins or role titles.
- Replace financial specifics, budgets, and retainer terms with ranges or TBC.

## Expected Outputs

- Evidence base and readiness check: what is known, what is missing, and what must be decided before strategy can proceed.
- Positioning options: two to three reasoned territories with a recommended direction and rationale, not a single pre-baked answer.
- Corporate brand platform/message architecture: core idea, narrative, and message house framed as a first build for client decision.
- Pillar architecture: derived from evidence and argued, including how many pillars and why.
- Stakeholder and executive thought-leadership map.
- Twelve-month roadmap/campaign platform linked to business moments.
- Measurement framework aligned to AMEC Barcelona Principles 4.0 and the AMEC Integrated Evaluation Framework.

## What Good Looks Like

- Input discipline: surfaces gaps before writing and flags that positioning is undecided.
- Strategic structure: pillars and positioning are reasoned from evidence, not borrowed from competitors.
- Review trail: every recommendation traces to input and separates fact from judgment.
- Honest about unsettled decisions: presents options for client decision rather than asserting a finished answer.
- Practical first artifact: message architecture small enough for a client decision meeting, but substantive enough to test the central strategic bet.

## Safety Note

This brief uses sanitized facts plus publicly grounded context. No confidential client documents, real names, real financials, or specifics of the leadership transition are included. The strategic problem is preserved while identifying and sensitive details are removed or generalized. The account team should review anything pulled into a live demo before it runs.

## How to use this pack

Terms, context and next steps orient the reader.

### Terms

- desk audit — the pre-conversation read of what public sources say about the client; six named passes over the material the workflow already has
- finding — something one of the audits established from those public sources
- gap — something one of the audits could not establish; it is listed as still to check rather than stated as a finding

*Why this step.* CD-S-002 judges the strategy against peers in the same market; the volume names three to five so the read is neither a spot check nor an industry map.

*Client fork.* CD-S-002's peer read forks by the client's own listing and regulation status -- a listed client's peers are other listed players; a regulated client's are other regulated players.

- Regulatory context. Bulgaria’s telecom sector is governed by EU rules including the European Electronic Communications Code, ePrivacy Directive, Net Neutrality Regulation, Roaming Regulation, Gigabit Infrastructure Act and EU termination-rate rules; Bulgarian core laws include the Electronic Communications Act and Electronic Communications Networks and Physical Infrastructure Act (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).
- Regulatory context. Telecom and adjacent digital activity in Bulgaria is also affected by the General Data Protection Regulation, Digital Services Act, Digital Markets Act, Cybersecurity Act, Artificial Intelligence Act, NIS2 Directive and Critical Entity Resilience Directive; this confirms the supplied brief’s legal and AI-policy constraints (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).
- Regulatory context. The Communications Regulation Commission is the independent telecom regulator; the Ministry of Transport and Communications and Ministry of e-Government set ICT, digital administration and cybersecurity policy; the National Radio Frequency Spectrum Council handles national spectrum-planning proposals (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).
- Regulatory context. CRC Decision No. 220 of 30 July 2024 found no effective competition in wholesale access to passive physical infrastructure, named Vivacom as having significant individual impact, and imposed access, non-discrimination, transparency, reference-offer and price-control duties (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
- Regulatory context. CRC launched a fourth-round analysis of local access at a fixed location, and by Decision No. 251 of 29 August 2025 ordered extra information on fixed access via mobile network for 2021-2023; this keeps fixed access and 5G-based home internet inside active review (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
- Regulatory context. CRC says Vivacom met all universal-service quality target values in 2024, did not request unfair-burden compensation by the 30 June 2024 statutory deadline, and had a 46% drop in universal-service complaints versus the prior period (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
- Regulatory context. CRC says 2024 universal-service complaints to Vivacom were mainly technical failures at 27% of complaints; termination complaints rose to 16% from 2% in 2023, and the other category rose 18 percentage points to 29% (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
- Regulatory context. CMS says CRC awarded 20-year 3.6 GHz licences to A1, Vivacom and Yettel in April 2021, and assigned 700 MHz and 800 MHz bands to the same three operators in December 2023 for 15 years; CMS says total licence payments were about BGN 13.4 million (https://cms.law/en/int/expert-guides/cms-expert-guide-to-5g-regulation-and-law/bulgaria).

Public electronic communications network providers are classed as essential entities. Essential-entity penalties can reach EUR 10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, with manager liability also introduced (https://www.schoenherr.eu/content/bulgaria-implements-nis-2-directive-key-changes-to-the-cybersecurity-act).

## Provisional hypothesis

Provisional: the research that follows can overturn it.

| What the AI drafts | What the human owns |
| --- | --- |
| A testable hypothesis. | Adding the point of view and choosing what to test. The engine's hypothesis is a suggestion. |

Vivacom's reputation problem is that its public story does not yet turn its strongest assets into one trusted national role. The open space is a clear story about useful Bulgarian digital infrastructure, grounded in fixed internet, television, coverage, satellite capacity, public-service duties, skills programmes and local digital projects. The claim must stay inside the evidence: Vivacom can credibly support leadership in fixed internet, pay TV, coverage and satellite growth, but it cannot claim total telecom leadership across every mobile, internet or customer-experience measure. A1, Yettel, CETIN and Neterra all carry credible network, quality, infrastructure or specialist claims, so Vivacom should not compete with another broad technology claim. It should prove the national outcomes that only its mix of incumbent infrastructure, United Group scale, EON, Bulsatcom, satellite assets, public-sector work and skills programmes can connect.

*Rests on.* The white space; Vivacom self-claim verdict; The narratives running about it; Category context; Each peer's narrative

| Confirmed if | Overturned if |
| --- | --- |
| The hypothesis holds if client data and stakeholder interviews show that decision-makers, employees, public-sector customers, and media accept Vivacom's infrastructure scale as useful national progress when it is tied to named outcomes rather than broad leadership language. | The hypothesis fails if audience research shows that Vivacom's scale mainly triggers former-incumbent, market-power, pricing, or service-friction associations that cannot be offset by fixed internet, television, satellite, public-sector, and skills proof. |

record.question: Vivacom now has fixed, mobile, television, satellite, smart-city, cloud, and digital-education proof in the public record; which of these businesses must sit at the centre of the corporate story, and which should stay as supporting proof?
record.finding:

United Group said in 2020 that Vivacom was the first telecommunications company in Bulgaria and supplied fibre broadband, mobile communications, and digital TV to private and commercial customers (https://united.group/united-group-welcomes-vivacom-the-largest-telecom-operator-in-bulgaria/).

Its business model. Vivacom’s revenue model is a telecom bundle model built around mobile, fixed broadband, fixed voice, pay TV, devices, business services, and public-sector solutions (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata; https://amcham.bg/member/vivacom/).

Netcracker says Vivacom uses Netcracker Revenue Management for billing, invoicing, and other revenue-related processes across postpaid mobile and fixed lines for B2C and B2B customers (https://www.netcracker.com/news/press-releases/netcracker-and-vivacom-extend-long-term-partnership-for-innovative-it-modernization-program).

Vivacom's insurance site says insurance products are provided through Vivacom Bulgaria EAD as a "застрахователен брокер с номер на удостоверение 552-ЗБ от 18.10.2022 г."; the Financial Supervision Commission register lists Vivacom Bulgaria EAD, company ID 831642181, among insurance brokers, so the broker status is corroborated (https://insurance.vivacom.bg/grazhdanska-otgovornost-online/; https://www.fsc.bg/zastrahovatelna-deynost/spisaczi-podnadzorni-licza/zastrahovatelni-brokeri/).

The narratives running about it. A customer-pain narrative is present in user reviews and crisis stories: Trustpilot reviews cluster around service, billing, contracts and support complaints, and Pikasa says one infrastructure failure generated more real response than months of planned announcements. A consolidation-and-market-power narrative is present around Vivacom's purchases of fixed broadband and TV operators, with A1 and PPF/Yettel criticising regulatory clearances and Vivacom rejecting the criticism. The banked record forms a clear reputation pattern: Vivacom’s strongest defendable story is infrastructure scale, but the same scale also feeds the former-incumbent and market-power concern. The narratives running about it. A media-pluralism narrative surrounds United Group’s Bulgarian position: Liberties’ 2025 Bulgaria report says telecom-media cross-ownership creates risks for editorial independence and fair competition, and names United Group as owner of Vivacom/BTC and Nova Broadcasting Group. The narratives running about it. A regulatory-power narrative is present beyond merger criticism: CRC defines Vivacom as having significant impact in passive physical infrastructure, and Sega reports a 2026 competition probe into alleged excessive duct-access prices. The narratives running about it. A public digital-inclusion narrative is present: the June 2025 government contracts with A1, Vivacom and CETIN target high-capacity networks where investment is lacking. The narratives running about it. A consumer-price-pressure narrative is present at category level: the Ombudsman tied public complaints to mobile operators’ price-indexation clauses and named Vivacom as one of the operators that followed Yettel’s late-2022 increase. record.question: Vivacom's digital presence spans My Vivacom, EON, Vivacom Support on Viber, Pay by Vivacom, Happy Call, GAME ON, and social channels; which digital services should prove the corporate story, and which are mainly sales or service channels?
record.finding:
Channels. Vivacom runs its main owned site at vivacom.bg with customer login, My Vivacom access, product areas, help pages, coverage maps, shop finder, EON, Arena and support paths (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/ekip).
Channels. The public news centre publishes Bulgarian-language items across promotions, company news, social responsibility, internship programme and Vivacom GAME ON (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini).
Channels. The LinkedIn company page had 22,015 followers and described Vivacom as a telecom operator for private and business customers in Bulgaria (https://bg.linkedin.com/company/vivacom).
Channels. The official Facebook page search result showed 291,877 likes and described itself as the official Facebook page of Vivacom (https://www.facebook.com/VIVAC0M/).
Channels. Instagram account @vivacombg showed 55K followers, 69 following and 1,594 posts in search results (https://www.instagram.com/vivacombg/?hl=en).
Channels. The YouTube channel @VIVACOMOfficial showed 15.3K subscribers and about 1.4K videos in search results (https://www.youtube.com/%40VIVACOMOfficial).
Channels. The X account @vivacom is listed as Bulgaria-based, linked to vivacom.bg/bg/5g and joined on August 6, 2010 (https://x.com/vivacom?lang=en).
Channels. The My Vivacom app is present on Google Play and Apple App Store, giving Vivacom a service channel beyond social and web publishing (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en_IE&id=bg.vivacom.mobile; https://apps.apple.com/bg/app/my-vivacom/id1297193461).
Channels. Pikasa monitored Vivacom on Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn and YouTube in Q1 2026, and said TikTok presence was negligible across all three Bulgarian operators (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war).
Channels. Vivacom GAME ON had a wider live-stream channel set than the banked 2026 YouTube evidence shows: in September 2024 the first two rounds were streamed in 9 online channels across YouTube, Twitch, Kick and TikTok (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/parvite-dva-runda-na-vivacom-game-on-s-blizo-180-000-gledania-online). In October 2025 a Roblox round was streamed in 11 channels across YouTube, Twitch, Kick and TikTok, so GAME ON uses creator and streaming channels beyond Vivacom's main owned social accounts (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/virtualniyat-svyat-na-roblox-otpravi-novo-izpitanie-za-otbornite-v-tretiya-onlain-rund-na-vivacom-game-on-2025).
Channels. My Vivacom is distributed beyond Google Play and the Apple App Store; Vivacom says users can install it from Google Play, App Store or Huawei AppGallery, and can register either inside the app or through the web version of My Vivacom (https://www.vivacom.bg/my-vivacom-app).
Channels. Happy Call is both a mobile app and a web route; Vivacom says users can open happycall.bg from phone or desktop, activate by SMS START to 1520, and stop by SMS STOP or in the app profile (https://www.vivacom.bg/dopalnitelni-uslugi/zabavlenie/happy-call).
Channels. Vivacom gives customers a Google Play carrier-billing route. Its owned page says users can add Vivacom billing in Google Play, pay for apps or subscriptions through their monthly Vivacom bill, and receive SMS verification from 1988 (https://www.vivacom.bg/dopalnitelni-uslugi/zabavlenie/google-play).
Channels. The banked record shows a three-operator attention contest: Vivacom, A1 and Yettel are tracked on Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn and YouTube, while TikTok was negligible across the three in Q1 2026 (banked findings: Channels; Presence).
Channels. Vivacom opened Vivacom Support on Viber at the start of March 2023 for direct customer questions, bill checks, payments and service information (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/vivacom-veche-e-vav-viber).
Channels. Vivacom called Viber its fourth fast digital customer-service channel after Facebook Messenger, chat on the official site and self-care chat in the web version of MyVivacom (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/vivacom-veche-e-vav-viber).
Channels. Viber's own public page confirms a Vivacom Support public account exists (https://chats.viber.com/vivacomsupport).
Channels. Nixanbal reported the Viber Support channel and said users would communicate with real people rather than a chatbot (https://nixanbal.com/vivacom-puska-viber-kanal-za-poddrazhka-na-klienti/).
Channels. The contacts page gives contact form, shop finder, customer-service number 123, My Vivacom profile, Vivacom Support, media email and central-office address as customer or media routes (https://www.vivacom.bg/pomosht/kontakti).
Channels. The mobile plans page makes vivacom.bg a sales channel by saying the online monthly fee is the lowest compared with Vivacom's other sales channels for the stated new mobile-contract offer (https://www.vivacom.bg/mobilni-uslugi/mobilni-planove).
Channels. Vivacom Arena is presented as a set of own TV channels inside EON packages, with Arena Action, Arena Comedy and Arena Life forming Arena Select (https://www.vivacom.bg/eon-tv/arena).

record.question: Pikasa found Vivacom strongest on Instagram but weak at turning YouTube reach into response; what audience behaviour should the new corporate platform change on each channel?
record.finding:
Presence. Vivacom says it has more than 2 million customers using more than 5.5 million services (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata).
Presence. Vivacom says it has invested nearly 3 billion leva in technology, innovation, people and the Bulgarian economy (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata).
Presence. Vivacom says it became part of United Group in 2020 (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata).
Presence. Pikasa tracked 134 Vivacom social posts in Q1 2026, with 15,770 total engagements and 118 average engagements per post (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war).
Presence. Pikasa said Vivacom led press volume among A1, Vivacom and Yettel in Q1 2026 with 198 articles, but that most were PR announcements with near-zero audience response (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war).
Presence. Pikasa said Instagram was Vivacom’s strongest platform in Q1 2026, averaging 327 engagements per post and forming the strongest platform-brand result in its dataset (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war).
Presence. Pikasa said Vivacom averaged only 9 engagements per YouTube video in Q1 2026 despite reaching 130,000 average views per video, the highest YouTube reach in the sector (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war).
Presence. The My Vivacom app was updated on Google Play on August 4, 2026, and the listing says it supports mobile, internet and TV service management, invoices, payment access, packages, EON profile settings, personalised online offers and support (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en_IE&id=bg.vivacom.mobile).
Presence. Gridinsoft detected vivacom.bg as an established 16.5-year-old domain with Google Tag Manager, social media links, multilingual support, structured page data and verified YouTube and X footprints; this is a technical signal, not a brand-performance measure (https://gridinsoft.com/online-virus-scanner/url/vivacom-bg).

The first two Vivacom GAME ON rounds in 2024 generated about 180,000 online views and more than 24,000 viewer hours, showing that the gaming platform can draw measurable audience attention outside ordinary telecom product posts (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/parvite-dva-runda-na-vivacom-game-on-s-blizo-180-000-gledania-online). The 2025 GAME ON YouTube series had more than 250,000 views after six episodes, according to Vivacom's own news centre; no independent source found in this pass tested that figure (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/virtualniyat-svyat-na-roblox-otpravi-novo-izpitanie-za-otbornite-v-tretiya-onlain-rund-na-vivacom-game-on-2025).
Presence. United Group said in July 2026 that Bulgaria's telecoms market reached 2.16 billion euros in the prior year and that IPTV had passed one million households nationally; this places Vivacom's EON presence inside a visible market shift toward IPTV (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/).
Presence. Happy Call had 100K+ Google Play downloads, a Teen rating, in-app purchases and a 27 July 2026 update date (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en&id=bg.allterco.fcm).
Presence. The Happy Call Google Play listing names VIVACOM Bulgaria as developer, gives happycall@vivacom.bg as support email, and links to a separate privacy policy at policy.teracomm.bg (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en&id=bg.allterco.fcm).
Presence. Pay by Vivacom's owned page shows the wallet as an active consumer-service presence, with household-bill payment, card controls, payment notifications, virtual debit card, personal IBAN, transfers between app users and point-of-sale payment listed on the page (https://www.vivacom.bg/drugi-uslugi/digitalen-portfeil).
Presence. Similarweb estimated vivacom.bg at 1.6 million visits and ranked it second in the Telecommunications category in June 2026 (https://www.similarweb.com/website/vivacom.bg/).

record.question: Vivacom's public tone moves from formal scale claims on corporate pages to warmer first-person plural language on LinkedIn and youth programmes; which version feels most like the voice the company wants in corporate reputation work?
record.finding:
Tone of voice. Vivacom’s corporate copy is in Bulgarian and often leads with scale, innovation and national role, as in the exact phrase “Vivacom е иноватор” (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata).
Tone of voice. Vivacom’s corporate page says its mission is to give customers high-quality telecom services and the best experience, and its vision is to be the preferred telecom provider in Bulgaria (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata).
Tone of voice. Vivacom’s LinkedIn page uses Bulgarian, first-person plural language, emojis, student quotes and soft calls to read more, which makes the social voice warmer and more human than the official press voice (https://bg.linkedin.com/company/vivacom).
Tone of voice. Vivacom’s LinkedIn content in August 2026 centred on internships, forest-fire prevention, Job Lab, leadership training, Game ON and product offers (https://bg.linkedin.com/company/vivacom).
Tone of voice. Pikasa found Facebook focused mainly on devices and plans, LinkedIn on cybersecurity, university partnerships and smart-city projects, and YouTube mainly on short promotional clips (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war).
Tone of voice. The news centre mix is highly commercial, with August 2026 items including smartphone offers, Samsung launches, online discounts, internships, GAME ON and cybersecurity training (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini).
Tone of voice. Vivacom’s 5G claim is proof-led in form: it names Ookla, the 417.27 Speed Score, 52,578 user tests and the July 1 to December 31, 2021 test period (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/vivacom-ima-nai-barzata-5g-mreja-v-bulgaria-spored-ookla).
Tone of voice. Telecompaper independently reported the same Ookla 5G result and 52,578 user-test basis, corroborating the speed claim while noting that the largest-network claim came from the operator (https://www.telecompaper.com/news/vivacom-named-fastest-5g-network-in-bulgaria-by-ookla--1410099).
Tone of voice. The My Vivacom app copy says it is “created with the customer in mind”; Google Play reviews and Apple App Store reviews challenge the experience with visible complaints about login, payment and reliability (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en_IE&id=bg.vivacom.mobile; https://apps.apple.com/bg/app/my-vivacom/id1297193461).
Tone of voice. Asen Velikov's 2019 interview used a customer-first and technology-change frame, calling Vivacom a "customer-oriented company" and saying customer experience had become a focus of investment because customers compare telecoms with Amazon and Google (https://www.economic.bg/bg/a/view/change-is-the-only-invariable-112562). This supports a voice route around customer experience and digital change, not only network scale (https://www.economic.bg/bg/a/view/change-is-the-only-invariable-112562).
Tone of voice. The Netcracker release carried a technical but customer-facing executive voice: Asen Velikov linked billing-system modernization to long-term stability, growth and the customer experience, while Netcracker framed the work around 5G monetization, AI, automation and vertical industries (https://www.netcracker.com/news/press-releases/netcracker-and-vivacom-extend-long-term-partnership-for-innovative-it-modernization-program).
Tone of voice. The GAME ON news voice is youth-culture and gaming-led, using named creators, Roblox, Minecraft, live streams, fan voting, prizes, finals and YouTube episodes to translate fibre-network proof into entertainment participation (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/parvite-dva-runda-na-vivacom-game-on-s-blizo-180-000-gledania-online; https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/virtualniyat-svyat-na-roblox-otpravi-novo-izpitanie-za-otbornite-v-tretiya-onlain-rund-na-vivacom-game-on-2025).
Tone of voice. Happy Call's product voice is casual and entertainment-led; Vivacom uses the exact phrases "Посрещни всеки с песен" and "Супер апликация за твоя телефон!" for caller-ring personalization (https://www.vivacom.bg/dopalnitelni-uslugi/zabavlenie/happy-call).
Tone of voice. Happy Call's Google Play copy uses self-expression language, saying the app has more than 3,000 songs and calling the service "Your music message for everyone who's calling you" (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en&id=bg.allterco.fcm).
Tone of voice. Pay by Vivacom's headline voice is ease-and-control led; Vivacom says, exactly, "Правим финансите по-лесни, достъпни и открити" (https://www.vivacom.bg/drugi-uslugi/digitalen-portfeil).
Tone of voice. Vivacom's Google Play carrier-billing page uses safety and convenience language, saying users can shop without giving bank-card details and pay later through the monthly Vivacom bill; no independent source opened in this pass tested that user-experience claim (https://www.vivacom.bg/dopalnitelni-uslugi/zabavlenie/google-play).
Tone of voice. Vivacom's Viber launch uses customer-closeness language, saying customers can contact the company quickly, easily and conveniently through their preferred communication platform (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/vivacom-veche-e-vav-viber).

Vivacom's Viber launch says, exactly, "Vivacom поставя клиентите си в центъра на всичко, което прави"; Nixanbal reported the service launch but did not test whether the service experience supports that claim (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/vivacom-veche-e-vav-viber; https://nixanbal.com/vivacom-puska-viber-kanal-za-poddrazhka-na-klienti/).
Tone of voice. Vivacom's careers headline says, exactly, "Започваш работа, получаваш кариера", which makes the employer voice direct and promise-led (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/karieri).
Tone of voice. Vivacom's careers page says, exactly, "Започваш работа. Получаваш свобода.", which gives the employer story a personal-growth frame (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/karieri).
Tone of voice. Vivacom's brand page is rule-led rather than campaign-led, giving logo form, spacing, contrast and corporate-colour rules for digital and print use (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/markata-vivacom).
Tone of voice. Vivacom's mobile-sales page says, exactly, "Най-добрата ни оферта е на vivacom.bg"; no independent source opened in this pass tested whether that price claim held across all Vivacom sales routes (https://www.vivacom.bg/mobilni-uslugi/mobilni-planove).
Tone of voice. Vivacom Arena uses a compact entertainment line, exactly, "Четири свята. Една сцена.", to frame four Arena channel worlds as one family offer (https://www.vivacom.bg/eon-tv/arena).

record.question: The peer map shows A1 and Yettel as national retail rivals, Neterra as an enterprise and infrastructure specialist, and CETIN as a wholesale network-infrastructure peer; which competitor set should the corporate platform be built to beat?
record.finding:
Three to five peers. A1 Bulgaria is a direct peer for Vivacom across mobile, fixed broadband, TV, entertainment, business ICT and IoT. A1 was founded in 1994, acquired by Telekom Austria Group in 2005, and A1 Group says it is second-largest in mobile and fixed-line segments and overall number one in the market (https://a1.com/a1-group-and-markets/a1-in-bulgaria/).
Three to five peers. A1's predecessor Mobiltel was bought by Telekom Austria in a 2005 transaction valued at up to EUR 1.6 billion. A1 later bought STEMO, with SeeNews citing industry sources that put the price around BGN 50 million, equal to about EUR 25.6 million (https://www.novinite.com/articles/48248/Telekom%2BAustria%2BAcquires%2BBulgaria%27s%2BMobiltel; https://seenews.com/news/a1-bulgaria-closes-buy-of-local-stemo-in-boost-to-corporate-it-services-1214760).
Three to five peers. Yettel Bulgaria is a direct peer for Vivacom in mobile, fixed wireless broadband and TV. It started as Globul in 2001, was sold by OTE to Telenor in 2013 for EUR 717 million, was bought as part of Telenor's CEE assets by PPF in 2018 for EUR 2.8 billion, and is now owned by e& PPF Telecom Group (https://www.telekom.com/en/media/media-information/archive/greece-ote-agrees-to-sell-globul-for-717-million-to-telenor-358962; https://en.yettel.hu/press/press-release/ppf-group-completes-acquisiton; https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/yettel-bulgaria).
Three to five peers. Yettel's current parent was formed after e& bought control of PPF Telecom assets outside Czechia, with the announced consideration at EUR 2.15 billion plus a possible earn-out of up to EUR 350 million. The European Commission conditionally approved the acquisition under the Foreign Subsidies Regulation on 24 September 2024 (https://en.yettel.hu/press/press-release/ppf-group-press-release-ppf-closes-a-major-transaction-and-forms-a-partnership-with-e-a-global-technology-group; https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/api/files/document/print/en/ip_24_4842/IP_24_4842_EN.pdf).
Three to five peers. Neterra is a narrower peer for Vivacom's enterprise, wholesale, satellite, cloud, data-center and managed-service audiences. Neterra was founded in 1996 in Sofia, owns and operates four data centers and a global network of over 220 points of presence, according to SeeNews (https://seenews.com/news/bulgarias-neterra-invests-12-mln-euro-in-data-network-upgrade-1289377).
Three to five peers. Neterra's own history says it built the first Bulgarian alternative connection to Turkey, created a Frankfurt point of presence, launched a large DWDM optical network in Bulgaria and operates Neterra.TV for Bulgarians abroad. CRC data places Neterra among the leading leased-line undertakings, which makes it a real B2B choice even if it is not a national mass-market mobile operator (https://neterra.net/about-us; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Three to five peers. A fourth direct peer is CETIN Bulgaria for Vivacom's public-sector, wholesale and network-infrastructure audiences. CETIN Bulgaria was established in July 2020 by separating telecom infrastructure from Telenor Bulgaria. It provides mobile network services for Yettel Bulgaria. Its parent reports 2025 revenue of EUR 170 million, EBITDA of EUR 123 million and CAPEX of EUR 76 million. It won rural digital network contracts alongside A1 and Vivacom under Bulgaria's 2025 BGN 433.6 million programme (https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/cetin-bulgaria; https://seenews.com/news/bulgaria-signs-222-mln-euro-digital-network-deals-with-a1-vivacom-cetin-1276695).
Three to five peers. The competitive set now reads as four practical choices by audience: A1 and Yettel for national consumer and business telecom, Neterra for enterprise, carrier, cloud and data-center buyers, and CETIN for wholesale and public-infrastructure buyers. This pattern is derived from the banked A1, Yettel and Neterra peer findings plus the CETIN findings in this pass (banked findings; https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/cetin-bulgaria).
Three to five peers. The four-peer map still holds. ICLG names A1, Yettel and Vivacom as the mobile operators, names Vivacom and A1 as the main fixed-internet providers, and says the rest of fixed internet is made up of many regional operators. No fifth present nationwide retail peer was established from this source (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).
Three to five peers. No new peer displaced the banked four-peer set. The new sources instead strengthen the same split: A1 and Yettel remain the national retail alternatives, CETIN remains the network-infrastructure peer behind Yettel, and Neterra remains the specialist enterprise and carrier peer (banked findings; https://www.cetinbg.bg/what-we-do/network; https://www.datocms-assets.com/56100/1771365178-fr39_20260217_eand_ppf_telecom_group_fy2025_annual_accounts_public.pdf).

verdicts.because: It directly uses the finding's four-peer map: A1 and Yettel as national retail rivals, Neterra as enterprise/infrastructure specialist, and CETIN as wholesale network-infrastructure peer.
The question directly uses the finding's four-peer split: A1 and Yettel as national retail rivals, Neterra as enterprise/infrastructure specialist, and CETIN as wholesale network-infrastructure peer.

record.question: A1 can claim breadth and speed, Yettel can claim certified mobile quality and employer trust, Vivacom can claim fixed internet, pay TV, coverage, and satellite proof, and Neterra can claim specialist infrastructure; which leadership claims are worth making, and which should we avoid?
record.finding:
The white space. The main national operators converge on network, technology, entertainment, ESG and employer claims. The supplied brief already flags that sameness, and the public record supports it through A1's market-scale and service-breadth claims, Yettel's certified network-quality claims and Vivacom's fibre, 5G and TV growth frame (SOURCE DOCUMENT: sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md; https://a1.com/a1-group-and-markets/a1-in-bulgaria/; https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/yettel-bulgaria; https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/).
The white space. A less occupied space is a national digital-infrastructure story that connects scale to people's daily and economic progress, not only to network claims. Vivacom has the assets for that story, but Pikasa's Q1 2026 analysis says much of its press volume was PR-led announcements with weak audience response (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war; SOURCE DOCUMENT: sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md).
The white space. Another open space is useful public service content. Pikasa says Yettel earned more varied coverage from tactile strips, digital literacy reaching 60,000 children, volunteering culture and entertainment stories, while A1 and Vivacom were more often present through sponsorship, product or announcement material (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war).
The white space. A B2B white space sits between mass telecom and specialist infrastructure. A1 owns ICT breadth through STEMO, Neterra owns enterprise-network credibility, and Vivacom can credibly connect national network scale with smart cities, cybersecurity, education, EON and fibre if it proves the role through named projects (https://newsroom.a1.com/news-a1-telekom-austria-group-announces-100-acquisition-of-stemo-a-bulgarian-ict-company?id=158471&l=english&menueid=14594; https://neterra.net/about-us; https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/).
The white space. The banked findings create a claim-tiering white space. A1 can claim breadth and speed; Yettel can claim certified mobile quality and employer trust; Vivacom can claim fixed internet, pay-TV and coverage; Neterra can claim specialist enterprise infrastructure. No player can safely own total leadership without qualifiers. This pattern is derived from the banked A1, Yettel, Vivacom and Neterra share and narrative findings plus Opensignal 2026 (banked findings; https://insights.opensignal.com/reports/2026/01/bulgaria/mobile-network-experience).
The white space. The rural digital-inclusion space is not empty. A1, Vivacom and CETIN all have public claims to the 2025 state-backed rural network build. Vivacom cannot make that story as if it acted alone. The open space is proof of the specific local outcomes Vivacom delivered within the shared programme (https://seenews.com/news/bulgaria-signs-222-mln-euro-digital-network-deals-with-a1-vivacom-cetin-1276695; https://www.cetin.international/w/expanding-bulgaria-s-digital-future-with-large-scale-fiber-deployment).
The white space. The wholesale-infrastructure story is occupied by CETIN and Neterra as well as by the retail operators. CETIN owns the separated Yettel network-service role. Neterra owns independent carrier and data-center proof. Vivacom's B2B story must connect national scale to named customer outcomes rather than just say infrastructure (https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/cetin-bulgaria; https://amcham.bg/2025/10/24/double-victory-for-neterra-and-netix-at-the-capacity-global-connectivity-awards-2025/).
The white space. The open space is not "best network" as a broad claim. SpeedGeo reports Vivacom as fastest fixed broadband in Bulgaria from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026, with 117 Mb/s average download, 85.2 Mb/s upload and 25 ms ping. The same source reports A1 as fastest mobile internet, with 190.7 Mb/s average download. This splits performance proof by service type (https://www.speedgeo.net/statistics/bulgaria).
The white space. A national-infrastructure story must avoid sounding like every peer's proof claim. The banked record shows A1 claiming breadth and speed, Yettel claiming certified quality and trust, Neterra claiming specialist infrastructure, and CETIN claiming wholesale infrastructure. The open space is the human and economic result of the infrastructure, with named local proof (banked findings: A1 narrative; Yettel narrative; Neterra narrative; CETIN narrative; Opensignal 2026 finding).
The white space. The ICLG 2026 Bulgaria chapter says fixed internet has strong infrastructure-based competition and many regional operators outside Vivacom and A1. This leaves room for a local-outcome story by town, school, enterprise or public service, because national share alone does not explain the regional customer experience (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).
The white space. The banked record plus new H1 2026 financials sharpen a white space around proof-backed national usefulness. A1 has the stronger current revenue proof, Yettel has mobile customer and employer proof, CETIN has infrastructure proof and Neterra has specialist continuity proof. Vivacom's safer open lane is not another best-network claim, but a named set of Bulgarian outcomes its network made possible (banked findings; https://a1.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/07/A1-Group_Half-Year-Financial-Report-2026-1.pdf; https://www.cetinbg.bg/what-we-do/network; https://www.datocms-assets.com/56100/1771365178-fr39_20260217_eand_ppf_telecom_group_fy2025_annual_accounts_public.pdf).
The white space. The device-and-app space is now more visibly occupied by Yettel. SeeNews carried a Yettel release saying Digitalk 101 ranked Yettel first in mobile device sales for 2023-2025, that smartphone sales through Yettel digital channels rose 56% in H1 2026, and that 95% of customer interactions were digitalised. Vivacom should not use digital customer experience as an ownable centre without proof stronger than Yettel's (https://seenews.com/news/yettel-leads-mobile-device-and-accessories-sales-for-the-third-consecutive-year-1299605).

verdicts.because: It directly uses the finding's claim-tiering facts: A1 breadth and speed, Yettel certified mobile quality and employer trust, Vivacom fixed internet/pay-TV/coverage, Neterra specialist infrastructure, and the caution about which leadership claims are safe or unsafe.

It directly uses the finding's claim-tiering facts: A1 breadth and speed, Yettel certified mobile quality and employer trust, Vivacom fixed internet/pay-TV/coverage, Neterra specialist infrastructure, and the need to decide which leadership claims are safe or should be avoided.

record.question: A1 and Yettel have both challenged Vivacom-linked consolidation, while the Supreme Administrative Court cleared the Bulsatcom infrastructure-assets transaction; how should the corporate story handle market-power scrutiny without repeating competitor framing?
record.finding: Competition clearance development. Bulgaria's Supreme Administrative Court issued a final ruling in February 2026 clearing United Group's acquisition of Bulsatcom telecom-infrastructure assets after appeals by A1, Yettel and CETIN. This changes the constraint from unresolved approval risk to a live concentration narrative that competitors can still use publicly (https://seenews.com/news/bulgarias-supreme-court-clears-united-groups-acquisition-of-bulsatcom-1290035). (bears on: Constraints, guardrails & AI permissions)

verdicts.because: The question directly uses the finding’s specific facts: A1 and Yettel challenges, the Supreme Administrative Court clearance, the Bulsatcom infrastructure-assets transaction, and the shift to a public market-power/concentration narrative.

It directly uses the finding’s facts: A1 and Yettel appeals, the Supreme Administrative Court clearance, the Bulsatcom infrastructure-assets deal, and the resulting competitor-driven market-power narrative.

record.question: The stakeholder map includes United Group and BC Partners, the Communications Regulation Commission, competition and consumer authorities, employees, media, municipalities, schools, public-sector customers, business customers, and civic organisations; which groups must approve, which must believe, and which must only not object?
record.finding:
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. Investors and owners matter because Vivacom is a subsidiary inside United Group. United Group is majority owned by BC Partners and has owned Vivacom since the 2020 closing. United Group says it is active in eight countries, has nearly 16 million users and 15,000 employees, and generated more than EUR 2.7 billion in annual revenue in its 2024 Bulsatcom announcement. (https://united.group/united-group-welcomes-vivacom-the-largest-telecom-operator-in-bulgaria/; https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/united-group-compretes-the-acquisition-of-bulsatcom)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. Owner relations matter because Vivacom sits under a parent with public governance conflict. Economic.bg reported in August 2025 that United Group had a control dispute between founder Dragan Sholak and majority shareholder BC Partners. It reported that Sholak filed a lawsuit after his removal and a dispute over EUR 200 million in bonuses. It also reported market speculation about a possible United Group sale at EUR 8 billion. (https://www.economic.bg/en/a/view/top-management-reshuffle-at-vivacom-director-leaves-spas-rusev-returns)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. The Communications Regulation Commission matters because it is the national sector regulator and source of market baselines. CRC said Bulgaria's electronic communications market was BGN 4.021 billion in 2024, up 5.7% from 2023. CRC said A1, Vivacom and Yettel formed 97.8% of fixed voice subscribers and 94.0% of fixed voice retail revenue. (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. CRC matters for Vivacom's market standing. CRC said Vivacom was the fixed internet leader in 2024 with 39.4% of subscribers and 37.1% of revenue. CRC said Vivacom was the pay TV leader in 2024 with 59.6% of subscribers and 56.5% of revenue after Bulsatcom and TVN Distribution Bulgaria were incorporated into Vivacom. CRC said Vivacom became second in mobile voice revenue in 2024 and its mobile voice revenue share rose from 25.4% in 2020 to 32.0% in 2024. (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. CRC matters for public-interest duties. CRC said Vivacom continued to provide public payphones at main entry points and high-traffic places such as airports, ports, railway and bus stations, motorways, hospitals and police stations. CRC said Vivacom continued free calls to emergency numbers from all public payphones. CRC said Vivacom continued tariff packages for low-income users, people with disabilities and people with special social needs. (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. The Commission for Protection of Competition matters because Vivacom's acquisitions have been contested. PPF Telecom Group said CPC approved transactions linked to Networx and Telnet despite court hearings and a court-ordered review. NERA said CPC cleared Vivacom's acquisition of Telnet and Networx unconditionally at Phase 2 on 29 June 2023. (https://www.ppf.eu/en/press-release/ppf-telecom-group-dismayed-by-regulatory-ruling-taken-in-bulgaria; https://www.nera.com/experience/2023/bulgarian-telco-vivacom-cleared-to-acquire-telnet-and-networx-.html)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. The European Commission matters for ownership control because United Group said the Vivacom acquisition followed European Commission approval in April 2020. It also matters for earlier history because Vivacom's own history says the 2012 restructuring received approval from the European Commission and other authorities. (https://united.group/united-group-welcomes-vivacom-the-largest-telecom-operator-in-bulgaria/; https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. Employees matter because the current strategy follows a management change. SeeNews reported that Asen Velikov replaced Nikolai Andreev as Vivacom CEO in August 2025. SeeNews also reported Stan Miller became supervisory board chair and Spas Rusev and Stan Miller joined the board, replacing Viktoriya Boklag and Yanez Zhivko. Vivacom's own management page lists Asen Velikov as CEO, Ognyan Toshmakov as CFO from 13 July 2026, Ivo Zlatev as chief legal officer, and Malina Chavdarova as head of human capital management. (https://seenews.com/news/bulgarias-vivacom-names-ceo-1279653; https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/ekip)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. Media matter both as channels and as parent-group context. United Group owns Vivacom in Bulgaria and also owns Nova Broadcasting Group in Bulgaria. Economic.bg reported that point when discussing Vivacom's management change and United Group's parent conflict. (https://www.economic.bg/en/a/view/top-management-reshuffle-at-vivacom-director-leaves-spas-rusev-returns)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. Communities and civic organisations matter because Vivacom frames public contribution around education, environment and local projects. Vivacom says its Regional Grant supports civic organisations across Bulgaria on education and environmental protection. Vivacom says it has supported 128 projects by 115 civic organisations with more than BGN 700,000. (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/sotsialna-otgovornost)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. Students, schools, STEM communities and local authorities matter because Vivacom names them in its social and business activity. Vivacom says Job Lab targets pupils in grades 11 and 12. Vivacom says it supports Bulgarian science olympiad teams. Vivacom says it creates smart-city and digital-modernisation options for more than 130 Bulgarian municipalities. (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/sotsialna-otgovornost; https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. Business customers and public-sector customers matter because Vivacom says it offers individual proposals for corporate clients and develops services in the Internet of Things and smart cities. The supplied brief also names business and enterprise customers, partners, regulators, government stakeholders, media, talent, the public, consumers and parent-group stakeholders as audiences to prioritise. (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata; sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. The banked record shows Vivacom’s stakeholder map is not only a customer and competitor map. It puts United Group and BC Partners above Vivacom, CRC and CPC around market conduct, the European Commission around ownership control, employees around the management change, media around both Vivacom and Nova Broadcasting Group, and civic organisations, schools and municipalities around social and local projects. (banked findings: owners and investors; CRC; CPC; European Commission; employees; media; communities; students; business and public-sector customers)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. The banked record shows ownership history is a live stakeholder issue, not background. Vivacom moved from state ownership to Viva Ventures, then AIG, then creditor and VTB-linked control, then United Group, with reported values ranging from EUR 130 million in restructuring-era sales to about EUR 1.2 billion in the United Group deal. The same record now links Vivacom to a 2025 United Group control dispute and reported EUR 8 billion sale speculation. (banked findings: company history and former names; ownership changes and reported prices; owner relations)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. Courts now matter alongside competition regulators. SeeNews reported on 19 February 2026 that Bulgaria’s Supreme Administrative Court issued a final ruling clearing United Group’s Bulsatcom infrastructure-assets acquisition after appeals by A1 Bulgaria, Yettel Bulgaria and Cetin Bulgaria. The court said the assessed deals did not form a notifiable concentration. (https://seenews.com/news/bulgarias-supreme-court-clears-united-groups-acquisition-of-bulsatcom-1290035)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. The Commission for Personal Data Protection matters for reputation and legal guardrails. Linklaters reported that Vivacom Bulgaria EAD was fined BGN 10,000 on 27 March 2025 for unlawful processing of personal data including names, addresses and personal identification numbers. Linklaters said the Commission required Vivacom to conduct a risk assessment and implement technical and work-process measures to prevent similar violations. (https://www.linklaters.com/en/insights/data-protected/data-protected---bulgaria)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. The Communications Regulation Commission matters for service-reliability pressure, not only market shares. Telecompaper reported that CRC requested Vivacom to conduct an internal investigation into a 25 April 2025 network and services incident. Telecompaper reported that CRC expected Vivacom to identify the causes, present risk-reduction measures and report results within seven days. (https://www.telecompaper.com/news/bulgarian-regulator-orders-vivacom-to-investigate-cause-of-network-failure--1535070)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. The Consumer Protection Commission matters for contract and pricing conduct. BNR reported that, from 2025, users may cancel mobile-service contracts without fees within 30 days when an operator announces inflation indexation. BNR said this followed meetings between the commission and telecom companies and an agreement regulating fee-free termination. (https://bnrnews.bg/en/post/104442/citizens-to-be-able-to-cancel-contracts-for-mobile-services-without-fees-from-2025)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. Civil society organisations remain a live stakeholder set around Vivacom’s social contribution. BAIT reported that the ninth Vivacom Regional Grant awarded BGN 100,000 to 10 civil society organisations in 2024, with BGN 10,000 for each finalist. BAIT reported a record 395 applications from 361 organisations. (https://www.bait.bg/en/novini/vivacom-regional-grant-supports-10-projects-with-bgn-100-000/)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. The Bulgarian Center for Not-for-Profit Law is more than a passive beneficiary in Vivacom’s local giving. BAIT quoted BCNL saying it had partnered with Vivacom since the start of the Regional Grant and that the ninth edition added an accelerator lab for finalists. (https://www.bait.bg/en/novini/vivacom-regional-grant-supports-10-projects-with-bgn-100-000/)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. Employees and future talent matter because Vivacom also talks to students as a workforce pipeline. United Group’s LinkedIn post said Vivacom’s Job Lab pilot would run from February to May 2026 in Sofia, Blagoevgrad, Varna and Veliko Tarnovo and include school workshops, independent student work, skills assessment, a Vivacom HQ visit and an AI and digital-skills module. (https://www.linkedin.com/posts/united-group-b.v._joblab-unitedgroup-vivacom-activity-7425125424449511424-1jtJ)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. The banked record shows Vivacom's stakeholder pressure has widened from ownership and merger approval into day-to-day public conduct. CRC appears around outages and universal service. KZP and the Ombudsman Institution appear around price increases and consumer complaints. The Commission for Personal Data Protection appears around personal-data handling. Courts appear around both Bulsatcom assets and consumer orders. (banked findings: CRC outage; KZP fee-free termination; Ombudsman; CPDP fine; Supreme Administrative Court Bulsatcom)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. The Consumer Protection Commission matters in Vivacom-specific pricing enforcement. KZP said the Supreme Administrative Court confirmed preliminary execution of its order banning Vivacom from applying indexed monthly fees. KZP said the ruling was final and not appealable. KZP said the beginning-of-year monthly-fee increases ranged from BGN 1.00 to BGN 2.00. (https://kzp.bg/bg/novini-mobilni-operatori/264)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. The Consumer Protection Commission also matters in contract-exit penalties. KZP said the Supreme Administrative Court confirmed the Sofia Administrative Court's rejection of Vivacom's second request to stop preliminary execution of KZP order 2594 of 4 September 2024. KZP said the order banned Vivacom from requiring more than one early-termination penalty or a penalty above the contractual maximum. (https://kzp.bg/bg/novini-mobilni-operatori/273)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. The Council for Electronic Media matters because Vivacom is a registered media-service provider, not only a telecom network operator. The CEM register lists Vivacom's management board as Asen Velikov, Stoyan Karanlakov, Nikolay Gavrilov, Ognyan Toshmakov and Ivo Zlatev. It lists the supervisory board as Spas Rusev, Stanley Miller, Roger Munger, Bernarda Trebusak Yetzel and Natalia Todorova. It lists United Group Luxembourg S.a.r.l. as sole owner of the capital. (https://www.cem.bg/linear_reg_docs.php?cat=1&id=428)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. The Bulgarian government and transport and communications ministry matter because Vivacom is one of the operators contracted for a national digital-network build. SeeNews reported six contracts with A1 Bulgaria, Vivacom Bulgaria and CETIN Bulgaria worth BGN 433.6 million, or EUR 221.7 million. SeeNews reported that BGN 390 million comes from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan. (https://seenews.com/news/bulgaria-signs-222-mln-euro-digital-network-deals-with-a1-vivacom-cetin-1276695)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. Rural, remote and sparsely populated communities matter because the national digital-network project is explicitly aimed at underbuilt areas. SeeNews reported that more than half of the targeted areas will be rural, remote or sparsely populated. Prime Minister Rosen Zhelyazkov said the project would support regional and demographic policy. (https://seenews.com/news/bulgaria-signs-222-mln-euro-digital-network-deals-with-a1-vivacom-cetin-1276695)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. Media-freedom organisations matter through Vivacom's parent-group media context. SafeJournalists published a 20 May 2026 warning about the potential Adria News Network sale. It called on the Luxembourg media regulator, the European Commission, BC Partners and United Group to scrutinise or avoid a sale that would harm editorial independence. (https://safejournalists.net/potential-sale-of-adria-news-network-threatens-media-freedoms/)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. The Ministry of Transport and Communications and the Ministry of e-Government matter for public-policy framing. ICLG says those ministries set Bulgarian policy for information and communication technologies. ICLG says the Ministry of e-Government is also responsible for public-administration digitalisation and cybersecurity. (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. The National Radio Frequency Spectrum Council matters for spectrum policy. ICLG says it proposes the National Plan for Radio Frequency Spectrum Allocation for approval by the Council of Ministers. (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/)
Who matters -- investors, regulators, employees, media, communities and non-governmental organisations. The foreign-investment screening system matters if United Group asset-sale options advance. ICLG says Bulgaria's Screening Council can permit, condition or prohibit covered foreign direct investments. record.question: United Group, regulators, competitors, customers, app-store users, and sector media all talk about Vivacom in different ways; whose voice most shapes the reputation problem today?
record.finding:
Who is talking. Vivacom talks through its corporate site, its management page, its social responsibility page and its sustainability page. Its current listed CEO is Asen Velikov, who joined Vivacom in 1999, became CFO in 2013, joined the management board in 2014, and is now member of the management board and CEO. (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/ekip)
Who is talking. United Group talks often about Vivacom as owner and parent. It announced the Vivacom acquisition in 2019, welcomed Vivacom into the group in 2020, announced the Bulsatcom completion in 2024, and published a July 2026 item backing Vivacom's fibre, 5G and television growth. (https://united.group/united-group-acquires-vivacom/; https://united.group/united-group-welcomes-vivacom-the-largest-telecom-operator-in-bulgaria/; https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/united-group-compretes-the-acquisition-of-bulsatcom; https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/)
Who is talking. Bulgarian regulators talk about Vivacom in annual market data and merger decisions. CRC names A1, Vivacom and Yettel as Bulgaria's three mobile voice providers in 2024. CRC also records Vivacom's fixed voice, fixed internet, pay TV, universal service and emergency-call duties. (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf)
Who is talking. Competitors and their owners talk about Vivacom in competition terms. PPF Telecom Group and Yettel Bulgaria criticised CPC decisions on Vivacom transactions in July 2023. Vivacom answered through a public denial carried by Broadband TV News. (https://www.ppf.eu/en/press-release/ppf-telecom-group-dismayed-by-regulatory-ruling-taken-in-bulgaria; https://www.broadbandtvnews.com/2023/07/04/vivacom-dismisses-unfounded-concerns-from-competitors/)
Who is talking. Business and sector media are active voices on Vivacom. SeeNews reported the August 2025 CEO change to Asen Velikov and the reshuffled supervisory board. Economic.bg linked the same reshuffle to United Group owner tensions and the return of former owner Spas Rusev to the board. Broadband TV News covered Vivacom's competition disputes and acquisitions. (https://seenews.com/news/bulgarias-vivacom-names-ceo-1279653; https://www.economic.bg/en/a/view/top-management-reshuffle-at-vivacom-director-leaves-spas-rusev-returns; https://www.broadbandtvnews.com/2023/07/04/vivacom-dismisses-unfounded-concerns-from-competitors/)
Who is talking. Technology partners talk about Vivacom's network and platform choices. Nokia announced a 2020 multi-year Vivacom fibre deal covering GPON and XGS-PON and more than 1.5 million households in major cities. Eutelsat and Vivacom announced a fourth European ground station in Bulgaria in 2023. (https://www.nokia.com/newsroom/nokia-helps-vivacom-bulgaria-deploy-next-generation-fiber-network/; https://united.group/vivacom-and-eutelsat-group-are-launching-in-bulgaria-the-fourth-european-ground-station/)
Who is talking. The Consumer Protection Commission is talking about mobile operators as a consumer-rights issue. BNR reported in 2025 that chair Maria Filipova ordered operators to stop unilateral contract changes without consumer consent and said fines could reach BGN 50,000 for each unfair commercial practice. BNR said two mobile operators had changed existing contract terms, including monthly charges, without written agreement from consumers. (https://bnrnews.bg/en/post/123374/cpc-issues-an-order-prohibiting-the-unilateral-price-increases-by-mobile-operators)
Who is talking. The Ombudsman Institution is talking about mobile operators as a citizen-harm issue. Its Secretary General said on 11 March 2025 that the institution had opposed controversial price increases for years and had acted after complaints from citizens. The same source named Yettel, Vivacom and A1 in the price-indexation sequence. (https://www.ombudsman.bg/en/n/ombudsmans-secretary-general-ombudsman-institution-sounds-years-long-alarm-a-2293)
Who is talking. Sector and legal media are talking about Vivacom through court and regulator decisions. SeeNews reported the final Supreme Administrative Court ruling on Bulsatcom in February 2026. BNR reported Consumer Protection Commission action on unilateral price changes in 2025. Telecompaper reported that CRC ordered Vivacom to investigate an April 2025 network failure. (https://seenews.com/news/bulgarias-supreme-court-clears-united-groups-acquisition-of-bulsatcom-1290035; https://bnrnews.bg/en/post/123374/cpc-issues-an-order-prohibiting-the-unilateral-price-increases-by-mobile-operators; https://www.telecompaper.com/news/bulgarian-regulator-orders-vivacom-to-investigate-cause-of-network-failure--1535070)
Who is talking. Technology and platform partners are talking about Vivacom’s operating base. Netcracker talked about a 2026 Vivacom IT modernisation extension. United Cloud talked about EON’s origin, features and regional use. United Group talked about Vivacom’s EON, fibre, 5G and television growth. (https://www.netcracker.com/news/press-releases/netcracker-and-vivacom-extend-long-term-partnership-for-innovative-it-modernization-program; https://united.cloud/latest/eon-tv-and-chill; https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/)
Who is talking. KZP is talking about Vivacom by name in consumer-protection enforcement. On 28 February 2025 it reported the final Supreme Administrative Court confirmation of preliminary execution of the order banning Vivacom monthly-fee indexation. On 19 March 2025 it reported the court rejection of Vivacom's second attempt to stop preliminary execution of the early-termination penalty order. (https://kzp.bg/bg/novini-mobilni-operatori/264; https://kzp.bg/bg/novini-mobilni-operatori/273)
Who is talking. The Council for Electronic Media is talking through its public register. It lists Vivacom Bulgaria EAD, EIK 831642181, its registered address, management board, supervisory board, sole owner United Group Luxembourg S.a.r.l., and registered cable, satellite and video-on-demand services. (https://www.cem.bg/linear_reg_docs.php?cat=1&id=428)
Who is talking. SeeNews and Capital are talking about possible United Group Bulgarian asset sales. SeeNews reported Capital's account that United Group was considering selling some or all Bulgarian assets, including Vivacom's fixed network and Nova Broadcasting Group. (https://seenews.com/news/see-focused-united-group-mulls-selling-bulgarian-assets-report-1294890)
Who is talking. SpeedGeo and V-SPEED are talking about Vivacom's broadband performance. Their 2025 Bulgaria broadband report ranked Vivacom first on average download speed and published the method behind the ranking. (https://www.speedgeo.net/storage/upload/award-pdf/en/broadband_bulgaria_2025.pdf)
Who is talking. SafeJournalists and a named group of Serbian civil society organisations are talking about United Group's media sale as a media-freedom issue. The signatories included the Independent Journalists' Association of Serbia, Transparency Serbia, A11 Initiative, Helsinki Committee for Human Rights in Serbia, YUCOM and CRTA. (https://safejournalists.net/potential-sale-of-adria-news-network-threatens-media-freedoms/)

United Group said Alpac had a record in international news assets and that ANN would have contractual safeguards for editorial independence. SafeJournalists challenged that confidence by citing concerns over Alpac's Euronews Serbia record and called for regulator scrutiny. (https://united.group/alpac-capital-and-united-group-announce-agreement-for-the-sale-of-adria-news-network/; https://safejournalists.net/potential-sale-of-adria-news-network-threatens-media-freedoms/)
Who is talking. Vivacom is talking heavily through LinkedIn as an employer, civic and youth-skills channel. Its LinkedIn page has 22,015 followers and shows 2,354 listed employees. Vivacom posted that 55 young people joined its 23rd summer internship edition from nearly 1,800 candidates. Vivacom posted that Job Lab reached 120 pupils in Sofia, Varna, Veliko Tarnovo and Blagoevgrad and added a module for young people from transition housing. (https://bg.linkedin.com/company/vivacom)
Who is talking. Vivacom's current chief executive is talking directly to interns and students. Vivacom's 8 August 2025 news item says Asen Velikov met summer interns for the third consecutive year. The item says interns asked about career development, innovation, infrastructure and the future of telecommunications. (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/stazhantite-na-vivacom-v-razgovor-s-glavniya-izpalnitelen-direktor-asen-velikov)

Opensignal's January 2026 Bulgaria report compares A1, Yettel and Vivacom across mobile experience awards. Who is talking. Customers are talking in high-volume app stores as well as Trustpilot. Google Play lists My Vivacom with 62.7K reviews and an update on 4 August 2026. (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en_IE&id=bg.vivacom.mobile; https://apps.apple.com/bg/app/my-vivacom/id1297193461?see-all=reviews&platform=iphone; https://www.trustpilot.com/review/www.vivacom.bg)
Who is talking. Legal and sector specialists are talking about Vivacom inside Bulgaria's wider telecom, media and internet rulebook. ICLG names Vivacom as a main fixed internet, mobile and pay-TV operator. ICLG also maps the regulators and laws that frame telecom, media, privacy, cybersecurity and artificial intelligence claims.
