record.question: Customers and public authorities criticise pricing, contracts, outages, and data handling, while United Group, partners, and network testers support the investment and infrastructure story; where must the new narrative carry a proof point rather than a promise?
record.finding:
Advocates and critics. United Group is a clear advocate for Vivacom's investment story. In July 2026, United Group said Vivacom's priority areas were fibre, 5G and television, and its CEO Stan Miller said the group would keep backing the Bulgarian team. (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/)
Advocates and critics. Vivacom's own management is an advocate for market consolidation. In July 2023, Vivacom rejected A1 and Yettel allegations as unfounded and said Bulgaria's fixed broadband and pay-TV markets remained multi-player markets. It said Vivacom held 31% of fixed broadband and 33% of pay TV by subscribers. (https://www.broadbandtvnews.com/2023/07/04/vivacom-dismisses-unfounded-concerns-from-competitors/)
Advocates and critics. PPF Telecom Group and Yettel Bulgaria are open critics of Vivacom's acquisition path. In July 2023, PPF said CPC approvals would put Vivacom near 70% of internet access in Rousse and near 50% in Varna, Razgrad, Silistra and Sofia City. PPF also said Vivacom held 32.9% of television distribution and 31.4% of fixed internet nationally before the Bulsatcom infrastructure question. (https://www.ppf.eu/en/press-release/ppf-telecom-group-dismayed-by-regulatory-ruling-taken-in-bulgaria)
Advocates and critics. A1 Bulgaria is a critic in the same competition dispute. Broadband TV News reported that Vivacom rejected allegations made by A1 and Yettel after CPC cleared Vivacom's acquisition of Networx and Telnet. (https://www.broadbandtvnews.com/2023/07/04/vivacom-dismisses-unfounded-concerns-from-competitors/)
Advocates and critics. The mayor of Stara Zagora was an advocate for Vivacom's satellite project with Eutelsat. United Group quoted Mayor Zhivko Todorov saying the project would stimulate the city and support digital inclusion across Eurasia. (https://united.group/vivacom-and-eutelsat-group-are-launching-in-bulgaria-the-fourth-european-ground-station/)
Advocates and critics. The banked record shows a three-sided argument around consolidation. United Group and Vivacom frame acquisitions as investment and service improvement. CRC, CPC, courts and the European Commission frame them as matters for approval, market definition and public-interest duties. PPF, Yettel and A1 frame them as concentration risk. (banked findings: United Group owner findings; CRC market-standing findings; CPC acquisition findings; PPF/Yettel/A1 critic findings; Vivacom denial finding)
Advocates and critics. A1 Group criticised Vivacom-linked acquisition activity in 2023 and said Vivacom could acquire over 60% of the TV distribution market and nearly 40% of the internet market. A1 Group said it had alerted the European Commission about concerns over what it called the hidden buyout of Bulsatcom by United Group. (https://newsroom.a1.com/news-a1-group-deeply-unsettled-by-an-unexpected-decision-of-the-bulgarian-commission-on-protection-of-competition?id=182022&l=english&menueid=14594)
Advocates and critics. The Supreme Administrative Court gave United Group a clear legal win on 19 February 2026. SeeNews reported that the court finally cleared the Bulsatcom infrastructure-assets acquisition after appeals by A1 Bulgaria, Yettel Bulgaria and Cetin Bulgaria. The court said the network deal and base-station infrastructure-assets deal did not form a notifiable concentration under Bulgarian competition law. (https://seenews.com/news/bulgarias-supreme-court-clears-united-groups-acquisition-of-bulsatcom-1290035)
Advocates and critics. Customers are visible critics in public review space. Trustpilot listed Vivacom with a 1.3 score from 203 reviews, 41 reviews in the previous 12 months and 92% one-star reviews. Trustpilot also marked the profile as unclaimed and warned that Vivacom had not invited customers, so the reviews may not be representative. (https://www.trustpilot.com/review/www.vivacom.bg)
Advocates and critics. The Ombudsman Institution criticised mobile-service price increases and named Vivacom as one of the operators that followed Yettel’s end-2022 indexation move. It said public discontent produced numerous complaints and that the Ombudsman referred issues to the Commission for Consumer Protection, the Communications Regulation Commission and other authorities. (https://www.ombudsman.bg/en/n/ombudsmans-secretary-general-ombudsman-institution-sounds-years-long-alarm-a-2293)
Advocates and critics. The banked record shows a split between supportive network proof and public conduct pressure. United Group, Vivacom, partners and SpeedGeo support the investment and network story. Regulators, courts, the Ombudsman Institution, customers and competitors put pressure on pricing, outages, data protection, contracts and consolidation. (banked findings: United Group advocate findings; regulator findings; customer review finding; PPF/Yettel/A1 critic findings; SpeedGeo 2025 source: https://www.speedgeo.net/storage/upload/award-pdf/en/broadband_bulgaria_2025.pdf)
Advocates and critics. KZP acted as a critic and enforcer on Vivacom monthly-fee indexation. On 28 February 2025, KZP said the Supreme Administrative Court confirmed preliminary execution of its order banning Vivacom from applying indexed monthly fees. KZP said the increases were between BGN 1.00 and BGN 2.00 and that customers could complain to Vivacom or KZP if the increase continued. (https://kzp.bg/bg/novini-mobilni-operatori/264)
Advocates and critics. KZP acted as a critic and enforcer on Vivacom early-termination penalties. On 19 March 2025, KZP said the Supreme Administrative Court rejected Vivacom's second attempt to stop preliminary execution of order 2594 of 4 September 2024. KZP said the order banned Vivacom from requiring more than one penalty, or a penalty higher than the contractual maximum, when consumers ended fixed-term contracts early. (https://kzp.bg/bg/novini-mobilni-operatori/273)
Advocates and critics. United Group and Alpac Capital advocated the Adria News Network sale by saying the buyer would protect editorial independence. United Group said Alpac was selected because it met the governance and independence principles. United Group said the agreement includes contractual safeguards for editorial and functional independence. SafeJournalists challenged the sale and called it a threat to media freedom in Serbia and the Western Balkans. (https://united.group/alpac-capital-and-united-group-announce-agreement-for-the-sale-of-adria-news-network/; https://safejournalists.net/potential-sale-of-adria-news-network-threatens-media-freedoms/)
Advocates and critics. Dragan Solak and Victoriya Boklag are critics of United Group's media-asset sale path. SeeNews reported on 26 May 2026 that they filed London proceedings against three BC Partners-owned entities to block the planned United Media sale. SeeNews said they claimed the sale breached shareholder-agreement consent rights over material changes to United Group's business. (https://seenews.com/news/united-group-founder-former-ceo-seek-to-block-sale-of-see-media-assets-1295343)
Advocates and critics. The banked record now shows competitors have several roles at once. A1 Bulgaria, Yettel Bulgaria and CETIN Bulgaria appear as critics of Vivacom-linked acquisitions, as co-contractors with Vivacom on state digital-network work, and as part of a possible buyer set through e& PPF. (banked findings: Supreme Administrative Court Bulsatcom; public digital-network project; fixed-network divestment possibility)
Advocates and critics. Independent network testers give Vivacom useful support, but not a clean all-network win. SpeedGeo ranked Vivacom first for fixed broadband from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026, with 117.0 Mb/s download, 85.2 Mb/s upload and 25 ms ping. SpeedGeo ranked Vivacom third in mobile download speed behind A1 and Yettel in the same period. Opensignal's January 2026 report says Vivacom dominated Coverage Experience while A1 was the fastest network and Yettel led Time on Network and Reliability. (https://www.speedgeo.net/statistics/bulgaria; https://insights.opensignal.com/reports/2026/01/bulgaria/mobile-network-experience)
Advocates and critics. Public app-store users are a large critic set around digital service and payment experience. Google Play lists My Vivacom at 3.9 stars, 62.7K reviews and more than 1 million downloads. Apple App Store Bulgaria lists My Vivacom at 3.6 out of 5 from 16K ratings. Recent app reviews on both stores raise login, payment, passcode and service-management complaints. (https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?hl=en_IE&id=bg.vivacom.mobile; https://apps.apple.com/bg/app/my-vivacom/id1297193461?see-all=reviews&platform=iphone)
Advocates and critics. ICLG gives a counterweight to the competitor concentration criticism. ICLG says Bulgaria's broadband market has strong infrastructure-based competition. ICLG says Vivacom and A1 serve 39.4% and 29.9% of fixed internet subscribers, while the rest of the market includes many regional operators. (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/)

verdicts.because: It directly uses the finding’s split between United Group/partners/network testers supporting the investment and infrastructure story and customers/public authorities criticising pricing, contracts, outages and data handling.

It directly uses the finding’s specific split between customers/public authorities criticizing pricing, contracts, outages and data handling, and United Group, partners and network testers supporting the investment and infrastructure story.

record.question: Vivacom faces telecom, competition, consumer, data, cyber, Digital Services Act, Digital Markets Act, and Artificial Intelligence Act scrutiny; which claim areas need mandatory Legal and Regulatory review before any client-facing use?
record.finding:
Regulatory context. Bulgaria’s telecom sector is governed by EU rules including the European Electronic Communications Code, ePrivacy Directive, Net Neutrality Regulation, Roaming Regulation, Gigabit Infrastructure Act and EU termination-rate rules; Bulgarian core laws include the Electronic Communications Act and Electronic Communications Networks and Physical Infrastructure Act (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).
Regulatory context. Telecom and adjacent digital activity in Bulgaria is also affected by the General Data Protection Regulation, Digital Services Act, Digital Markets Act, Cybersecurity Act, Artificial Intelligence Act, NIS2 Directive and Critical Entity Resilience Directive; this confirms the supplied brief’s legal and AI-policy constraints (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).
Regulatory context. The Communications Regulation Commission is the independent telecom regulator; the Ministry of Transport and Communications and Ministry of e-Government set ICT, digital administration and cybersecurity policy; the National Radio Frequency Spectrum Council handles national spectrum-planning proposals (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).
Regulatory context. CRC Decision No. 220 of 30 July 2024 found no effective competition in wholesale access to passive physical infrastructure, named Vivacom as having significant individual impact, and imposed access, non-discrimination, transparency, reference-offer and price-control duties (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Regulatory context. CRC launched a fourth-round analysis of local access at a fixed location, and by Decision No. 251 of 29 August 2025 ordered extra information on fixed access via mobile network for 2021-2023; this keeps fixed access and 5G-based home internet inside active review (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Regulatory context. CRC says Vivacom met all universal-service quality target values in 2024, did not request unfair-burden compensation by the 30 June 2024 statutory deadline, and had a 46% drop in universal-service complaints versus the prior period (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Regulatory context. CRC says 2024 universal-service complaints to Vivacom were mainly technical failures at 27% of complaints; termination complaints rose to 16% from 2% in 2023, and the other category rose 18 percentage points to 29% (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Regulatory context. CMS says CRC awarded 20-year 3.6 GHz licences to A1, Vivacom and Yettel in April 2021, and assigned 700 MHz and 800 MHz bands to the same three operators in December 2023 for 15 years; CMS says total licence payments were about BGN 13.4 million (https://cms.law/en/int/expert-guides/cms-expert-guide-to-5g-regulation-and-law/bulgaria).
Regulatory context. Bulgaria’s Supreme Administrative Court issued a final ruling in February 2026 clearing United Group’s acquisition of Bulsatcom telecom infrastructure assets after appeals by A1 Bulgaria, Yettel Bulgaria and Cetin Bulgaria; the court said the deal and base-station infrastructure asset deal were not a notifiable concentration under Bulgarian competition law (https://seenews.com/news/bulgarias-supreme-court-clears-united-groups-acquisition-of-bulsatcom-1290035).
Regulatory context. A1 Group publicly objected in July 2023 to CPC approval of Vivacom acquisitions of Networx-Bulgaria and six smaller operators, saying the deals could give Vivacom more than 60% of TV distribution and nearly 40% of internet; CRC’s 2024 market data later reported Vivacom at 59.6% of pay-TV subscribers and 39.4% of fixed internet subscribers (https://newsroom.a1.com/news-a1-group-deeply-unsettled-by-an-unexpected-decision-of-the-bulgarian-commission-on-protection-of-competition?id=182022&l=english&menueid=14594; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Regulatory context. The banked record shows a regulatory pattern: Vivacom is being treated both as a regulated infrastructure holder and as the main object of consolidation scrutiny. The banked record says CRC imposed access, non-discrimination, transparency, reference-offer and price-control duties on Vivacom for passive physical infrastructure; rivals objected to or appealed Vivacom-linked acquisitions; and the Supreme Administrative Court cleared United Group’s acquisition of Bulsatcom infrastructure assets as not notifiable under Bulgarian competition law (banked findings: CRC Decision No. 220 of 30 July 2024; A1 objection; Supreme Administrative Court Bulsatcom ruling).
Regulatory context. On 27 June 2025, the Commission on Protection of Competition, the Commission for Consumer Protection and CRC signed a cooperation agreement for consumer protection, market transparency and price-increase scrutiny before and after euro adoption. CRC said it had agreements with telecom undertakings on a working model. The consumer regulator said mobile-service prices would be included in the unified consumer portal, and that rules for consumer protection in electronic communications had already been revised with CRC. The competition authority said it was about to start a sector analysis of the telecommunications services market (https://crc.bg/en/news/1699/cpc-ccp-and-crc-join-forces-for-better-consumer-protection-and-market-transparency).
Regulatory context. Bulgaria’s amended Cybersecurity Act entered into force on 13 February 2026 and transposed NIS2, 16 months after the original deadline. Public electronic communications network providers are classed as essential entities. Regulated entities must give an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notice within 72 hours and a final report within one month. Essential-entity penalties can reach EUR 10 million or 2% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, with manager liability also introduced (https://www.schoenherr.eu/content/bulgaria-implements-nis-2-directive-key-changes-to-the-cybersecurity-act).
Regulatory context. The European Commission sent Bulgaria a reasoned opinion on 7 May 2025 for failing to notify full NIS2 transposition by the 17 October 2024 deadline. The Commission says NIS2 covers public electronic communications services and other critical sectors (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/nis2-directive-bulgaria; https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/news/commission-calls-19-member-states-fully-transpose-nis2-directive).
Regulatory context. The AI Act entered into force on 1 August 2024 and became applicable on 2 August 2026, with earlier rules for prohibited practices, AI literacy and general-purpose AI. From 2 August 2026, the AI Office and member-state authorities enforce the Act. High-risk systems in sensitive areas now apply from 2 December 2027, and high-risk systems embedded in regulated products apply from 2 August 2028 (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai).
Regulatory context. The banked record shows a new regulatory pattern when read together with CRC’s Digital Services Act role: scrutiny is widening from telecom market duties into consumer protection, cyber incident reporting, online-safety coordination and euro-adoption price monitoring. CRC imposed passive-infrastructure duties on Vivacom. CPC, CCP and CRC agreed joint consumer and price scrutiny. Bulgaria transposed NIS2 with 24-hour early warning and 72-hour incident notice duties. CRC was appointed Digital Services Coordinator but said it could not perform the role in full without national Article 49 legislation (banked findings: CRC Decision No. 220, CPC-CCP-CRC cooperation, Cybersecurity Act; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Regulatory context. CRC says Council of Ministers Decision No. 405 of 13 June 2024 appointed CRC as Bulgaria’s Digital Services Coordinator. CRC says it joined all 12 meetings of the European Board for Digital Services in 2024. CRC says the lack of a law imposing the specific obligations under Article 49 of the Digital Services Act prevented it from performing the coordinator role in full (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Regulatory context. CRC says 612 undertakings provided retail internet access in 2024. CRC says its analysis of reports under Articles 3 and 4 of the open-internet regulation found the requirements were met. CRC says the nettest.crc.bg portal and the CRC Network Quality app have been available to end users since 2023 for fixed and mobile internet quality measurement (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Regulatory context. CRC says it adopted a position on free spectrum resources in the 1.5 GHz, 2.6 GHz, 3.6 GHz and 26 GHz bands after public consultation. CRC says it amended rules for 900 MHz and 1800 MHz to support technological neutrality. CRC says 2025 priorities include WRC-23 implementation and completing the fourth review of wholesale local access at a fixed location (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Regulatory context. CRC says it began building a specialised electromagnetic-compatibility laboratory in 2024. CRC says the site opened on 9 May 2024 and the structure-acceptance certificate was drawn up on 23 December 2024. CRC says procurement also started for robotic SAR measuring equipment (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Regulatory context. The EU Gigabit Infrastructure Act applies from 12 November 2025, with some rules applying earlier from February and May 2026 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/EN/legal-content/summary/gigabit-infrastructure-act-gia.html).
Regulatory context. CRC Decision No. 185 of 22 May 2025 opened public consultation on draft conditions for Vivacom, A1 and Yettel permits in the 900 MHz and 1800 MHz bands (https://crc.bg/en/news/1685/crc-has-opened-a-procedure-for-public-consultations-on-the-draft-conditions-to-be-included-in-the-permits-of-mobile-companies-for-the-use-of-radio-frequency-spectrum-in-the-900-mhz-and-1800-mhz-bands).
Regulatory context. CRC said the 900 MHz and 1800 MHz permits lacked coverage obligations and proposed adding coverage and speed duties in the public interest (https://crc.bg/files/URChS/ObstObsazhdane/2025/20250522_reshenie_185.pdf).
Regulatory context. The draft permit conditions require 99.9% coverage of settlements below 3,000 residents with 30 Mbps within three years of the permit change (https://crc.bg/files/URChS/ObstObsazhdane/2025/20250522_proekt_uslovia_razreshenia_900_1800_MHz.pdf).
Regulatory context. The draft permit conditions require coverage of all highways, first-class roads and railway lines with 50 Mbps within three years of the permit change (https://crc.bg/files/URChS/ObstObsazhdane/2025/20250522_proekt_uslovia_razreshenia_900_1800_MHz.pdf).
Regulatory context. The draft permit conditions require 99.5% national territory coverage with 50 Mbps, 99.5% coverage of all settlements with 100 Mbps, and road and rail coverage duties within five years of the permit change (https://crc.bg/files/URChS/ObstObsazhdane/2025/20250522_proekt_uslovia_razreshenia_900_1800_MHz.pdf).
Regulatory context. The draft permit conditions allow the operators to meet the duties through infrastructure sharing, active-network sharing, spectrum sharing, national roaming, joint network build and access for mobile virtual network operators (https://crc.bg/files/URChS/ObstObsazhdane/2025/20250522_proekt_uslovia_razreshenia_900_1800_MHz.pdf).
Regulatory context. CRC Decision No. 198 of 12 June 2025 ordered United Fiber Bulgaria to keep 31 December 2022 price terms until prices are set under an approved passive-infrastructure reference offer (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2025_BG.pdf).
Regulatory context. The banked record and this pass show that Vivacom should be assessed through three separate regulatory lenses: wholesale access duties, merger and asset-deal scrutiny, and retail concentration claims (banked findings: passive-infrastructure duties; fixed access review; Bulsatcom clearance; A1 objection; Vivacom market shares; this pass: CRC Decision No. 198 and 900 MHz and 1800 MHz consultation).

record.question: United Group has quantified environmental proof, while Vivacom-specific environmental, social, and governance proof is stronger in social programmes than in audited Bulgaria-only climate data; what group-verified data can we use safely?
record.finding:
ESG context. United Group says its 2024 sustainability results included 61% electricity from renewable sources, a 52% cut in Scope 1 and 2 emissions against its 2020 baseline, a 13% improvement in its Network Efficiency Index, 25% refurbished customer premises equipment among installed devices, more than 2,300 kg of e-waste recovered, and more than 1,500 smartphones recovered through customer take-back programs (https://united.group/united-group-releases-2024-sustainability-report-highlighting-tangible-progress-across-esg-priorities/).
ESG context. United Group says it is building three solar plants and one wind farm in Bulgaria; by 2027 these assets are planned to supply 160% of electricity needed for the Group’s Bulgarian operations, cover 65% of total Group electricity use, remove about 120,000 tonnes of CO2 from Bulgaria’s grid each year, reach 124 MW combined capacity, and produce 310,000 MWh a year (https://united.group/united-group-enters-renewable-energy-production/).
ESG context. A Vivacom careers page says United Group Energy develops renewable power plants to supply United Group telecom and media operations with 100% green electricity, and says Bulgaria has more than 120 MW of renewable projects under development, construction and operation (https://www.vivacom.bg/bg/residential/za-nas/karieri/obiavi-za-rabota/31166/senior-electrical-engineer-high-voltage-substations-sofia).
ESG context. Vivacom says its management system is certified to ISO 9001:2015, ISO 14001:2015, ISO 45001:2018, ISO/IEC 20000-1:2018, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, and ISO/IEC 27018:2019; I did not find an independent certificate register for each standard in this pass, so this is a client claim awaiting document proof (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata).
ESG context. The banked record shows a proof split: United Group has quantified group-level environmental proof, while Vivacom-specific certificates still need document proof. United Group reported 61% renewable electricity, a 52% Scope 1 and 2 cut against 2020, 25% refurbished customer premises equipment among installed devices, and e-waste and phone take-back figures; Vivacom’s ISO claims were not independently proved in the banked pass (banked findings: United Group 2024 sustainability results; Vivacom certification claim).
ESG context. United Group says its 2040 net-zero target was approved by the Science Based Targets initiative in February 2024. United Group says its near-term targets are a 90% absolute Scope 1 and 2 cut by 2030 from 2020 and a 40% Scope 3 cut by 2030 from 2022. United Group says its long-term target is a 90% Scope 3 cut by 2040 from 2022. The Science Based Targets initiative says targets in its dashboard are reviewed and validated by SBTi Services, but this pass did not extract the United Group row from the dashboard itself (https://united.group/united-groups-net-zero-target-gains-approval-from-the-science-based-targets-initiative-sbti/; https://sciencebasedtargets.org/target-dashboard).
ESG context. Vivacom says it follows United Group targets including 100% renewable electricity sourcing by 2027, zero waste to landfill by 2030, 40% women in managerial positions by 2030, average 40 learning hours per employee annually by 2030, annual Code of Responsible Business Conduct and Ethics training for 100% of employees, and five annual on-site supplier-standard audits through 2030. Independent public proof in this pass corroborated the climate target validation only, not the social and governance targets (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/ustojchivo-razvitie; https://united.group/sustainability-our-vision-esg-targets-progress/).
ESG context. United Group’s H1 2026 update says Vivacom ran the Bulgarian pilot of Job Lab with 120 students in Sofia, Varna, Veliko Tarnovo and Blagoevgrad. The same update says Vivacom completed the 16th Technical Academy with new artificial-intelligence and cybersecurity courses, held a Private 5G Hackathon, took 55 people into its Summer Internship Programme, and extended its partnership with the Association of Olympic Teams in Natural Sciences to 2028 with an extra EUR 30,000 donation (https://united.group/updates-from-united-groups-operations-h1-2026/).
ESG context. The European Commission says Bulgaria’s 2026 digital record has strong infrastructure but weak use. It reports 38.3% of people with at least basic digital skills versus 60.4% for the EU. It reports 38.3% of SMEs with basic digital intensity versus 71.4% for the EU. It reports 15.7% business cloud use, 8.6% AI use and 27.1% data analytics use (https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-10476-2026-ADD-32/en/pdf).
ESG context. The European Commission says cybersecurity maturity in Bulgaria remains uneven, especially among SMEs. It recommends stronger cybersecurity preparedness in SMEs and critical sectors. Bulgarian citizens put online privacy and security first: 91% named it as the top digital priority for the next decade (https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/factpages/bulgarias-2026-digital-decade-country-report).
ESG context. Vivacom says it is the "първият телеком в България" to offer Eco Half SIM cards made from 100% recycled plastic. Vivacom says supplier data shows the cards can cut carbon emissions by up to 18% versus Half SIM and 43% versus standard SIM cards. Vivacom says earlier Half SIM use cut plastic waste by 50%, cut emissions by 30%, reached more than 380,000 cards, and e-invoicing saved 10 tonnes of paper per month in 2023. I did not find an independent public source verifying those Vivacom-specific figures in this pass (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/novini/vivacom-vavejda-parvite-v-bulgaria-eco-half-sim-karti-ot-100-retsiklirana-plastmasa).
ESG context. Vivacom says it began replacing paper monthly invoices with electronic invoices in October 2024 for private customers and part of its business customers. Vivacom says invoices are available through My Vivacom and up to 12 months of electronic invoices can be accessed there. I did not find an independent public source measuring the customer effect of this change in this pass (https://www.vivacom.bg/e-bill).
ESG context. Vivacom Regional Grant began in 2015 and supports civil-society projects in education, environment, social issues, culture, sport and health (https://www.bblf.bg/en/initiatives/112/project/3117/vivacom-regional-grant).
ESG context. From its seventh edition, Vivacom Regional Grant narrowed its priority areas to education and environment (https://www.bblf.bg/en/initiatives/112/project/3117/vivacom-regional-grant).
ESG context. By January 2024, Vivacom Regional Grant had funded 108 projects by 98 organizations for more than BGN 500,000 (https://amcham.bg/2024/01/31/the-9th-edition-of-the-vivacom-regional-grant-has-been-launched/).
ESG context. The ninth Vivacom Regional Grant doubled the maximum NGO grant from BGN 5,000 to BGN 10,000 and set a total donation pool of BGN 100,000 (https://amcham.bg/2024/01/31/the-9th-edition-of-the-vivacom-regional-grant-has-been-launched/).
ESG context. Vivacom won BBLF’s 2024 Investor in Human Capital and Working Conditions award for its Summer Internship Programme (https://www.bblf.bg/en/bblf-and-partner-news/1855/bblf-announced-the-winners-of-the-21st-annual-responsible-business-awards).
ESG context. Bulgaria’s circular-economy transition remains slow, with weak resource efficiency and risk of missing 2025 municipal-waste recycling targets (https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/europe-environment-2025/countries/bulgaria).
ESG context. Bulgaria’s updated national energy and climate plan sets a 34.96% renewable share of gross final energy consumption by 2030 (https://climate-laws.org/document/bulgaria-updated-final-national-energy-and-climate-plan-necp-2021-2030_c0db).
ESG context. The banked record and this pass show that Vivacom-specific ESG proof is strongest in social programmes, while climate proof remains mainly at United Group or Bulgarian renewables-project level (banked findings: United Group 2024 sustainability results; Vivacom certification claim; United Group energy assets; Vivacom targets; Vivacom H1 2026 social programmes; this pass: Vivacom Regional Grant and BBLF award).

record.question: Bulgaria's category context shows strong fibre coverage, rising internet revenue, IPTV growth, and concentrated bundled services; which market shifts should the strategy turn into a business case for reputation work?
record.finding:
Category context. Bulgaria’s electronic communications market reached EUR 2.06 billion in 2024, up 5.7% on 2023, according to the ICLG Bulgaria telecoms chapter citing CRC data (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).
Category context. United Group said in July 2026 that Bulgaria’s telecom market grew close to 5% last year to EUR 2.16 billion, and said the growth came in fibre, 5G and television (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/).
Category context. CRC reported bundled-service revenue of BGN 2.064 billion in 2024, up 10.6% year on year; A1, Vivacom and Yettel accounted for 97.8% of bundled-service revenue and 98.3% of bundled-service subscribers (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Category context. Vivacom’s bundled-service subscriber share rose from 30.7% in 2023 to 32.9% in 2024, and its bundled-service revenue share rose from 27.6% to 30.2%; CRC says Bulsatcom was deleted from the CRC register and its activity was reported by Vivacom (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Category context. CRC reported retail fixed internet and data-transfer revenue of BGN 1.879791 billion in 2024; Vivacom led retail fixed internet access with 39.4% of subscribers and 37.1% of revenue, up 7.2 and 8.3 percentage points year on year (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Category context. CRC reported 2.02 million pay-TV subscribers at the end of 2024; Vivacom led pay TV with 59.6% of subscribers and 56.5% of revenue after the incorporation of Bulsatcom and TVN Distribution Bulgaria (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Category context. CRC reported IPTV subscribers grew 9.4% in 2024 and IPTV reached 47.8% of pay-TV subscribers; Vivacom, A1 and Yettel together made up 95.0% of IPTV subscribers (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Category context. CRC reported satellite TV subscribers fell 8.4% in 2024; after Bulsatcom was incorporated into Vivacom, Vivacom’s satellite-TV subscriber share exceeded 80.0% by the end of 2024 (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Category context. The banked record shows a category pattern: growth, consolidation and concentration are moving together. The banked record reports market growth in fibre, 5G and TV; Vivacom share gains in bundled services, fixed internet, pay TV and satellite TV; Bulsatcom and TVN activity incorporated into Vivacom; and rival objections to acquisitions and market shares (banked findings: CRC 2024 market data; United Group July 2026 market growth statement; A1 objection; Bulsatcom incorporation findings).
Category context. ICLG says 62.4% of fixed internet subscribers in Bulgaria used fibre-optic access at the end of 2024. ICLG says Vivacom and A1 served 39.4% and 29.9% of fixed internet subscribers, respectively, while the rest of the market included many regional operators. ICLG says Bulgaria has strong infrastructure-based competition in broadband, and mobile shares sit in the 30% to 37% range across A1, Yettel and Vivacom (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).
Category context. Vivacom says it is an "иноватор" and says it invested close to BGN 3 billion in technology, innovation, people and the Bulgarian economy. Vivacom says more than 2 million clients use more than 5.5 million services. Independent sources in this pass corroborate Vivacom’s leading shares in fixed internet and pay TV, but did not verify the BGN 3 billion investment claim (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata; https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).
Category context. The European Commission says Bulgaria reached 93.53% fixed very high-capacity network coverage in 2025, above the EU average of 85.54%. It says Bulgaria reached 93.53% fibre-to-the-premises coverage, above the EU average of 74.13%. It says Bulgaria reached 94.83% basic 5G coverage, slightly below the EU average of 96.79% (https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-10476-2026-ADD-32/en/pdf).
Category context. The European Commission says Bulgaria’s 3.4-3.8 GHz 5G coverage was 79.62% in 2025, above the EU average of 74.75%. It says Bulgarian 1 Gbps fixed-broadband subscriptions were only 2.92% of fixed-broadband subscriptions, below the EU average of 26.97%. It says Bulgarian 5G SIM penetration reached 41.25%, below the EU average of 55.55% (https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-10476-2026-ADD-32/en/pdf).
Category context. United Group says Bulgaria’s internet revenue rose more than 9% to EUR 1.21 billion in 2025. United Group says IPTV passed one million households and became Bulgaria’s most widely used television platform. United Group says cable and satellite TV are declining. These details were not in the banked record, but the underlying CRC 2025 table was not found in the CRC annual-reports page in this pass (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/; https://crc.bg/en/rubrics/375/annual-reports).
Category context. Yettel says it connects more than 3 million users in Bulgaria and has more than 180 stores. Yettel reports 2025 revenue of EUR 557 million, EBITDA of EUR 162 million, CAPEX of EUR 47 million, 1,989 employees, 3.208 million mobile subscribers, 141,000 fixed-broadband subscribers and 104,000 pay-TV subscribers. CETIN Bulgaria reports 2025 revenue of EUR 170 million, EBITDA of EUR 123 million and CAPEX of EUR 76 million (https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/yettel-bulgaria; https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/cetin-bulgaria).
Category context. Bulgaria’s electronic communications market reached BGN 4.220 billion in 2025, up 4.9% on 2024 (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2025_BG.pdf).
Category context. Data-transfer and internet-access revenue reached BGN 2.376 billion in 2025 and made up 56.3% of the Bulgarian electronic communications market (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2025_BG.pdf).
Category context. Retail internet subscribers reached 11.216 million at 31 December 2025, with the increase partly affected by a changed bundled-service definition that added prepaid mobile users (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2025_BG.pdf).
Category context. Bulgaria had 3.169 million 5G subscriptions at 31 December 2025, equal to 37.5% of mobile-internet subscriptions (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2025_BG.pdf).
Category context. CRC data put 5G coverage at 92% of population and almost 66% of territory at the end of 2025 (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2025_BG.pdf).
Category context. Fixed broadband delivered over mobile networks reached 23.3% of fixed-broadband subscribers in 2025 (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2025_BG.pdf).
Category context. xDSL, provided only by Vivacom, fell to just above 2% of fixed-broadband subscribers at the end of 2025 (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2025_BG.pdf).
Category context. IPTV was the only TV-distribution revenue line to grow in 2025, rising 1.4% year on year (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2025_BG.pdf).
Category context. SpeedGeo says Vivacom led Bulgarian broadband speed for 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026, while A1 led mobile download speed and lowest mobile ping in the same period (https://www.speedgeo.net/statistics/bulgaria).

verdicts.because: It directly uses the finding’s specific facts about fibre coverage, internet revenue growth, IPTV growth, and concentration in bundled services.

record.question: Vivacom's reputation problem is that its public story does not yet turn its strongest assets into one trusted national role. The open space is a clear story about useful Bulgarian digital infrastructure, grounded in fixed internet, television, coverage, satellite capacity, public-service duties, skills programmes and local digital projects. The claim must stay inside the evidence: Vivacom can credibly support leadership in fixed internet, pay TV, coverage and satellite growth, but it cannot claim total telecom leadership across every mobile, internet or customer-experience measure. A1, Yettel, CETIN and Neterra all carry credible network, quality, infrastructure or specialist claims, so Vivacom should not compete with another broad technology claim. It should prove the national outcomes that only its mix of incumbent infrastructure, United Group scale, EON, Bulsatcom, satellite assets, public-sector work and skills programmes can connect.
record.finding:
The white space. The main national operators converge on network, technology, entertainment, ESG and employer claims. The supplied brief already flags that sameness, and the public record supports it through A1's market-scale and service-breadth claims, Yettel's certified network-quality claims and Vivacom's fibre, 5G and TV growth frame (SOURCE DOCUMENT: sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md; https://a1.com/a1-group-and-markets/a1-in-bulgaria/; https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/yettel-bulgaria; https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/).
The white space. A less occupied space is a national digital-infrastructure story that connects scale to people's daily and economic progress, not only to network claims. Vivacom has the assets for that story, but Pikasa's Q1 2026 analysis says much of its press volume was PR-led announcements with weak audience response (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war; SOURCE DOCUMENT: sanitized-telecom-blank-slate-brief.md).
The white space. Another open space is useful public service content. Pikasa says Yettel earned more varied coverage from tactile strips, digital literacy reaching 60,000 children, volunteering culture and entertainment stories, while A1 and Vivacom were more often present through sponsorship, product or announcement material (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war).
The white space. A B2B white space sits between mass telecom and specialist infrastructure. A1 owns ICT breadth through STEMO, Neterra owns enterprise-network credibility, and Vivacom can credibly connect national network scale with smart cities, cybersecurity, education, EON and fibre if it proves the role through named projects (https://newsroom.a1.com/news-a1-telekom-austria-group-announces-100-acquisition-of-stemo-a-bulgarian-ict-company?id=158471&l=english&menueid=14594; https://neterra.net/about-us; https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/).
The white space. The banked findings create a claim-tiering white space. A1 can claim breadth and speed; Yettel can claim certified mobile quality and employer trust; Vivacom can claim fixed internet, pay-TV and coverage; Neterra can claim specialist enterprise infrastructure. No player can safely own total leadership without qualifiers. This pattern is derived from the banked A1, Yettel, Vivacom and Neterra share and narrative findings plus Opensignal 2026 (banked findings; https://insights.opensignal.com/reports/2026/01/bulgaria/mobile-network-experience).
The white space. The rural digital-inclusion space is not empty. A1, Vivacom and CETIN all have public claims to the 2025 state-backed rural network build. Vivacom cannot make that story as if it acted alone. The open space is proof of the specific local outcomes Vivacom delivered within the shared programme (https://seenews.com/news/bulgaria-signs-222-mln-euro-digital-network-deals-with-a1-vivacom-cetin-1276695; https://www.cetin.international/w/expanding-bulgaria-s-digital-future-with-large-scale-fiber-deployment).
The white space. The wholesale-infrastructure story is occupied by CETIN and Neterra as well as by the retail operators. CETIN owns the separated Yettel network-service role. Neterra owns independent carrier and data-center proof. Vivacom's B2B story must connect national scale to named customer outcomes rather than just say infrastructure (https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/cetin-bulgaria; https://amcham.bg/2025/10/24/double-victory-for-neterra-and-netix-at-the-capacity-global-connectivity-awards-2025/).
The white space. The open space is not "best network" as a broad claim. SpeedGeo reports Vivacom as fastest fixed broadband in Bulgaria from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026, with 117 Mb/s average download, 85.2 Mb/s upload and 25 ms ping. The same source reports A1 as fastest mobile internet, with 190.7 Mb/s average download. This splits performance proof by service type (https://www.speedgeo.net/statistics/bulgaria).
The white space. A national-infrastructure story must avoid sounding like every peer's proof claim. The banked record shows A1 claiming breadth and speed, Yettel claiming certified quality and trust, Neterra claiming specialist infrastructure, and CETIN claiming wholesale infrastructure. The open space is the human and economic result of the infrastructure, with named local proof (banked findings: A1 narrative; Yettel narrative; Neterra narrative; CETIN narrative; Opensignal 2026 finding).
The white space. The ICLG 2026 Bulgaria chapter says fixed internet has strong infrastructure-based competition and many regional operators outside Vivacom and A1. This leaves room for a local-outcome story by town, school, enterprise or public service, because national share alone does not explain the regional customer experience (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).
The white space. The banked record plus new H1 2026 financials sharpen a white space around proof-backed national usefulness. A1 has the stronger current revenue proof, Yettel has mobile customer and employer proof, CETIN has infrastructure proof and Neterra has specialist continuity proof. Vivacom's safer open lane is not another best-network claim, but a named set of Bulgarian outcomes its network made possible (banked findings; https://a1.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2026/07/A1-Group_Half-Year-Financial-Report-2026-1.pdf; https://www.cetinbg.bg/what-we-do/network; https://www.datocms-assets.com/56100/1771365178-fr39_20260217_eand_ppf_telecom_group_fy2025_annual_accounts_public.pdf).
The white space. The device-and-app space is now more visibly occupied by Yettel. SeeNews carried a Yettel release saying Digitalk 101 ranked Yettel first in mobile device sales for 2023-2025, that smartphone sales through Yettel digital channels rose 56% in H1 2026, and that 95% of customer interactions were digitalised. Vivacom should not use digital customer experience as an ownable centre without proof stronger than Yettel's (https://seenews.com/news/yettel-leads-mobile-device-and-accessories-sales-for-the-third-consecutive-year-1299605).
Vivacom self-claim verdict. Vivacom's parent presents it as a leading provider of mobile, fixed broadband and television services in Bulgaria. CRC data corroborates leadership in fixed internet subscribers at 39.4% in 2024 and pay-TV subscribers at almost 60%, but not mobile subscriber leadership, where A1 held 36.5% in 2024 (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf). (bears on: Reputation problem / desired perception)
The narratives running about it. The strongest volume narrative is planned corporate and product news: Pikasa says Vivacom's Q1 2026 media presence was dominated by PR-driven announcements about devices, jobs, satellite rankings and employer awards. (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war)
The narratives running about it. A network-performance narrative is present but contested: OpenSignal gives Vivacom coverage awards, while A1 wins speed awards in January 2026. (https://insights.opensignal.com/reports/2026/01/bulgaria/mobile-network-experience)
The narratives running about it. A fixed-network and TV growth narrative is present: United Group says Bulgaria's market growth is in fibre, 5G and television, and says Vivacom has backed that shift through EON. (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/)
The narratives running about it. A global-satellite narrative is present: United Group says Vivacom operates Plana and Mogila ground stations, broadcasts more than 600 TV channels, and serves Europe, Africa, South America, Asia and Antarctica. (https://united.group/vivacom-satellite-global-growth/)
The narratives running about it. A social-contribution narrative is present through the Regional Grant, which funded education and environmental projects and had supported 118 projects since launch by April 2024. (https://www.bait.bg/en/novini/vivacom-regional-grant-supports-10-projects-with-bgn-100-000/)
The narratives running about it. A customer-pain narrative is present in user reviews and crisis stories: Trustpilot reviews cluster around service, billing, contracts and support complaints, and Pikasa says one infrastructure failure generated more real response than months of planned announcements. (https://www.trustpilot.com/review/www.vivacom.bg; https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war)
The narratives running about it. A consolidation-and-market-power narrative is present around Vivacom's purchases of fixed broadband and TV operators, with A1 and PPF/Yettel criticising regulatory clearances and Vivacom rejecting the criticism. (https://www.telecompaper.com/news/a1-ppf-telecom-criticise-bulgarian-clearance-of-vivacom-takeovers--1468688; https://www.broadbandtvnews.com/2023/07/04/vivacom-dismisses-unfounded-concerns-from-competitors/)
The narratives running about it. The banked record forms a clear reputation pattern: Vivacom’s strongest defendable story is infrastructure scale, but the same scale also feeds the former-incumbent and market-power concern. (banked findings: company origin; banked findings: CRC 2024 pay-TV and mobile positions; banked findings: acquisition-clearance criticism; banked findings: United Group growth narrative)
The narratives running about it. The banked record forms a second pattern: rivals can credibly attack from different sides. A1 has speed and engagement strengths, Yettel has employer and customer-quality signals, and Vivacom has coverage, fixed internet, TV and satellite proof. (banked findings: OpenSignal; banked findings: nPerf; banked findings: WhereWeWork; banked findings: WTA-linked satellite ranking; banked findings: Pikasa social dataset)
The narratives running about it. The Balkan eCommerce Summit recap says Vivacom’s social communication in the telecom case study leaned toward entertainment, YouTube video production, Instagram giveaways, promotions and transaction-led content. This adds a more consumer-promotion-led narrative than the banked corporate-news pattern. (https://balkanecommerce.com/sessions-recaps-2026/signal-vs-noise-what-5-million-digital-conversations-reveal-about-your-brand-across-different-markets/)
The narratives running about it. A media-pluralism narrative surrounds United Group’s Bulgarian position: Liberties’ 2025 Bulgaria report says telecom-media cross-ownership creates risks for editorial independence and fair competition, and names United Group as owner of Vivacom/BTC and Nova Broadcasting Group. (https://dq4n3btxmr8c9.cloudfront.net/files/x8dqq8/Liberties_Rule_of_Law_Report_2025_Bulgaria.pdf)
The narratives running about it. A regulatory-power narrative is present beyond merger criticism: CRC defines Vivacom as having significant impact in passive physical infrastructure, and Sega reports a 2026 competition probe into alleged excessive duct-access prices. (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf; https://www.segabg.com/hot/category-economy/kzk-proveryava-vivakom-za-monopolni-ceni)
The narratives running about it. A public digital-inclusion narrative is present: the June 2025 government contracts with A1, Vivacom and CETIN target high-capacity networks where investment is lacking. (https://seenews.com/news/bulgaria-signs-222-mln-euro-digital-network-deals-with-a1-vivacom-cetin-1276695)
The narratives running about it. A consumer-price-pressure narrative is present at category level: the Ombudsman tied public complaints to mobile operators’ price-indexation clauses and named Vivacom as one of the operators that followed Yettel’s late-2022 increase. (https://www.ombudsman.bg/en/n/ombudsmans-secretary-general-ombudsman-institution-sounds-years-long-alarm-a-2293)
The narratives running about it. A consolidation-clearance narrative shifted in 2026: competitors had challenged the Bulsatcom asset deals, but the Supreme Administrative Court gave a final clearance. (https://seenews.com/news/bulgarias-supreme-court-clears-united-groups-acquisition-of-bulsatcom-1290035)
The narratives running about it. A satellite-growth narrative continued into 2026: WTA ranked Vivacom third in its 2025 Fast 10 and twentieth in its Global Top 20. (https://www.worldteleport.org/news/717850/World-Teleport-Association-Publishes-Top-Operator-Rankings-for-2025.htm)
The narratives running about it. An incumbent public-service narrative is present: CRC says Vivacom continued to provide public payphones, free emergency-number calls, an electronic telephone directory and social-price packages in 2024. (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf)
The narratives running about it. A vulnerable-customer access narrative is present: CRC set appropriate universal-service broadband at 5 Mbps in 2024 and framed access as part of participation in social and economic life. (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf)
The narratives running about it. A talent and skills narrative expanded in H1 2026: United Group says Vivacom’s Job Lab pilot engaged 120 students across Sofia, Varna, Veliko Tarnovo and Blagoevgrad. (https://united.group/updates-from-united-groups-operations-h1-2026/)
The narratives running about it. United Group says Vivacom completed the 16th edition of its Technical Academy, added artificial intelligence and cybersecurity courses, and ended with a Private 5G Hackathon. (https://united.group/updates-from-united-groups-operations-h1-2026/)
The narratives running about it. United Group says Vivacom welcomed 55 participants to its Summer Internship Programme in H1 2026. (https://united.group/updates-from-united-groups-operations-h1-2026/)
The narratives running about it. A youth science and gaming-community narrative is present: United Group says Vivacom GAME ON released its first mobile game and its first two YouTube episodes generated more than 87,000 views. (https://united.group/updates-from-united-groups-operations-h1-2026/)
The narratives running about it. United Group says Vivacom extended its partnership with the Association of Olympic Teams in Natural Sciences to 2028 and added a EUR 30,000 donation. (https://united.group/updates-from-united-groups-operations-h1-2026/)
The narratives running about it. A business-modernisation narrative is partner-backed: Netcracker announced on 11 February 2026 that Vivacom extended its long-term partnership for a revenue-management platform programme. (https://www.netcracker.com/news/press-releases/netcracker-and-vivacom-extend-long-term-partnership-for-innovative-it-modernization-program)
Category context. Bulgaria’s electronic communications market reached EUR 2.06 billion in 2024, up 5.7% on 2023, according to the ICLG Bulgaria telecoms chapter citing CRC data (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).
Category context. United Group said in July 2026 that Bulgaria’s telecom market grew close to 5% last year to EUR 2.16 billion, and said the growth came in fibre, 5G and television (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/).
Category context. CRC reported bundled-service revenue of BGN 2.064 billion in 2024, up 10.6% year on year; A1, Vivacom and Yettel accounted for 97.8% of bundled-service revenue and 98.3% of bundled-service subscribers (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Category context. Vivacom’s bundled-service subscriber share rose from 30.7% in 2023 to 32.9% in 2024, and its bundled-service revenue share rose from 27.6% to 30.2%; CRC says Bulsatcom was deleted from the CRC register and its activity was reported by Vivacom (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Category context. CRC reported retail fixed internet and data-transfer revenue of BGN 1.879791 billion in 2024; Vivacom led retail fixed internet access with 39.4% of subscribers and 37.1% of revenue, up 7.2 and 8.3 percentage points year on year (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Category context. CRC reported 2.02 million pay-TV subscribers at the end of 2024; Vivacom led pay TV with 59.6% of subscribers and 56.5% of revenue after the incorporation of Bulsatcom and TVN Distribution Bulgaria (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Category context. CRC reported IPTV subscribers grew 9.4% in 2024 and IPTV reached 47.8% of pay-TV subscribers; Vivacom, A1 and Yettel together made up 95.0% of IPTV subscribers (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Category context. CRC reported satellite TV subscribers fell 8.4% in 2024; after Bulsatcom was incorporated into Vivacom, Vivacom’s satellite-TV subscriber share exceeded 80.0% by the end of 2024 (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Category context. The banked record shows a category pattern: growth, consolidation and concentration are moving together. The banked record reports market growth in fibre, 5G and TV; Vivacom share gains in bundled services, fixed internet, pay TV and satellite TV; Bulsatcom and TVN activity incorporated into Vivacom; and rival objections to acquisitions and market shares (banked findings: CRC 2024 market data; United Group July 2026 market growth statement; A1 objection; Bulsatcom incorporation findings).
Category context. ICLG says 62.4% of fixed internet subscribers in Bulgaria used fibre-optic access at the end of 2024. ICLG says Vivacom and A1 served 39.4% and 29.9% of fixed internet subscribers, respectively, while the rest of the market included many regional operators. ICLG says Bulgaria has strong infrastructure-based competition in broadband, and mobile shares sit in the 30% to 37% range across A1, Yettel and Vivacom (https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).
Category context. Vivacom says it is an "иноватор" and says it invested close to BGN 3 billion in technology, innovation, people and the Bulgarian economy. Vivacom says more than 2 million clients use more than 5.5 million services. Independent sources in this pass corroborate Vivacom’s leading shares in fixed internet and pay TV, but did not verify the BGN 3 billion investment claim (https://www.vivacom.bg/za-nas/za-kompaniyata; https://iclg.com/practice-areas/telecoms-media-and-internet-laws-and-regulations/bulgaria/).
Category context. The European Commission says Bulgaria reached 93.53% fixed very high-capacity network coverage in 2025, above the EU average of 85.54%. It says Bulgaria reached 93.53% fibre-to-the-premises coverage, above the EU average of 74.13%. It says Bulgaria reached 94.83% basic 5G coverage, slightly below the EU average of 96.79% (https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-10476-2026-ADD-32/en/pdf).
Category context. The European Commission says Bulgaria’s 3.4-3.8 GHz 5G coverage was 79.62% in 2025, above the EU average of 74.75%. It says Bulgarian 1 Gbps fixed-broadband subscriptions were only 2.92% of fixed-broadband subscriptions, below the EU average of 26.97%. It says Bulgarian 5G SIM penetration reached 41.25%, below the EU average of 55.55% (https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-10476-2026-ADD-32/en/pdf).
Category context. United Group says Bulgaria’s internet revenue rose more than 9% to EUR 1.21 billion in 2025. United Group says IPTV passed one million households and became Bulgaria’s most widely used television platform. United Group says cable and satellite TV are declining. These details were not in the banked record, but the underlying CRC 2025 table was not found in the CRC annual-reports page in this pass (https://united.group/united-group-backs-vivacoms-growth-as-bulgarias-telecoms-market-expands/; https://crc.bg/en/rubrics/375/annual-reports).
Category context. Yettel says it connects more than 3 million users in Bulgaria and has more than 180 stores. Yettel reports 2025 revenue of EUR 557 million, EBITDA of EUR 162 million, CAPEX of EUR 47 million, 1,989 employees, 3.208 million mobile subscribers, 141,000 fixed-broadband subscribers and 104,000 pay-TV subscribers. CETIN Bulgaria reports 2025 revenue of EUR 170 million, EBITDA of EUR 123 million and CAPEX of EUR 76 million (https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/yettel-bulgaria; https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/cetin-bulgaria).
Category context. Bulgaria’s electronic communications market reached BGN 4.220 billion in 2025, up 4.9% on 2024 (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2025_BG.pdf).
Category context. Data-transfer and internet-access revenue reached BGN 2.376 billion in 2025 and made up 56.3% of the Bulgarian electronic communications market (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2025_BG.pdf).
Category context. Retail internet subscribers reached 11.216 million at 31 December 2025, with the increase partly affected by a changed bundled-service definition that added prepaid mobile users (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2025_BG.pdf).
Category context. Bulgaria had 3.169 million 5G subscriptions at 31 December 2025, equal to 37.5% of mobile-internet subscriptions (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2025_BG.pdf).
Category context. CRC data put 5G coverage at 92% of population and almost 66% of territory at the end of 2025 (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2025_BG.pdf).
Category context. Fixed broadband delivered over mobile networks reached 23.3% of fixed-broadband subscribers in 2025 (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2025_BG.pdf).
Category context. xDSL, provided only by Vivacom, fell to just above 2% of fixed-broadband subscribers at the end of 2025 (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2025_BG.pdf).
Category context. IPTV was the only TV-distribution revenue line to grow in 2025, rising 1.4% year on year (https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2025_BG.pdf).
Category context. SpeedGeo says Vivacom led Bulgarian broadband speed for 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026, while A1 led mobile download speed and lowest mobile ping in the same period (https://www.speedgeo.net/statistics/bulgaria).
Each peer's narrative. A1's narrative is breadth plus market scale: mobile, fixed, TV, sport, payment, ICT, cloud and IoT under one provider. A1 calls itself "overall, the number one in the market"; CRC corroborates A1 as the largest mobile voice operator by subscribers, but CRC shows Vivacom leading fixed internet and pay-TV, so the self-claim is segment-dependent (https://a1.com/a1-group-and-markets/a1-in-bulgaria/; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Each peer's narrative. A1 also runs a challenger-regulator narrative against Vivacom concentration. It says Vivacom acquisitions could create a dominant TV and broadband player, and CRC later shows Vivacom's 2024 pay-TV share near 60% after Bulsatcom and TVN Distribution Bulgaria were incorporated (https://newsroom.a1.com/news-a1-group-deeply-unsettled-by-an-unexpected-decision-of-the-bulgarian-commission-on-protection-of-competition?id=182022&l=english&menueid=14594; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Each peer's narrative. Yettel's narrative is mobile quality, reliability and employer credibility. Yettel calls itself the "largest mobile telecommunications provider in Bulgaria by revenue"; CRC corroborates that Yettel held the highest 2024 retail mobile voice revenue share at 40.9% (https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/yettel-bulgaria; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Each peer's narrative. Yettel also publishes a human-use narrative around accessibility, digital literacy, volunteering, sustainability content and original YouTube series. Pikasa says this gave Yettel the most genuinely varied media coverage among the three national operators in Q1 2026 (https://pikasa.ai/post/149/the-platform-bet-how-bulgarian-telecoms-are-winning-and-losing-the-attention-war).
Each peer's narrative. Neterra's narrative is business-grade infrastructure rather than mass consumer telecom. It says its mission is to empower customers everywhere through information technology and customer care, and CRC corroborates its business-network role through a 10.4% share of retail leased lines by line count and a 33.7% share of wholesale leased-line revenue in 2024 (https://neterra.net/about-us; https://crc.bg/files/Annual_Report_CRC_2024_EN.pdf).
Each peer's narrative. The peer pattern is acquired scale versus built specialist depth. A1, Yettel and Vivacom are now parts of larger cross-border groups after major transactions, while Neterra's banked history presents a Sofia-founded specialist that built its own international network. This pattern is derived from banked findings: A1 2005 acquisition; Yettel OTE-to-Telenor-to-PPF-to-e& PPF chain; Vivacom United Group acquisition; Neterra founded in Sofia and expanded through network build-out (banked findings).
Each peer's narrative. CETIN's narrative is separated infrastructure serving retail operators. It was created from Telenor Bulgaria's infrastructure in 2020. Its own materials frame the rural broadband project as equal digital access for remote areas. SeeNews corroborates the state programme, the BGN 433.6 million contract value and the A1, Vivacom and CETIN participants (https://www.eandppftelecom.eu/our-companies/cetin-bulgaria; https://www.cetin.international/w/expanding-bulgaria-s-digital-future-with-large-scale-fiber-deployment; https://seenews.com/news/bulgaria-signs-222-mln-euro-digital-network-deals-with-a1-vivacom-cetin-1276695).
Each peer's narrative. Yettel's 25-year anniversary narrative moves beyond certified network quality. It says Globul's 2001 entry brought real competition to Bulgaria. It says Yettel introduced the iPhone in Bulgaria, launched 4G and ran the first public 5G test. It says its strategic direction is to become "more than a telecom". SeeNews labels the item as a Yettel press release, so the source reports the claim but does not independently test it (https://seenews.com/news/yettel-bulgaria-has-invested-eur-1-7-billion-over-25-years-1296648).
Each peer's narrative. The peer pattern is group strength plus local proof. A1 uses service breadth and parent scale. Yettel uses e& PPF ownership, CETIN network support and certified quality. CETIN uses separated infrastructure. Neterra uses its NetIX, data-center and network ecosystem. The pattern means Vivacom's story must show Bulgarian outcomes, not only group scale (banked findings: A1 narrative; Yettel narrative; CETIN narrative; Neterra narrative; Vivacom current ownership).
Each peer's narrative. The banked record creates a new ownership pattern: A1, Yettel and Vivacom are foreign-owned converged operators built through major transactions, while Neterra is the Sofia-founded specialist and CETIN is the separated infrastructure company. That means each peer can claim scale, expertise or neutrality from a different origin story, and Vivacom's former-state-operator history remains the only incumbent-origin story in the set (banked findings: A1 acquisition history; Yettel ownership chain; Vivacom origin and current ownership; Neterra origin; CETIN creation).
Each peer's narrative. Yettel's 2026 Code of Conduct adds an ethics-and-responsibility line to its network and employer story. It says, "doing good is good business", and links growth to people, trust and responsibility. This is Yettel's own language; the source does not independently test the claim (https://www.yettel.bg/sites/default/files/2026-08/Yettel_CodeOfConduct_EN.pdf).
Each peer's narrative. Neterra's 2026 content uses a business-continuity story, not only a network-asset story. Its Digitalk 101 article titles one angle "Business Without Geographic Limits" and says hybrid internet combines fibre, 5G, Starlink and other technologies into one service, one device and one contract. This is Neterra's own article; AmCham carried the ranking story, but not every operating detail (https://neterra.net/news/neterra-and-netix-take-leading-positions-in-the-digitalk-101-2026-rankings; https://amcham.bg/2026/08/12/neterra-and-netix-take-leading-positions-in-the-digitalk-101-2026-rankings/).

The factual pieces named in the claim are carried by the findings: Vivacom’s fixed internet, pay-TV, coverage, satellite, public-service, EON/Bulsatcom, public-sector and skills-programme proof is established, while the broader 'trusted national role' point is a provisional judgement rather than an extra unsupported fact.

compose-debrief-write-up.output:
# Debrief Write-Up

What the conversation established, tracked against the eight question sets, and what is still missing from each. A set with nothing under it was not covered -- that is a finding, not an omission from this document.

**Voices heard.** Elitza Georgieva, Chief Communications Officer  Only one voice. The volume asks for more than one where possible.

## A — essentials / the ask

What we now know:
- The ownable line offered was: "You can't do without it."
- The work needs to cut the old BTK association and avoid generic technology, environmental, social and governance, or employer-brand claims.
- The desired shift is from moderate, activity-led presence to more emotional, more digital, higher-quality storytelling.
- Share of voice alone is no longer enough as the success measure.

Still to get:
- The material does not state the final decision owner for this phase beyond the wider briefing pack.
- The material does not define the exact outputs, deadline, approval meeting, or budget.
- The material does not confirm which audience is the first business priority.

Questions for this set:

- What decision do you need this corporate story to support first: customer preference, leadership trust, employee belief, parent-group confidence, or regulatory comfort?
- When you say Vivacom should be seen as something people cannot do without, what must the audience believe after one sentence?
- Which deliverables will help you move from a blank slate to a decision: territories, a platform line, proof pillars, message architecture, a leader story, or a channel plan?
- Who must approve the first version: the chief executive officer, parent-group communications, legal, regulatory affairs, or another owner?
- What is the one outcome this work must change in 2026 so the engagement has paid for itself?

## B — business & organizational context

What we now know:
- Vivacom wants to be seen as the solid, stable telecom that successfully stepped into the role of innovator.
- Elitza Georgieva said the transformation itself is under-told: a heavy incumbent became faster and pushed the sector forward.
- She named first commercial 5G, first 10-gigabit network, wide high-speed city footprint, first unlimited consumer plans, EON, smart home, smart-city work, satellite communications, Regional Grant and Job Lab as proof pools.
- She said the company is waiting for a sale and that divestment due diligence makes leaders cautious.

Still to get:
- Several proof points are marked for verification and need exact source, date and claim wording.

The five prompts the volume asks this conversation to surface, each answered from the material or named as not yet surfaced.

- **The ownable line:** The ownable line offered in the conversation is: "You can't do without it." The surrounding meaning is that Vivacom should be presented as useful, reliable infrastructure for daily life, not as another broad technology leader.

- **What the client walks away from (defines the edge):** Vivacom walks away from "the BTK" and from the old state-telecom identity. It also walks away from broad market-leader boasting across segments because that invites regulator and government attention.
- **Why the company exists (origin / purpose):** Vivacom exists to let people do what matters most to them in the best possible way, through connectivity anywhere, any time, with everyone who matters, plus strong support. Vivacom's problem is no longer only that it lacks a corporate story; it lacks a shared, public-ready way to turn indispensability into trust while sale uncertainty, old BTK associations, customer friction and regulatory sensitivity constrain what it can safely say. The conversation sharpened the task from finding a positioning territory to proving a warmer national role: Vivacom must show why people and institutions cannot do without it, using legally safe proof and human stories that existing customers, employees and critical urban audiences can believe.

## Client & context

_Who they are, business model, markets, moment._

Vivacom is a Bulgarian telecommunications provider in a mature, regulated and price-pressured market. It serves consumers, business customers, enterprise customers and public-sector customers through mobile, fixed internet, television, satellite, smart-city, cloud and digital services, and it has been part of United Group since 2020.

## Organisational objective

_The business change and by when; the story change that delivers it._

Business objective: The material says growth must come from preference and value, not volume, but it does not set a commercial target or deadline. Communications objective: Move Vivacom from moderate, activity-led presence to one warmer, more digital and more trusted company story that makes existing customers believe, in Elitza Georgieva's words, "Vivacom, that's my telecom."

Deliverable. # Final-brief board -- report

**Outcome: CLEARS the Board.** only low concerns stand.

Rule applied: Proceeds to the human ship gate with the Board report attached.

Two personas, convened on the Step 3 pair before the final-brief hard stop. The CFO asks where the business and the number are behind every measure; the Journalist asks which claim outruns the evidence the material actually supplies. The pair is adjudicated, not advised: a critical finding or a block from either stops the run before approval is even requested.

Convened on the Step 3 pair: The CFO / Board · The Journalist

## The verdicts

| persona | position | verdict | findings that survived the referee |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The CFO / Board | So what — where's the business and the number? | PASS | 0 |
| The Journalist | Where's the substance? I'm going to check. | PASS | 0 |

## The findings

No finding survived the referee pass.
## Struck by the referee

No attack counts unless it quotes the exact target. 0 were discarded before triage.


## How the findings were triaged

The system — not the operator — triages by these fixed rules. The one that fired is marked; the rest are shown so the outcome can be read against what did not happen.

| condition | outcome |
| --- | --- |
| Any CRITICAL finding (legal red line, factual falsehood, greenwashing, reputational landmine) | HARD BLOCK — fix before anything else, regardless of all other verdicts |
| Competitor returns BLOCK on distinctiveness | RETURN to Insight/Strategy — a table-stakes strategy cannot ship |
| Target Audience returns BLOCK (insight not held / unvalidated) | RETURN to Insight — trigger M7 validation |
| ≥ 2 High concerns, or ≥ 4 Medium | MUST REVISE — auto-revise loop |
| **Only Low concerns, or all PASS** | CLEARS the Board → proceeds to the human ship gate with the Board report attached |

## The review loop

1. Draft
2. Attack
3. Referee
4. Triage
5. Fix
6. Re-review
7. Clear

Bounded to 3 rounds. Round 1 of 3 ran here. If it still cannot clear, it escalates to a human — the one place seniority is invoked, and only on genuinely hard deadlocks.

## Keeping the Board honest

It is AI, so it can flatter or hallucinate.

- **Grounding.** Each persona is fed real data, not imagination — the competitor's real positioning, the client's real record, actual audience evidence.
- **Specificity requirement.** No attack counts unless it quotes the exact target; the referee discards the rest.
- **Severity calibration.** Anchored to worked examples so verdicts are consistent run to run — no drifting standards.
- **Validate the validators.** Periodically check the Board's findings against real senior reviews: does it catch what seniors catch, without crying wolf?

## Operator-independence

The operator never scores the Board and never adjudicates a finding. The triage above is a fixed rule, not a judgement, so a novice and a veteran get the same scrutiny and the same fix set.
